Our 10 favorite scenes from T2: Judgment Day

Ars Technica Long form August 28, 2026

James Cameron’s 1991 sci-fi blockbuster returns to theaters this weekend for its 35th anniversary.

I’m on record declaring James Cameron’s Terminator 2: Judgment Day (1991) to be The Best Damn Sequel of All Time, and I stand by that assessment. August 29, the fictional date (in 1997) of the franchise’s original nuclear holocaust, is fast approaching, and Judgment Day is celebrating its 35th anniversary this year. So StudioCanal has decided to mark both occasions with a special theatrical rerelease of the film this weekend. What better time to revisit some of our favorite scenes from this seminal sci-fi action blockbuster?

(Many, many spoilers below.)

Nobody really expected 1984’s The Terminator to be a hit, but it racked up an impressive $78 million at the box office against its modest $6.4 million budget. Star Arnold Schwarzenegger was keen to do a sequel, but Cameron was busy with other projects, including Aliens in 1986 (another killer sequel). There were also legal complications over the film rights until Schwarzenegger convinced Carolco Pictures, the studio behind Total Recall (1990), to buy everyone out and hire Cameron to make Judgment Day.

Cameron wrote the script in about six weeks, diverging significantly from the stripped-down feel of its predecessor (which some have described as a “science fiction slasher”). Instead, Cameron chose to make his original Terminator the reprogrammed hero of the sequel, serving as a mechanical father figure to a young John Connor (Edward Furlong). Cameron likened the transformation to the Tin Man getting a heart in The Wizard of Oz. Linda Hamilton agreed to reprise her role as Sarah Connor, and this “found family” triad became the emotional core of the film. Hamilton worked out like a fiend for the role, and her resulting lean-yet-ripped physique made her an action heroine on par with Sigourney Weaver’s Ripley.

Released over the July 4th holiday weekend in 1991, Terminator 2: Judgment Day was a critical and financial smash hit, despite predictions that the film would bomb and lose its estimated $70 million production budget. It ended up grossing $520 million, which sadly was not enough to protect Carolco from other film losses. (The studio went bankrupt in 1995.) It’s the perfect sci-fi action film, expertly paced with well-drawn character dynamics, amazing special effects, emotional beats, and humorous touches to keep things from getting too grim. No subsequent film in the franchise even comes close.

The film also has one of the best villains in cinema with the shapeshifting T-1000 (Robert Patrick). Cameron actually had the idea for a Terminator made of liquid metal when he was writing the first film, but the technology available at the time wasn’t up to the task. Then Cameron made The Abyss in 1989, which featured a flowing, water-like alien at the very end created by Industrial Light & Magic (ILM). ILM made a major investment, expanding its staff and spending over $3 million on new equipment and specially designed software just for Judgment Day.

The gamble paid off. The T-1000 and other visual effects earned critical raves and an Oscar (the film snagged four in all) and helped usher in the golden age of CGI. Audiences loved the character, which had as much to do with Cameron’s expert pacing as the effects. The T-1000’s abilities are only gradually revealed. Initially, the slender Patrick seems no match for Schwarzenegger’s heavily muscled T-800, even if he can take on anyone’s form. Then we see its liquid metal form is impervious to bullet wounds, healing them instantly—even when a gunshot blast splits its head in two. Cameron keeps upping the ante, until one becomes convinced the T-1000 is well-nigh invincible.

“T2 was made for theaters, and our lovingly prepared 3D version, coming back to the big screen, is the absolute best way to see the film,” Cameron told Deadline Hollywood via statement. “I believe it’s safe to do spoilers after 35 years, so SPOILER ALERT: the good guys win against the AI super intelligence. And maybe that’s a message of hope we could use this summer.”

There is a staggered global rollout for the rerelease. It’s now available in Germany, Latin America, the Czech Republic, the US, Italy, and Poland. The film will be released in France on September 2; Australia, New Zealand, the Netherlands, Sweden, and Hungary on September 3; and the United Kingdom on September 4.

And now, we give you 10 of our favorite scenes:

Judgment Day‘s eye-popping special effects certainly provide plenty of highlights, but Cameron didn’t skimp on the story either. This is a prime example of how the director used touches of levity to make even the film’s more workmanlike segments entertaining. The T-800 arrives from the future naked as a jaybird and must acquire clothing, transportation, and weaponry. Naturally, he wanders into a biker bar—to the delight of the female patrons—finds a dude his size, and demands the biker’s clothes and motorcycle.

The biker thinks it’s a joke at first and refuses, extinguishing his cigar on the T-800’s bared pectoral muscle—with no effect. The outcome of the ensuing bar fight is a given. The T-800 walks away with cool leather clothing, a motorcycle, a shotgun, and a pair of stylish black sunglasses as George Thorogood and the Destroyer’s “Bad to the Bone” plays. The song’s been overused in films since then, but it was the perfect grace note for this scene.

This is the first major chase sequence, with both the T-800 and the T-1000 trying to get to a fleeing John Connor first. John’s little motorbike proves no match for the large truck commandeered by the T-1000, which blasts through a cinder block wall at one point. The T-1000 never falters in its single-minded pursuit, but the arrival of the T-800 saves the boy. The truck eventually explodes, seemingly incinerating the T-1000. It’s only after the T-800 and John ride away that we see the T-1000 emerge from the flames and resume his police officer appearance.

The sequence was filmed over nine hours in LA’s San Fernando Valley. The T-800’s big stunt involved jumping a motorcycle 60 feet (at an altitude of roughly 15 feet) to the flood control channel below. Stunt coordinator Joel Kramer rigged up a support mechanism for the 750-pound motorcycle, since otherwise the jump was deemed too dangerous. The rigging and wires were erased during post-production.

This is one of those “upping the ante” moments. We’ve seen the T-1000’s amazing shapeshifting abilities, taking on the form of a policeman and John’s foster mother in quick succession. We’ve seen his arms transform effortlessly into weapons. We’ve seen him heal bullet holes instantly. When he arrives at the psychiatric hospital to take out Sarah Connor, he must briefly hide as a team of detectives exits. A lone security guard goes into the hall to get coffee from the vending machine. The T-1000 is nowhere to be seen—until it slowly oozes up out of the checkerboard hospital floor tiles right behind the unsuspecting guard.

The shot required a special bit of software capable of reshaping specific regions of a 2D image using 3D geometry, mapping a computer-generated replica of the floor to the actual footage. This was combined with animation of the T-1000 taking shape. As for the T-1000 taking on the guard’s shape—that was achieved the old-fashioned way, since the actor Don Stanton had a twin brother (Dan).

This is where flipping the script to make the T-800 John’s protector instead of the hunter really pays emotional dividends. Sarah Connor has reshaped her entire persona (not just her physique) in the wake of what happened to her in the first film. Everything centers on protecting John from the machines. Her obsession gets her locked up in a psychiatric hospital, and her odds of release are not good.

She’s in the middle of breaking out on her own—quite effectively—and has made it to the elevator, which opens to reveal the T-800, her former adversary, back (in her mind) to kill her and John. Horrified, Sarah flees back the way she came and is briefly subdued by hospital staff until the T-800 tosses them aside like rag dolls. She sees John is safe, and the T-800 reaches down and repeats the line her protector uttered in the first film: “Come with me if you want to live.”

Bonus: Sarah’s psychiatrist and everyone else who thought she was crazy rattling on about killer machines from the future must confront the fact that she was right all along, especially when the T-1000 shows up.

This powerful dream sequence shows Sarah and the rest of Los Angeles utterly annihilated by a nuclear blast. It starts with children and their mothers—including a younger, more innocent Sarah Connor—on a playground, oblivious to the danger, as a distraught Sarah soundlessly tries to warn them by banging on the chain-link fence. Then the blast hits, burning Sarah alive (actually a full-sized puppet) and reducing those children to ash.

It took a ton of special effects work to pull off the sequence, combining practical effects, miniatures, and CGI enhancements. The team built a mini-Los Angeles based on the live-action footage, including skyscrapers and an overpass. Some of the model buildings stood 5 feet tall, and many were designed to break away to mimic the effects of a blast. The nuclear fireball was actually a backlit, 8-foot plexiglass column. The most powerful visual effect is the ashy remains of the playground victims, still intact—until a shock wave scatters the ashes to the wind.

Sarah’s dream is sufficiently traumatic to compel her to leave John with the T-800 and seek out Miles Dyson (Joe Morton), Cyberdyne’s director of special projects and the scientist most responsible for developing what would become Skynet. Her plan is to kill Miles and stop Judgment Day from ever happening—hence the film’s catchphrase, “No fate but what we make.” But she can’t go through with it, even as John and the T-800 arrive to stop her.

To prove to Miles that Sarah is telling the truth—that his work will lead to humanity’s near-annihilation—the T-800 removes the skin from his hand and forearm, revealing the cyber skeleton underneath. As he flexes the mechanical fingers in front of a horrified Miles and his wife, the T-800 intones, “Now listen to me very carefully….” I’m sure Miles was hanging on his every word.

John, Sarah, and the T-800 enlist Miles’ help to break into Cyberdyne headquarters and steal the salvaged arm and computer chip left behind by the T-800 in the first film. They are working against the clock, since pretty much every law enforcement unit in the city arrives at the building to stop them. John’s hacking skills prove useful, as does the T-800’s extensive firepower—although per John’s instructions, there are zero human fatalities.

Ultimately, Miles sacrifices himself so that the others can escape, holding onto the detonator that sets off a massive explosion until his final breath. The filming site was an empty office building in Fremont, California, and the explosion was real; pyrotechnician Tom Fisher used hundreds of gallons of gas to create that giant fireball. Respect.

The carefully orchestrated high-speed chase down a highway that immediately precedes this scene deserves its own spot on the list, just for the ingenuity of the stunt design. That chase ends with a semitruck pulling a tank of liquid nitrogen overturning and skidding into an active steel mill, spilling liquid nitrogen all over the street. The T-1000 resolutely wades toward its targets anyway, only to start to freeze from the feet up, breaking its legs off at the knees and losing a hand before it solidifies, a look of shocked surprise on its face. The T-800 blasts it to smithereens with a well-timed, “Hasta la vista, baby.”

That should be the end of the T-1000, right? RIGHT? But within minutes the scattered shards start to melt in the heat of the steel mill and begin to coalesce yet again. “We don’t have much time,” the T-800 observes—and indeed, the T-1000 soon reassembles. The frozen shards were actually made of serabin, a material used as ballast for model railroad cars that resembles chrome when it’s polished. Frozen mercury didn’t work because it turned white. But globs of liquid mercury worked just fine to show the melting shards coming together, even though its toxicity meant the special effects crew had to wear protective gear over the two-day shoot.

Spoiler alert: The T-1000 is not quite unbeatable. Sure, he recovers nicely from a hole in the head, courtesy of Sarah, and being cleaved in two by the T-800 wielding a piece of rebar—the former achieved with a mechanical head and shoulders replica of Patrick (“Donut Head”), the latter with a maquette sculpture (“Cleave Man”), both augmented with CGI. Just when things are looking dire for John and Sarah, the T-800 reboots on auxiliary power and shoots the T-1000 with a grenade launcher. The torso explodes and creates “Pretzel Man” (achieved with three full-sized puppets).

A teetering T-1000 then topples into a vat of molten steel and slowly melts into oblivion, running through each of the human forms it took on over the course of the film (foster mom, security guard, etc.) before vanishing in a howl. This was the most difficult sequence for the special effects team and took weeks to complete, matching carefully choreographed movements of all the actors in the live-action pit with splashing liquid filmed in a separate miniature version of the vat. The illusion of molten steel was basically water and mineral oil mixed with a little powdered sugar; creative lighting and heaters placed below the cameras—plus a few CGI sparks in the background—did the rest.

The result didn’t quite satisfy Cameron, but the rendering shots took so long that the director ran out of time, even with the production crew working 24-hour shifts. The final print wasn’t delivered to theaters until the night before the official release. But audiences were blown away. It was the perfect way to bring about the T-1000’s demise.

After that spectacular special effects achievement, Cameron closed things out with an emotional, well-earned farewell. John drops the first T-800 arm and chip into the vat of molten steel to destroy them. But there is one chip left: the one in the new T-800’s head. Since it cannot self-terminate, Sarah is tasked with lowering the machine into the vat, against John’s anguished objections. It’s the final payoff to the relationship Cameron has painstakingly built between John and the machine—and the T-800 goes out in style, giving a gloved thumbs-up as its hand slowly sinks into the liquid steel.

As demand for Meta AI glasses explodes, it’s harder to avoid creepy recordings

Ars Technica Long form August 21, 2026

Ars looks at Zuckoff, the latest free app detecting Meta AI glasses amid privacy backlash.

Can you tell when someone nearby is wearing Meta AI glasses?

As millions of people buy into the smart glasses fad each year, the odds are increasing that you could be secretly recorded while simply going about your day.

Meta is not the only smart glasses maker, but its AI glasses are by far the most popular. And as the devices become more common, some public places, including schools, courts, restaurants, and entertainment venues, have begun to ban them. Even tech lovers have rejected Meta glasses in certain settings. The hackers behind DEF CON 2026 reportedly banned smart glasses with no exceptions, reminding attendees with prescription pairs to “be sure to pack non-violating eyewear if you need them.”

But a ban is only as effective as the people enforcing it. Spotting a pair of smart glasses can require tech-savvy security staff, and enforcement may depend on users voluntarily disclosing their devices—or on watchful observers speaking up.

Those bans are an important way to push back against the potential for abuse. But privacy advocates know that increasing the social friction around nonconsensual recording can’t stop the practice by itself.

Until comprehensive consumer privacy laws are passed, the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) has warned that Meta seems prepared to make the tech even more invasive in its bid to sell more glasses and stay ahead of rivals in the burgeoning industry.

And as AI advances, EFF staff technologist Cooper Quintin told Ars, potential new features such as facial recognition could raise the stakes further, potentially allowing the devices to be used to create convincing deepfakes or nonconsensual intimate imagery of people who may not be aware that cameras are rolling.

“I think that there are a lot of other concerns there beyond just being recorded without your knowledge,” Quintin told Ars.

EFF has warned that smart glasses makers will likely be tempted to add facial-recognition features unless lawmakers intervene and give people a private right to sue companies whose products violate their biometric privacy rights. In the meantime, the group has released a guide for smart-glasses users that lays out ways to resist facial recognition, develop responsible recording habits, and better understand the privacy risks of continuous recording. It also urges users to consider blurring strangers’ faces before posting videos online.

For people unknowingly targeted in secret recordings, the only safety feature Meta provides is nearly “useless,” Quintin told Ars.

A tiny recording light that can be easily covered with a sticker is unlikely to deter bad actors intent on abusing the glasses, whether that’s stalkers or creepy partners secretly recording women in public bathrooms or private bedrooms. The tech has also controversially been used in immigration raids, 404 Media reported, and to harass sex workers and retail workers. And on social media, videos show a range of other unwanted recordings, from relatively inoffensive pranks to more harmful videos featuring bullying or harassment.

The volume of these videos online suggests the LED feature “is better than nothing, but not by much,” Quintin said.

Experts have noted that Meta may already have plans to diminish that limited safety feature. The company is supposedly “testing a prototype of ‘super sensing’ AI glasses that would use cameras and audio recordings to capture a wearer’s every moment,” the Financial Times reported last month. According to sources familiar with Meta’s thinking, executives “are planning not to activate the LED when the super-sensing features are being used,” even though “that would make it harder for bystanders to know when they were being recorded.”

Meta execs’ plans may change if the public’s privacy concerns remain a sticking point, though, sources have suggested. And backlash will likely be sustained as more people wear the glasses, since digital rights experts have accused Meta of failing to consider civil rights or privacy ramifications when designing new features. Perhaps most troublingly, Meta recently backpedaled and deleted an unreleased facial recognition system from its smart-glasses app that Wired and EFF revealed had been quietly installed on 50 million phones in June.

It’s unclear if or when Meta might try to bring the facial recognition system back. Meta did not respond to Ars’ request to comment on this story.

As Meta glasses have become more commonplace, hobbyist programmers have been building apps to detect when smart glasses are nearby so people can steer clear of them.

These civil defense apps, Quintin said, aren’t a perfect solution to the social problem of smart-glasses recording without consent. But when used in combination with bans, the apps can offer wary members of the public a way to check if a ban is being enforced or whether a nearby device may begin recording at a sensitive time. Society needs both solutions, Quintin said, especially because the most popular and recognizable smart glasses available today will likely one day come in a wider assortment of trendy models, making them harder to spot in the wild.

“You need to have the social construct around these being unwelcome, and you also need to be able to find when people are using these,” Quintin said. “Right now, they’re pretty easy to just detect with your eyes. They’re pretty obvious, but that might not always be the case. So technologies like this are also important to supplement that.”

Since February, engineers have been releasing and updating apps that help people detect glasses like Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, or Snap Spectacles.

“It is completely unsurprising that people are building apps to fight back against Meta glasses and other surreptitious public recording,” Quintin told Ars. Many people “have a deep revulsion to being recorded without their consent, which is understandable,” and that remains “the biggest problem with these glasses,” Quintin said.

Smart-glasses detector apps aren’t perfect. At best, they can alert users when nearby glasses are turned on by detecting the Bluetooth signal used to pair the glasses with a phone. Most importantly, the apps cannot determine whether the glasses are actively recording, and users are cautioned to never assume that someone wearing smart glasses is recording them. App makers also advise against confrontation and accept no liability for false positives or misunderstandings. Additionally, detection may be unreliable if a wall or other obstacle, like a human body, interferes with a signal.

Users don’t seem to consider these flaws deal-breakers. They simply want some way to scan a room, and some are eager to provide feedback to improve the apps, even expressing an emotional investment in seeing the technology develop.

One of the first apps, Nearby Glasses, is available for free on both iOS and Android. It has been downloaded more than 100,000 times from the Play Store and remains the most popular such app, despite the developer, Yves Jeanrenaud, warning on GitHub that he’s “no pro developer” and that “detecting Bluetooth LE devices might sometimes just not work as expected,” and “false positives are likely.” More recently, the detection functionality has been updated, moving beyond earlier versions that only looked for a manufacturer ID, Jeanrenaud told Ars.

Released in response to online content showing that smart glasses are “an intolerable intrusion, consent neglecting, horrible piece of tech,” Jeanrenaud said, he kept his goals humble. On GitHub, he wrote, “I hope this app is useful for someone,” but “I do not want to promote techsolutionism, nor do I want people to feel falsely secure. It’s still an imperfect approach,” and it probably “always will be.”

By July, another detector, Antizuck Smart Glasses Scanner, was nearing the top of iPhone charts, also charging $3 for the service. One high school teacher reviewing the app called it the “best $3 I’ve spent,” writing that she was concerned that her students could use AI glasses to take unwanted recordings in class.

Ars tested the most recently released app, Zuckoff, which launched for free on iPhone in early August and is currently seeking 12 testers to launch on Android devices later this year.

Already, thousands of users have downloaded the iPhone app, with some eagerly submitting feedback that has helped improve key functionality, including the ability to detect AI glasses and receive alerts when the app is closed. Perpetual scanning is an optional feature that costs about $10 a year. The subscription helps cover the costs of “continuous support” for the app, Zuckoff’s creator, Pawel Szydlowski, told Ars.

Like Jeanrenaud’s app, Zuckoff collects no data and was created partly in response to the toxic Meta glasses content that is flooding social media. Szydlowski told Ars that he built the app in one week after finishing another project that scans for nearby Bluetooth devices and deciding, “Let’s see how far we can go with detecting those glasses.”

Without researching whether other apps had already sought to solve the problem, Szydlowski decided to put his 10 years of iPhone developer experience to work. “I was like, ‘I can do something about it, so let’s go,’” Szydlowski told Ars.

Szydlowski’s biggest challenge was collecting the unique identifiers that manufacturers use to label different products for regulatory purposes. Zuckoff uses these identifiers to help users detect specific smart-glasses models while ignoring Bluetooth signals from less creepy devices. To compile as comprehensive a list as possible, Szydlowski crawled Instagram and Reddit for photos of people wearing different types of smart glasses.

“I see you have those glasses,” Szydlowski would say in messages to early Meta glasses adopters, who agreed to help despite presumably approving of the technology. “Can you help me with this little name? I want to know the unique identifier that’s broadcasting.”

To catch glasses with identifiers that Zuckoff hasn’t yet logged, Szydlowski created a workaround that first flags devices by their advertised names. It’s less precise, he said, but it gives users some indication that a pair of smart glasses may be nearby, even without a known identifier. He’s currently working on another solution that should widen discovery even further, he told Ars.

Szydlowski’s app first alerted him to nearby smart glasses when he ran into two colleagues wearing them at a recent Apple event in Poland. That helped him confirm the tech was working as he hoped.

When you load Zuckoff, the app “estimates distance from signal strength and puts a confidence level on every hit rather than a hard yes or no,” Szydlowski explained. Estimates tell users if glasses are very close (within arm’s length), close (in the same room), near (nearby), and far. This feature also makes it possible to see when you may be approaching an area with a larger concentration of smart glasses, like in a tourist trap like the Las Vegas strip.

Ars replicated the test, thanks to this writer’s brother-in-law, who agreed to use the app to detect his own Ray-Bans. He likes to use his smart glasses to record nature sightings when he goes boating or to take action shots of his bulldog playing fetch along the lake, and he had the glasses on him when I called to see if he could run the test.

After putting the glasses on, my brother-in-law loaded the app, which detected the glasses in minutes and warned that “one possible pair” was “within arm’s length.” (In this case, the message was very literal, since he was wearing the glasses while looking at the phone in his hand.)

The app then references the identifier to help the user detect exactly which model is nearby, and my brother-in-law confirmed that Zuckoff correctly labeled his smart glasses.

For Szydlowski, the toughest challenge was figuring out how Apple might allow the app to run in the background, since the company is “very strict when it comes to apps working in the background all the time.” He worried some users wouldn’t find the app as beneficial without that functionality. Eventually, he settled on a solution that scans continuously, but rather than flagging all known devices the moment they’re turned on, Apple allows only a fixed list of known Bluetooth service identifiers to be detected in that mode. Extra-cautious users should therefore also open the app to see the full list of potential devices in the area.

“This background feature, it’s so crucial,” Szydlowski said.

Android may allow him to offer faster detection through background functionality, Szydlowski suggested, because unlike Apple devices, Android allows background activities to be “possible to exempt from battery optimization,” Szydlowski said. That means Zuckoff “can continue using the battery in the background” without Android protocols that “wipe out the apps that are consuming your battery,” he said.

Although people have mostly grown accustomed to the idea of being recorded without consent in public, smart glasses have the potential to expand mass surveillance in ways that deeply concern privacy advocates.

Meta could introduce technical solutions, like automatically blurring faces, as Google does in Street View images, but Szydlowski doubts Meta would voluntarily make such a privacy-conscious change without regulatory or public pressure. The creator of Zuckoff, a name that takes a cheeky dig at Meta’s founder, also said that “I’m pretty sure they’re not going to be happy with this app existing.”

He likens malicious smart-glasses recording to the earliest harms of Apple’s AirTags. When that technology was released in 2021, the easy-to-hide tracking devices were soon implicated in stalking cases. But there still is no federal law targeting AirTag abuses, and it took the first states to act on the emerging privacy threat roughly three to five years to pass legislation to prohibit the invasive tracking.

Szydlowski worries lawmakers will be similarly slow to react to threats from Meta glasses. He told Ars he thinks the best solution might be rules mandating companies like Meta advertise a specific Bluetooth service identifier while recording. That would improve civil defense apps like his.

In the meantime, he hopes people will find the detector app that they like best and use it to spread awareness that smart glasses may be present in a room where they’re unexpected or explicitly forbidden.

“The goal of this app was just making people aware because a lot of people won’t be aware until it becomes a major problem, which was the case with AirTags, basically,” Szydlowski said.

Last December, analysts forecasted that 2026 would be a breakthrough year for smart glasses. And it’s clear by now that Meta wants this to be the year that AI glasses are suddenly everywhere you look.

The tech giant invested heavily in promoting them, collaborating with celebrity influencer Kylie Jenner on a pair of Ray-Bans featuring an AI assistant that speaks in her voice. The campaign featured billboard ads and a video spot showing Kylie simply enjoying wearing the glasses, without necessarily highlighting their practical features. The partnership was rumored to have paid Jenner millions of dollars and was intended to position the technology as a fashionable, practical accessory—and perhaps buff out the public perception of them as “pervert glasses.” But critics have argued that the ads seem narrowly designed to encourage more people to use their glasses for continuous recording.

Though the Jenner campaign was supposedly viewed as a success internally at Meta, it also prompted global backlash. On social media, the protest collective “Everyone Hates Elon” razed Jenner, The Huffington Post reported, saying that “recording everything we see and do constantly? It’s giving fascism, not fashion, hun.” And pop singer Lorde stopped a festival performance to tell her fans, “Fuck the glasses. Don’t get the glasses. Not sexy.”

Salon’s Andi Zeisler slammed the Kylie Edition glasses for trying to lull women into a false sense of security, even as Meta knows the technology has been used to record women without their knowledge, both in public and private. In London, activists took that criticism a step further, replacing bus stop ads of Jenner smiling in the glasses with a spoof in which her face transforms into a skeletal grin above the warning that at Meta, “We’re always watching.”

But despite protests, the glasses aren’t going away any time soon, as Meta plans to move millions more into production. In 2025, the company sold more than 7 million AI glasses—up from 2 million sold in the prior two years combined—then quickly made plans to double its Ray-Ban outputs, Bloomberg reported. By the end of 2026, Meta expects to start producing at least 20 million glasses annually to meet demand, or perhaps as many as 30 million if the market continues trending strongly.

Beyond the backlash, regulating the glasses is a touchy subject, Quintin told Ars. No civil rights group would advocate banning recording in public, a practice that can be crucial for holding police and government officials accountable. What may prove just as useful as thoughtful privacy regulations, Quintin suggested, is a broader effort to ban the technology at the community level.

Szydlowski told Ars that he’s personally not bothered by Meta’s AI glasses, only by the gross content made with them. But other critics, like Quintin, think the tech is “disgusting” and “unacceptable,” and he has little hope that technical solutions can solve the problem and abundant concern that the privacy risks will compound as enthusiasm for the technology grows.

Right now, there’s less social friction around using glasses to record than there was when people first started using phones to record public interactions, Quintin suggested. As a father of young children, he recently saw another dad using glasses to film kids at a birthday party, a moment that illustrates how smart glasses have shifted the power dynamic.

Previously, “if you wanted to record somebody, you had to take out your phone, shove it in their face,” Quintin said. “And they know they’re being recorded. That is a useful social friction. And the glasses remove that and put the friction on the other end. The friction is now on me, calling you a pervert for wearing glasses and telling you to stop recording my kids.”

Szydlowski somewhat agreed. He told Ars there’s value in being able to record hands-free from eye level, but he created Zuckoff because he draws the line at posting harmful smart-glasses recordings online.

“People are using it in a bad way,” Szydlowski said. “That was the first part that annoyed me. I was like, ‘I don’t like it. I just don’t enjoy the content, and I don’t think it’s valid,’ because myself, I wouldn’t have a way to react to being recorded because I’m used to people holding the phone and actually pointing at me. Then I can say, ‘Hold on a second. This is not scrolling. Someone is actually recording.’”

This story was updated on August 25 to note that the Nearby Glasses app has been updated and is free.

Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra review: The ultra foldable with an ultra price

Ars Technica Long form August 14, 2026

Samsung didn’t have to change much this year because its hardware is just that good.

Samsung has largely defined the foldable phone category, but it’s no longer alone in releasing flexible devices. Google, Motorola, and a raft of Chinese OEMs have their own take on this form factor. Is the new Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra really “ultra” enough to remain on top?

This phone doesn’t have the wide frame of the new Z Fold 8, instead matching the approximate size and shape of the company’s last few tablet-style foldables. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is not a big leap, but it continues Samsung’s pattern of iterative foldable improvements. At this point, there’s very little left to improve. The compromises of going with a foldable over a regular flat phone have largely been erased with the Z Fold 8 Ultra. Well, except for the price.

Foldables used to be real pocket-busters, almost like carrying two phones glued together. Samsung has successively shaved a few millimeters off every year, taking a leap last year with the Z Fold 7. The Z Fold 8 Ultra is even a bit slimmer than that phone, but the difference is basically imperceptible. It still has the same buttons in the same places, including a fingerprint sensor in the power button.

The 2026 Samsung flagship foldable is barely thicker than the average flat phone when folded, which is impressive considering the powerful hardware inside. The two halves come together with no gap, and the hinge feels smooth and springy. The phone almost seems to “leap” into the unfolded configuration when you pry it open, and it ends up flatter than the Galaxy Z Fold 7, which didn’t quite reach 180 degrees. It’s structurally solid in this state, even though it’s barely 4 mm thick. It feels like a small tablet, not a phone that folds in half, but somehow, it is. You can fold it back up, and it fits in your pocket like any regular phone. It’s a very cool piece of hardware.

The 6.5-inch 1080p cover OLED is about the same size and shape as any non-foldable smartphone on the market today. It has the latest Gorilla Glass Ceramic coating, and it’s plenty bright for outdoor use. The real star of the show is the 8-inch internal foldable screen. Its resolution is 2256 x 2504, a bit higher than last year’s phone, and its peak brightness has increased to 3000 nits.

Even very bright foldable screens can be hard to read in bright light because the plastic top layer is so reflective. Samsung has addressed that somewhat with the Z Fold 8 Ultra with its new anti-reflective layer. Reflections aren’t gone, but like the treated glass on Samsung’s flat Ultra phones, the intensity of reflections is much reduced. This makes the big internal screen more legible outdoors.

The other screen update tackles the classic foldable crease. Early on, foldable screens had a veritable chasm running down the middle. That has been minimized to varying degrees, with some phones showing almost no crease at all. Samsung is now in that group with the Z Fold 8 Ultra thanks to its “Titanium Flex” technology. This metallic layer apparently supports the OLED better, eliminating the crease. If you look from the right angle in the right lighting, you may be able to see a bit of distortion, but you can’t really feel it while using the screen.

The only truly clunky aspect of the phone’s design is the camera module. Because the internals are so tightly packed, the camera hardware pokes way out past the rear glass. It stands out in the wrong way and can get snagged on your pocket when you try to put the phone away. The three modules are lined up in the corner in usual Samsung fashion, which makes the phone a wobbly mess when you set it down.

Samsung’s One UI is a known quantity at this point. It comes loaded with some duplicative apps and junk you may not want, like Facebook and LinkedIn. The interface can be a little cluttered, and there are features buried in the settings that you’ll probably never touch. But Samsung doesn’t change much year-to-year, so if you’ve used a Samsung phone in the past few years, the learning curve will be minimal.

Samsung makes a big deal out of multitasking on its foldables, offering robust window management that goes beyond what you get from Google or Motorola. It’s a snap to move apps around, break them out into floating windows, and save configurations. You can also have three apps running live in split-screen on the Fold, whereas most other foldables limit you to two.

Android itself has more foldable optimizations than it once did, and Samsung has taken full advantage of that. For example, the taskbar on the Z Fold 8 Ultra is easy to bring up while using the phone, and you can pin it to the screen. It also shows more recent apps than the standard Google version of this feature.

And then there’s the AI. Samsung has been all-in on Galaxy AI for the last couple of years, and it’s expanded that feature set even further with the 2026 foldables. Samsung does at least still offer the option to run its AI features solely through on-device processing. This keeps your data from going to the cloud but limits the AI features that are available.

Samsung is again pushing its Now Brief feature, and it’s one of the most perplexing AI features I’ve seen on a phone. It’s all over the device—the home screen comes with a widget, it appears on the lock screen, and it sends you notifications. But it still does almost nothing. The pitch is that Samsung uses on-device AI to ingest your data and produce actionable suggestions. More often than not, all you get are links to anxiety-inducing news stories, your calendar, the weather, and maybe some videos. I feel like I’m living in the “c’mon do something” meme every time I open Now Brief.

Samsung’s Now Nudge feature offers proactive suggestions powered by on-device AI. For example, you may see a suggestion to add an event to your calendar based on a text conversation. In general, this feature seems better at completing tasks correctly, but it still doesn’t show up very often. It is, however, nice that nudges now open apps in split-screen instead of taking you away from the content you’re viewing.

Samsung also gets even deeper Gemini AI integration with this release. Gemini Notebook (formerly NotebookLM) is preloaded, and it’s optimized for drag-and-drop and split-screen usage. That’s cool if you are a fan of Google’s AI research tool, which is admittedly one of the better things the company has done with LLMs.

More questionable is the expanded support for app automations, which debuted earlier this year on the Galaxy S26 series. The idea is that you can ask Gemini to complete a task for you, and it will use the appropriate app to get it done in the background. The list of supported apps has expanded to more than 40, including DoorDash, Temu, Airbnb, Delta, and Best Buy.

Unsurprisingly, having Gemini operate even simple apps is very slow and fraught with errors. It gets there most of the time, but it’s nowhere near good enough that I’d trust the results without a thorough double-check. And at that point, why not just do it myself?

It’s not all AI retreads, though. Samsung has added something genuinely fantastic to its Galaxy AI portfolio, but it’s not the kind of AI it wants everyone talking about. As of the last version of One UI (and continuing in the version on the Fold), Samsung’s phone app does Google-style call screening. This is one of the biggest selling points for Pixel phones in this age of endless phone spam, and Samsung is finally on board.

As on Pixel phones, you have the option of directing a robot to answer a suspicious call. It transcribes what the caller says, giving you the option of answering or getting more information before picking up. This alone almost makes up for the issues I have with One UI.

Like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, Samsung’s new flagship foldable runs on a version of the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 optimized specifically for its devices. This is functionally the fastest mobile processor in the world, featuring eight high-speed Oryon CPU cores and an Adreno GPU that can rival some laptop chips.

You won’t find yourself waiting on the Z Fold 8 to get things done (unless you ask Gemini to use an app). It’s a snappy experience, even when running multiple apps side by side. Games also run flawlessly on this device, as long as you don’t mind a toasty phone.

In benchmarks, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra scores very near the top of all current phones (see below). While the chip is identical to the one in the S26 Ultra, it doesn’t quite match that phone’s scores. This is most likely due to thermal constraints in the foldable.

Heat is a problem in all smartphones—the benchmark scores you see bandied about are all based on full performance for short periods. When you stress a device for more than a minute or two, such as when you play a high-end game, performance will drop dramatically. In the past, some Samsung phones have throttled by more than half when heating up. The Z Fold 8 Ultra isn’t that bad, but you can expect to lose about 30 to 40 percent of that peak speed. However, that still leaves the Z Fold 8 with higher overall performance compared to, for example, a Google Pixel.

Samsung’s new foldable still comes with 12GB of RAM in the base model. You can upgrade to 16GB with more storage, but the phone is already very expensive. Overall, apps remain in memory long enough, and I haven’t noticed issues with multitasking. Still, at this price, 16GB of RAM would make more sense. Perhaps if we were not in the midst of the great AI RAM shortage, Samsung would have stepped up to 16GB.

There aren’t many hardware improvements in this year’s Fold, but the battery and charging did get some attention. Having finally gone the silicon-carbon route, Samsung has increased the capacity to 5,000 mAh (up from 4,400 mAh last year). That’s on par with most non-folding flagship phones. It’s not a night-and-day difference in longevity, and you can still drain it quickly by using only the big internal display, but you don’t have to worry about whether the Z Fold 8 Ultra will make it to bedtime most days.

If the Z Fold 8 Ultra doesn’t quite make it all the way to bedtime, you won’t be terribly inconvenienced. Samsung has boosted the charging from the measly 25 W peak speed of past foldables to a much more reasonable 45 W. That’s nothing compared to what you get with certain Chinese smartphones, but it’s much more livable. Samsung says you can go from empty to 67 percent in about 30 minutes with a compatible USB-PD charger.

One of the main selling points of the Z Fold 8 Ultra over the Z Fold 8 is the camera setup. While the wide-body foldable only has two rear cameras (both 50 MP), the Z Fold 8 Ultra has an upgraded triple setup with a 200 MP primary, a 10 MP 3x telephoto, and a new 50 MP ultrawide.

The 200 MP camera is the same as last year’s foldable, and the sensor is identical to what’s in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. However, the aperture is narrower (less light collection) due to the constraints introduced by foldables. Photos are binned to 12 MP, showing good dynamic range and brightness, although Google does have Samsung beat there. They still have that distinctive vibrant and sometimes too contrasty look we associate with Samsung cameras.

Capture speed has always been a challenge for Samsung phones, which seem to lean toward being brighter, even at the expense of some blur. Things are better than they once were with the Z Fold 8 Ultra, but you should take a few snaps of any subject that is moving around to make sure you get one that’s crisp. Luckily, Samsung’s burst mode is quick and reliable.

You don’t get a telephoto camera with Samsung’s wider foldable, but this sensor increasingly feels like an afterthought for the Ultra. It’s still just 10 MP, and the sensor is tiny at 1/3.94 inches. it will get you a bit closer to your subject, but the results often look overprocessed. That’s doubly true if you zoom beyond 3x and count on Samsung’s processing to clean up the image.

The new 50 MP ultrawide does offer a nice upgrade over last year’s Fold, though. The field of view is wide enough that it offers a different perspective than the main camera but not so wide that the edges look distorted. The boosted resolution speeds up captures in low light and results in slightly better detail with the expected pumped-up Samsung colors. This sensor is also used for macro shots on the Z Fold 8 Ultra, and the detail you get close up is noticeably better than the last Fold.

While the still photos may have some foibles, Samsung’s video recording on the Z Fold 8 with the main sensor is a step up from almost any other phone. It can handle up to 8K resolution at 30 fps, and the enhanced stabilization available at lower resolutions is great for recording on the move. Video is crisp across the board, with great range and colors.

In some ways, it’s amazing that a device like this exists. It’s hardly any more bulky than a traditional smartphone, but it’s a tablet that fits in your pocket. There’s almost no crease in the screen, and the hinge is rock-solid. Heck, you can even drop it in a pool, and it will keep ticking (IP48). The cameras, battery life, and performance aren’t as compromised as they were with past foldables, either.

The slow pace of change in mobile technology has prompted many of us to become a bit jaded, but if foldables of this caliber were somehow remarkably cheaper, they would be in everyone’s pocket. But that’s the problem—they’re not cheaper. In fact, all computing devices are getting more expensive.

The $100 price bump is quickly becoming a 2026 tradition, but that’s a bigger chunk of the price when you’re talking about a flat phone that used to cost $800 or $900. At $2,100, the Z Fold 8 Ultra is only a little more expensive than last year’s version. If you were willing to spend $2,000 on a foldable, $2,100 is not a big leap.

The dream of foldable mass adoption may be slipping away, but that doesn’t mean these devices don’t have a place. If you do most of your computing on a phone and could benefit from the added screen real estate, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a killer device. It won’t weigh down your pocket, and it lets you easily multitask and use apps with tablet-style interfaces. You’ll pay handsomely for that ability, but enough people are willing to do so that Samsung’s 2026 foldables are seeing record sales—though they still trail flat phones by a wide margin.

For people who would consider spending two grand on a phone, this is a good option. But it’s not so much better than the Z Fold 7 that you need to rush out and get the new model. For Z Fold 6 owners who like the experience, though, this is a worthy upgrade.

Could United Launch Alliance’s money problems finally force its owners to sell?

Ars Technica Long form September 11, 2026

ULA is preparing to resume launching the Vulcan rocket in the coming weeks.

Pretty much every rocket company in the United States, save one, has embraced two fundamental tenets: reusability and diversification.

Most famously, SpaceX branched out from reusable rockets to pursue and dominate a growing spectrum of space services: cargo delivery, human spaceflight, satellite production, broadband, and, perhaps soon, orbital data centers and in-space manufacturing. Blue Origin is evolving from a pure rocket company into a satellite manufacturer, robotics developer, and, most recently, a potential competitor for SpaceX’s Starlink network.

Rocket Lab used a different approach to diversify after achieving success with its small Electron launch vehicle. The company relocated its headquarters from New Zealand to Southern California, started building spacecraft and payloads, and then went on a spree of corporate acquisitions to expand into satellite communications and take on a new role as a merchant supplier of satellite components and sensors. It’s now in a stage of advanced development of its partially reusable next-generation Neutron launch vehicle.

The list goes on. Firefly Aerospace started as a launch company and now builds Moon landers and space tugs. Relativity Space is already looking beyond rockets before ever putting anything into orbit.

They all realize an enduring truth in the space business. Launch is a low-margin business. SpaceX’s financial statements, now open to inspection after the company went public earlier this year, shine a light on this fact. Just 8 percent of the company’s $12.5 billion in revenue during the first half of this year came from launch services. Another 5 percent came from “launch and development” activities, which include SpaceX’s work on things like NASA’s lunar lander program.

SpaceX attributes the rest of its revenue to Starlink and AI. The potential of the latter is almost solely responsible for SpaceX’s post-IPO valuation of approximately $1.8 trillion.

Rocket Lab’s financials paint a similar picture. It reported $434 million in revenue for the first half of 2026 and credited a quarter of it to launch services.

Given all this, what are we to make of the company that SpaceX supplanted as the country’s leading launch provider?

United Launch Alliance, founded in 2006, was born in an era when the US government was the dominant force in the domestic launch market. Commercial launch demand was on the wane, and what demand there was often went to launch providers in Europe or Russia. Executives at the two leading US launch companies—Boeing and Lockheed Martin—knew they were in trouble. Boeing’s Delta IV rocket program, in particular, was in danger of going out of business.

The situation jeopardized the US government’s policy of ensuring two separate rocket types are available to launch national security payloads into orbit. With the government’s blessing, Boeing and Lockheed entered into a 50-50 joint venture, merging their Delta and Atlas rocket programs under one roof. The merger all but erased competition from the US launch market. However, the sole-source paradigm proved lucrative for ULA’s corporate parents, which each reported hundreds of millions of dollars in earnings from ULA per year in the first decade of the company’s existence.

SpaceX sued the US Air Force in 2014 for the right to compete for military launch contracts, and the Pentagon relented the following year, making SpaceX eligible to bid against ULA. SpaceX won its first high-priority military launch contract in 2016, a few months after the company landed its reusable Falcon 9 booster for the first time.

This moment was a turning point for ULA and the start of a long slide from dominance for the Boeing-Lockheed venture. Around the same time, ULA kicked off development of a new rocket, the Vulcan, to replace the legacy Atlas V and Delta IV rockets. But officials did not prioritize reusability in Vulcan’s design, with no plans to reuse the rocket’s booster stage and only tentative plans to eventually recover and reuse Vulcan’s main engines. A decade later, ULA’s half-hearted stab at reusability hasn’t gone anywhere.

Aside from ULA’s initial design decisions, the company faltered in its execution of the Vulcan rocket’s development, which was co-funded by the Pentagon. Vulcan’s first launch was delayed more than four years from ULA’s original target of 2019. Boeing and Lockheed Martin at first provided only tentative funding for Vulcan’s development, then ULA waited until 2018 to select an engine for Vulcan, deciding on Blue Origin’s BE-4 over Aerojet Rocketdyne’s AR1. Until then, engineers pursued two different designs for the Vulcan rocket—one with a methane-fueled first stage and another, narrower rocket for kerosene.

In the meantime, ULA shelved plans for an advanced, long-duration upper stage, a feature that, at least on paper, appeared to be one of the Vulcan rocket’s advantages over SpaceX’s Falcon rocket family. Delays in testing and qualifying Blue Origin’s BE-4 engine and an explosion of the rocket’s Centaur upper stage during a ground test in 2023 eventually pushed Vulcan’s first test flight into early 2024.

Still, ULA’s stellar track record for reliability proved a key selling point for the Pentagon, which awarded the company more than half of the military’s next batch of launch contracts in 2020, 27 missions worth some $4.5 billion. SpaceX got the rest of the contracts, with 22 launches booked on Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets for a total value of $4 billion. The situation flipped with the Pentagon’s next round of launch procurement in 2025, when SpaceX won the lion’s share.

ULA’s streak of reliability continued with a near-flawless debut launch of the Vulcan rocket. But ULA ran into trouble on the rocket’s second flight in October 2024 when the exhaust nozzle on one of its Northrop Grumman-built solid rocket boosters shattered moments after liftoff. The rocket kept flying after the anomaly and still reached orbit. An investigation concluded that the nozzle failed due to a “manufacturing defect” in an insulator, leading to the melting and burn-through of the booster nozzle.

But the nozzle problem wasn’t actually fixed. A similar failure on the fourth Vulcan launch last February has grounded the rocket for more than six months. ULA aims to return to flight with the Vulcan rocket soon, perhaps by the end of this month, on a commercial flight with a batch of Amazon Leo broadband satellites. The US Space Force has not cleared Vulcan to resume launches with military payloads, and the program’s cumulative delays have forced military officials to reassign several missions from ULA to SpaceX. Military officials aren’t happy, and they’ve let Boeing and Lockheed know.

A ULA spokesperson said the investigation into the solid rocket booster anomaly is “ongoing” and did not confirm a target launch date for the next Vulcan flight. “We will share the Vulcan Leo 1 mission launch date upon the completion of the investigation and coordination with our customer,” the representative said.

Vulcan’s technical issues are cropping up as launch prices rise at United Launch Alliance. It’s not surprising that the Vulcan rocket, with a fully expendable design, is on average more expensive than SpaceX’s mostly reusable Falcon rocket. But ULA’s launch prices have increased significantly over the last few years—from $112 million to more than $200 million per Vulcan mission—while SpaceX’s prices have remained relatively stable.

At the same time, the financial situation at ULA is not great. Lockheed Martin said its earnings “primarily” attributable to ULA dipped from $325 million in 2016 ($436 million in 2025 dollars) to $100 million in 2022 ($109 million in 2025 dollars). Double that to get an idea of ULA’s net income. Last year, Lockheed reported its share of earnings from ULA was “not significant.” ULA was responsible for a quarter of the operating profit in Lockheed’s space business a decade ago. It dropped to less than 10 percent over the last five years, then to virtually nothing in 2025.

It isn’t as easy to parse ULA’s financial situation from Boeing’s financial statements, which lump ULA’s earnings with several other Boeing joint ventures. But the overall trajectory at Boeing has also trended down.

Boeing and Lockheed’s shareholder equity in United Launch Alliance in 2025 was half of what it was 10 years ago, adjusted for inflation. Shareholder equity, or book value, is a measure of a company’s assets minus liabilities. It’s the amount of money a company’s shareholders would receive after liquidation. The chart below shows the change in how Boeing and Lockheed have valued their equity stakes in ULA since 2016.

Book value isn’t the same as market value, an unknowable figure for an equity-based joint venture like ULA. Market value is typically higher than book value for profitable companies, but Boeing and Lockheed’s earnings suggest that ULA’s finances are, to put it delicately, fragile.

The concerns from ULA’s corporate owners became public in July, when Boeing and Lockheed Martin revealed they guaranteed a loan to sustain ULA through the grounding of the Vulcan rocket. In SEC filings, Boeing and Lockheed wrote that the suspension of Vulcan launches is “negatively affecting ULA’s financial condition and results of operations.”

Lockheed revised down this year’s profitability forecast for its space division by $45 million in July, citing “lower ULA equity earnings.” United Launch Alliance opened 2026 with a forecast of 18 to 22 launches this year. Eight months later, the company has launched five times, and just once with the Vulcan rocket. The lull in launches means fewer customer payments and lower revenue.

ULA’s owners “each agreed to guarantee $500 (million) of certain ULA credit facilities” in May, Boeing said. “We and Lockheed expect to provide additional financial support and could incur losses if ULA is unable to resume Vulcan launches consistent with ULA’s assumptions.” In a footnote, Boeing added that it “generally” issues such credit guarantees on behalf of “parties with less than investment-grade credit.”

Bloomberg reported last month that ULA was looking to raise $1.5 billion, three times the original amount. It’s a remarkable turnabout for Boeing and Lockheed Martin, which have long tapped ULA for a steady flow of revenue.

“ULA’s financial position has been impacted due to the performance challenges associated with the anomaly with the solid rocket booster nozzle experienced on two of the Vulcan launches,” a ULA spokesperson told Ars. “While this is a challenging time bringing our Vulcan rocket up to its optimal launch rate, ULA is well positioned for the future and continues to be laser-focused on our customers’ needs and achieving a reliable and sustainable manifest.”

“Our board continues to view ULA as a national asset providing critical launch capability supporting key government and commercial customers and is supportive of ULA’s continued growth and innovation,” the spokesperson said. “We already have strong commitments from our customers, with more than 80 launches on contract, ULA’s manifest is nearly sold out for the foreseeable future.”

Boeing and Lockheed’s efforts to shore up ULA’s finances come after a multiyear sales pitch shopping ULA to potential buyers. None agreed to pay the sum of roughly $5 billion that ULA’s owners were originally asking. Speculation in the launch industry at the time was that a fairer selling price might be $2 billion to $3 billion.

Blue Origin, Jeff Bezos’ space company and a key supplier for the Vulcan rocket, appeared for a time to be the leading contender for buying up United Launch Alliance. That was when ULA was riding high, soon after the successful first flight of Vulcan in 2024. Industry chatter about the potential sale quieted after Vulcan’s recent booster woes.

Other candidates for taking over ULA included Amazon, Vulcan’s biggest commercial customer. Amazon has already funded a significant expansion in ULA launch capability to support the Amazon Leo constellation. Two other ULA suppliers, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris, could also be interested, as could a private equity firm or even a buyout by one of ULA’s current owners. The list of prospective buyers is largely conjecture. Company officials usually don’t speak publicly about mergers and acquisitions until they’re ready to announce them.

A Boeing spokesperson responded to questions from Ars, saying, “Consistent with our corporate practice, we don’t comment on potential market rumors or speculation about financial activities.” Lockheed Martin and ULA did not provide a statement by late Thursday.

It would also be foolish to rule out the US government taking a stake in ULA amid a rush of state-backed investments under the Trump administration.

Engine-builder Aerojet Rocketdyne, now split into separate companies, submitted an unsolicited offer to buy ULA for $2 billion in 2015. Boeing and Lockheed dismissed the bid. $2 billion was probably below market value at the time.

Today, the sale price for any potential acquisition of ULA is almost certainly lower than it was a few years ago, but ULA still has a strong pedigree, with a rocket that is actually (kind of) flying, something many US launch companies can’t say. This could open the possibility of new dark-horse contenders for purchasing United Launch Alliance.

One company to watch is AST SpaceMobile, a Texas-based firm in the early stages of deploying a network of broadband satellites to beam signals directly to smartphones from low-Earth orbit. SpaceX’s Starlink network already does this, and Amazon is pursuing the direct-to-device connectivity market with its Amazon Leo constellation.

AST officials hinted last month that they are interested in getting into the launch business. The company raised more than $1 billion in a convertible bond sale in July, and AST executives wrote in their most recent quarterly earnings report that they are looking for ways to spend it. The company said it is pursuing an “expanding universe of growth initiatives” to “further vertically integrate our business and mitigate risks associated with third-party launch providers.”

AST’s primary launch providers are SpaceX and Blue Origin. Both are potential competitors in the satellite broadband business. The growth initiatives AST said it was interested in would allow it to “secure additional access to orbit” for its own constellation. AST listed “partnerships and/or acquisitions” as possibilities. A company spokesperson did not respond to questions on the matter.

The balance sheet in AST’s latest quarterly filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission showed the company had approximately $2.3 billion in cash and cash equivalents on hand at the end of June, equal to or more than ULA’s publicly traded subcontractors, Northrop Grumman and L3Harris. That was before AST closed its $1 billion bond sale in July.

There are reasons to question AST’s long-term business outlook, especially as it goes head-to-head against SpaceX and Amazon, two of the most well-capitalized US tech firms. However, vertical integration has served most space companies well, and the same may be true with AST. But there’s a catch. ULA itself is not vertically integrated, with suppliers providing key parts, like engines, payload fairings, and avionics.

AST would surely improve its position with more control of its own access to space. AST already builds its own satellites—each with enormous 2,400-square-foot phased-array antennas—and manages much of its frontend connectivity service, working alongside mobile phone telcos like AT&T and Verizon. T-Mobile is SpaceX’s largest domestic partner on Starlink direct-to-cell.

A buyer for ULA outside of the launch business would also maintain competition in the US launch market. Any sale would have to be approved by the Federal Trade Commission and Department of Justice to ensure it does not substantially reduce competition. Some companies in other sectors are aiming to complete mergers and acquisitions under the Trump administration, which they see as providing a favorable regulatory environment for such transactions.

The launch market would lose a competitor if a company like Blue Origin, with its own heavy-lift rocket, acquired ULA. This would be unwelcome news for the US military as SpaceX prepares for the retirement of its workhorse Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets in favor of the newer, more powerful Starship rocket. Starship is unlikely to be certified any time soon for the US government’s most critical national security missions.

United Launch Alliance boasts a substantial order book, a backlog of approximately 80 missions with its Vulcan rocket and the soon-to-retire Atlas V, a number only rivaled by SpaceX.

ULA hopes to resume burning down its backlog in the coming weeks, with the return-to-flight of Vulcan slated for as soon as the end of September. This will be the first of 38 launches Amazon has reserved on the Vulcan rocket and comes as the company faces a bottleneck in launch capacity due to Vulcan’s grounding and the explosion of Blue Origin’s New Glenn rocket on the launch pad in May.

The upcoming launch will be ULA’s first under the direction of its new CEO, Mark Peller, who was named to the position last month. Peller replaces Tory Bruno, who retired from ULA last December to take a job overseeing national security business at Blue Origin. Peller is a 36-year veteran of the launch industry, including 20 years at United Launch Alliance, where he led development of the Vulcan rocket from its inception through its certification for US government missions in 2025.

“ULA has a tremendous history of launching some of the nation’s most important national security and exploration missions, and the future is limitless with the new capabilities and performance of our Vulcan rocket,” Peller said in a statement announcing his new role as CEO.

In the near term, this “limitless future” is in the hands of the engineers preparing to return the Vulcan rocket to flight. The next launch of Vulcan will require the thrust from six solid rocket boosters, the most ever on a Vulcan flight to date. That means six data points to show ULA and Northrop have a path to overcoming the booster nozzle problem.

Upon clearing that hurdle, ULA needs a buyer willing to invest in innovation. It would help if the presumed new owner had some skin in the game as an anchor customer for the Vulcan launch vehicle, and more importantly, for what should undoubtedly come next—a reusable rocket.

Story updated to add comments from United Launch Alliance.
