Police searching for six men over anti-migrant protest

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:51:35 GMT

Police have released images of six men they want to speak to in connection with an anti-migrant protest in Portsmouth.

Hampshire police attended Eastney Marina on 6 September after hundreds of demonstrators blocked roads in an attempt to stop coaches carrying 120 migrants, who had crossed the Channel in a dinghy, from leaving the city.

The force said several police, coastguard and Border Force vehicles had been damaged during the evening. Seven officers were treated at the scene for injuries, but no-one in attendance was seriously hurt.

Assistant Chief Constable Tony Rowlinson urged anyone who recognised the six men to contact police.

The government condemned "intimidating and thuggish behaviour" at the demonstration, while stressing the right to peaceful protest.

On Friday, a 42-year-old man from Paulsgrove was charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police officer in connection with the incident. He has been remanded into custody.

A 16-year-old boy was arrested on Saturday in connection with the disorder. He has been released on bail pending further enquiries.

Rowlinson said: "The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences."

The force had reviewed "hundreds of hours' worth" of footage, he said, adding: "The actions we have been taking as part of our investigation send a clear warning to anyone intent on causing disruption and disorder at any future events."

Around 500 anti-migrant protesters took to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday and were met by hundreds of counter-protesters from Stand up to Racism.

Migrants intercepted in the Channel are typically brought to Dover for initial processing.

However, the dinghy that arrived at Eastney Marina had set off from near Cherbourg in the Bay of the Seine, about 170 miles (274km) west of Calais and significantly further west than the usual departure points.

Taking those on board to Dover would have added another four to five hours to a journey that had already lasted around 10 hours. It would also have required lifeboats to operate outside their normal patrol area for longer.

As a result, Border Force and the coastguard opted to bring the group ashore at Eastney Landing in Portsmouth, with lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth on the Isle of Wight assisting in the operation.

Migration analysts say people smugglers may be experimenting with new departure points to avoid a heavy police presence in Calais and Dunkirk.

Crew members from the RNLI were later targeted by protesters, sharing their photos and names in posts on social media accusing them of treason.

McInnes delivers togetherness & intensity in Old Firm gobsmacker

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:08:09 GMT

Fifty-five minutes into this Rangers romp at Ibrox, Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney stood beside each other in the Celtic technical area, chin-stroking, head-scratching, pointing, waving, drowning.

To them, in this moment, this Premier Sports Cup quarter-final must have felt like a surreal and nightmarish occasion - and it was only 1-0 at the time. Rangers had really only started to wreak their havoc.

Such was Rangers' dominance, their complete owning of their visitors in every conceivable category, the Celtic managerial brains trust seemed just as lost as every one of their players on the field.

Man for man, Rangers won every battle, not for 45 minutes but for the full ninety.

Rangers overwhelm meek Celtic to clinch semi-final spot

No away fans, of course. Not that that had anything to do with it. Being locked out of Ibrox might have seemed like a curse to Celtic folk. In the end, it must have felt like the greatest blessing.

In his early months in the job, Derek McInnes has been looking for a marquee performance. Now he has it. He was looking for a formation that worked and personnel that were big enough and bold enough to execute it and he got that, too. This was 3-0 going on more. Plenty more.

The simplicity of their progression to the semi-final was a touch surreal. Neither of these were in particularly good form coming into this. They were both winning, yes, but they haven't been all that convincing.

This season, in their last eight domestic features combined - all won, in fairness - there was only a goal in it at the end in seven of them. Both sides had got themselves into a cycle of missed chances and, at times, uncomfortable days.

So the smart money was on a tight contest. Extra-time, maybe. Penalties? You wouldn't have ruled that out either. O'Neill is such a winning machine that many would have expected Celtic to find a way, somehow. So much for that.

Few Old Firm games surprise you anymore, but this one was a gobsmacker.

Rangers had all the intensity and all the togetherness. They had six players making their Old Firm debut from the start but if inexperience can be a challenge in this fixture then it was a challenge they met with gusto.

McInnes and his driven and vastly superior players neutralised Celtic, shut them down, rendered them impotent. Celtic captain Callum McGregor lords it over days like this, but the supreme central midfielder was Dan Neil, not just in his outstanding goals but in the control and the leadership he exerted.

With Nico Raskin beside him it was a no-contest in the middle of the pitch. James Penrice did a power of really good work in there, too.

Camilo Duran, playing wide again instead of through the middle, has been one of the players of the season so far, but he hardly existed, totally bossed by Olwethu Makhanya - calm in the maelstrom, classy in nearly everything he did.

Kasper Hogh needed a goal having scored in just one game in six - a hat-trick, albeit - but the record signing spent much of his day in Emmanuel Fernandez's pocket. He had no service and no sniff.

Where did this come from? Lord knows, but it makes life very interesting now, not just in the destination of the League Cup - Rangers will be massive favourites against Aberdeen in their semi-final - but in the race for the league title.

McInnes might have hit on something substantial. The big task, of course, is to repeat that energy, that belief, that ruthlessness.

You expected Celtic to stir and make a game of it, but they were never allowed to, in part because of their own awful shortcomings with the ball and in other part because Rangers didn't allow them to settle. They hunted them down, right from the opening minutes.

A mood, of sorts, was set as early as the fourth minute when Sam Johnstone, Celtic's jumpy new goalkeeper, passed a clearance straight to Kevin Kelsy, who slashed it wide.

Johnstone had been harried by Rangers' press, a big theme of the day. For Kelsy, it was a great chance to strike early, but if he failed then he made amends later on.

Kelsy is only in the door, but he looks to have personality and desire. He was playing with Ryan Naderi, an oft-criticised striker, a player you hear constantly is not Rangers class. Naderi was one of the totems of the day, a work rate that never stopped, a constant menace in hunting and gathering. Naderi might have changed a few Rangers minds on Sunday.

Martin O'Neill and Shaun Maloney could not get a response from their team

The opener was a microcosm; Naderi robbing Cameron Carter-Vickers, Kelsy then picking out Neil for a sumptuous finish. Rangers were physically and creatively on top, but there's always a feeling that one goal needed to become two to halt Celtic's assumed purple patch, a response that never came.

That was the bizarre thing. Total authority for an entire game is a rare enough thing in this contest. Usually there's a spell when the team that's ahead has to weather some kind of storm. Celtic couldn't throw a bucket of water in Rangers' direction not to mind a tempest. When McInnes' side made it two it was only what they deserved.

Penrice put in the cross, Naderi flicked it on and Kelsy banged in the volley. Neil's second and Rangers' third was a peach, a sign of confident uninhibited players enjoying themselves. The smallest of mercies for Celtic was that it stayed at three.

The second part of this drama comes on Sunday, a league game that could not have been better set up had Eddie Hearn been involved in the promotion. Rangers looking to lay down another marker going to Celtic's home, full of 60,000 folk baying for revenge. Given some of the vile songs that were directed at O'Neill at Ibrox then McInnes is in for some treatment. Sadly, he's heard it all over before, as has O'Neill.

McInnes was measured in the aftermath, more low-key than you might have expected and there was sense in that. This was one game and he knew it. They won nothing on the back of it and he knew that, too.

Apart from, that is, precious momentum and self-belief and the knowledge of what their standard can be when they get it right. And on Sunday, they got it spectacularly right.

'Finally got our points' - Hull and Woad shine in European Solheim win

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:54:44 GMT

This video can not be played

How Europe won the 2026 Solheim Cup

Charley Hull got the ball rolling as Europe's big names finally came to the fore in Sunday's singles as they wrested the Solheim Cup back from the USA with a 15-13 victory in the Netherlands.

Hull, who had garnered just half a point across the first two days in an unprofitable partnership with fellow Englishwoman Lottie Woad, led Europe out again on Sunday and claimed a 3&2 win over American livewire Megan Khang.

It delivered an immediate boost to Anna Nordqvist's team in the singles format that they have been unbeaten in since their last home defeat in 2015.

Woad, who alongside Hull is ranked among the top 10 players in the world, also delivered, with her 2&1 win over fellow debutant Auston Kim sparking wild celebrations on the 17th green at Bernardus Golf Club.

With Carlota Ciganda three holes up heading on to the 16th, it assured the hosts of reaching the 14½-point tally required to triumph in the biggest team competition in women's golf.

"It was the no-brainer to put Charley first," said Nordqvist.

"We saw the stats and Charley and Lottie were actually top-four players that made the most birdies for the week. They just played really tough matches.

"People don't understand how good all these players are and how good the golf has been in the past three days.

"So Charley was a no-brainer, and then finishing strong with Carlota. As we know, she's done it in the past."

Any question marks over Nordqvist's captaincy had revolved around repeatedly pairing her two star English players together over the first two days.

And Hull was one of the first on the scene to congratulate Woad, with the quip, "finally got our points didn't we Lottie".

Veteran Ciganda officially carrying her side over the winning line by beating Jennifer Kupcho could not have been more fitting as she became just the second player to secure the decisive point twice - having done so in 2023 - joining Catriona Matthew who did the same for Europe in both 2003 and 2013.

On Saturday evening Kupcho had hushed the crowd and yelled "vamos" as she drained a 91-foot putt on the 17th and then knocked in a 30-footer on the 18th green to steal a point from the Spaniard in the fourballs.

It felt like a moment that had turned the momentum of the match towards Angela Stanford's team but fewer then 24 hours later, Kupcho and her US team-mates had little to cheer with all the euphoria draped around those wearing blue and yellow.

"I was really happy to see that I was playing against Kupcho," said Ciganda. "She's a fighter, I'm a fighter, and what she did was amazing on 17 and 18.

"But [on Sunday] I knew she had no chance. I was like, I want to kill you," joked the Spaniard.

Lottie Woad won her first full point in the singles for Europe

Having started the day level at 8-8, Europe's quartet of rookies deserve huge credit.

Having impressed in the foursomes and fourballs, Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez and France's Nastasia Nadaud once again demonstrated their suitability for the biggest of stages.

Lopez Ramirez defeated Yealimi Noh 3&2, while Nadaud always looked in control against Andrea Lee to win by the same scoreline.

Mimi Rhodes, who had partnered Nadaud to two victories, was only downed by a superb performance from world number one Nelly Korda, while Lauren Coughlin, Lindy Duncan, Alison Lee were the only others to put splashes of red on Sunday's scoreboard.

Coughlin, who had already earned two-and-a-half points this week, ended Leona Maguire's unbeaten singles record.

Duncan beat Maja Stark, while Alison Lee came from four holes down to complete the biggest singles comeback in the history of the Solheim Cup, with a final-hole victory over Esther Henseleit.

But it was simply not enough for the visitors, whose wait for a first win on European soil since 2015 continues.

"The Europeans played great, and that's the way it goes," said Stanford.

"Their backs were against the wall, they had nothing to lose, and that's exactly what they did, they came out and played well."

By the time Rose Zhang concluded her win on the 18th against Celine Boutier in the last match on the course, the European party was in full swing.

This video can not be played

Woad putt helps Europe seal Solheim Cup win

As the US team returned to their team hotel on Saturday, a picture was posted on social media of them celebrating Kupcho's heroics on the 17th and 18th greens with a crate of beer.

Those scenes will have certainly inspired Europe on Sunday and the home team managed the wet early conditions perfectly as the US toiled on the greens.

"When we showed up in July here, they were faster. And I don't think it had anything to do with the rain either," said Stanford when asked about the speed of the greens.

"It's my responsibility to get the team ready. This is the one thing I am kicking myself [over] is that I just didn't keep pushing. We got to figure out how to hit our putts a little bit harder, which is really difficult, to change the way you putt.

"So I'm a little frustrated with myself that I didn't drive that point home. We don't play on greens this slow usually,

"I don't think we played bad. I think we just didn't make enough putts. If you listen to everything I've ever said, Europeans always putt better.

"I don't know why. I still don't know why. I mean, I have a good idea, but I'm not going to say it right now. Apparently I didn't get to know the superintendent as well as I should have."

Reform confident it won't need to repay any of £72m under proposed new donor rules

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:40:38 GMT

Reform UK believes the £72m in donations it has received from two cryptocurrency billionaires were "entirely in line with the law", the party's economic spokesman has said.

Robert Jenrick told the BBC he did not expect that the party will have to return any of the money from Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne, who are both British and have spent time living overseas.

The government is seeking to change the law on donations to UK political parties from British expats, including a £100,000 cap backdated to 25 March.

"These two donations are entirely in line with the law as it is and, as far as we know, the law as it's going to be in the future," Jenrick said.

As well as limiting how much British citizens can donate to political parties from overseas, the government has proposed a minimum residency period in which the £100,000 cap would still apply for those who move back to the UK.

This would be in place for the remainder of the calendar year and the following calendar year after the person returns.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that the rule changes would apply retrospectively and anyone not complying with them would have "to return that money".

Rayner added she was not commenting specifically on Delo and Harborne as she does not "understand" their "circumstances".

Answering questions about the donations following Rayner's remarks, Jenrick said: "It might be that Angela Rayner or the government keep trying to change the law to make it even harder for people to donate to Reform, nothing would surprise me.

"But, as it stands, we believe these are entirely in line with the law."

BBC News has been told that both Delo and Harborne have returned to the UK. Delo is understood to have been back in the country since last year.

Jenrick said Delo had returned to the UK "in part so that he can comply with the changes to the law".

In a statement after the programme, a Reform UK spokesman said: "We are 100% confident both [donations] are legal and won't ever have to be handed back."

One person familiar with the government's proposed changes said the issue of whether Delo and Harborne are affected would likely come down to how ministers choose to define UK residency.

They said one way would be to adopt the same definition used in tax laws, but stressed how complex the rules around residency are.

The government's proposed changes were added to the Representation of the People Bill after they were approved by MPs this month. The bill still needs to be scrutinised in the House of Lords.

Rayner said the proposals were "directly as a result" of a review by former top civil servant Philip Rycroft, published on 25 March.

Rayner said: "We said that because of the intention of the legislation and the recommendations, which we accepted, was known in the public domain that it would be retrospective to that date.

"That legislation is going through Parliament at the moment and we've also written to the Electoral Commission, which is an independent body, to see what further measures we need to take to protect our democracy."

There are currently no restrictions on the amount of money UK-based donors can give to political parties.

The government has previously said it was "determined to tackle" the issue of "mega-donors", and has established a new taskforce to do this.

It did not support calls from some MPs for a cap but Rayner left the door open to the possibility of further restrictions.

"It's not as simple as we're saying we won't put a cap [on donations], it's a question of making sure that the task and finish group look at how we implement this."

Rayner said the aim would be to "protect our democracy in the spirit of individuals not being able to overpower and buy their way into democracy at the expense of those people that are at the ballot box".

Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it was important to ensure "we do not end up with a sort of Americanisation of politics where money just sort of runs free".

He said people should be able to support the democratic movements they wished but added that "what we've got to be careful about is where different industries, where different financial sources raise questions".

Liberal Democrat Cabinet Office spokeswoman Lisa Smart said there should be emergency legislation to cap campaign donations and spending.

She said: "No politician should be able to buy the keys to Number 10."

A Green Party spokesperson said there needed to be "more robust laws" around political donations, adding: "The Labour Party urgently needs to find its spine and support a tight cap on donations from individuals."

Jenrick said Delo and Harborne - who each gave £36m to the party in two days and now share the record for the largest ever donation given to a UK political party - were "not buying anything, they simply support our agenda".

Both men had already donated millions of pounds to Reform ahead of the announcement of their latest contributions.

The Times reported in June that Harborne, who has been based in Thailand, had registered to vote in the UK, while Delo had told the Telegraph in April that he was moving back from Hong Kong.

Harborne wrote in the Telegraph on Saturday that Reform was a "start-up party" that lacked "the benefit of hundreds of years of patronage". Delo had written in the newspaper the day prior that he wanted to enable Reform to put up a "fair fight at the next election.

The £72m from the two is more than the total received by all UK political parties last year.

Delo was pardoned by US President Donald Trump last year over a breach of anti-money laundering laws at his crypto trading platform, BitMex, to which he had pleaded guilty in 2022.

Reform's fundraising has come under scrutiny in recent months. This includes police announcing an investigation over allegations the party broke foreign funding laws in a broadcast by Channel 4 News last week.

The party's leader Nigel Farage is also under investigation by the parliamentary standards commissioner over whether he should have declared a £5m gift he received from Harborne ahead of the 2024 election.

Both Reform and Farage have denied any wrongdoing in both instances.

The Great North Run (GNR) returned to Tyneside this weekend, with 63,000 runners taking part in the world's biggest half marathon - including Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

England star and Newcastle captain Dan Burn rang the starter's bell, with famous faces including football personality Chris Kamara and fitness coach Joe Wicks taking on the challenge.

The 13.1-mile (21km) event saw runners and wheelchair users race from Newcastle through Gateshead and South Tyneside, before finishing in South Shields.

Britons David Weir and Melanie Woods won the men's and women's elite wheelchair races respectively. Brigid Kosgei won the elite women's contest and Zouhair Talbi won the men's race.

"You see the causes people are running for, all pulling together for the bigger cause," Burnham said. "It's just a day that reminds you how good this country is when it's together like this.

"This part of the world, it doesn't half shine on a day like this. The warmth of the people comes out - the people in the race with you, the people on the sidelines."

As always, runners donned a variety of costumes in the bid to raise funds for good causes. Among them were nuns, horses and a pair of ovaries.

The Tyne Bridge is undergoing a major restoration project so large parts of it were covered in scaffolding.

The 2026 medal was designed by local artist Alex Mulholland - known as Mul - and features the Tyne Bridge.

"The design celebrates the stories behind each runner, and the incredible causes that inspire so many people to take on the event," he said.

Turkish police detain dozens in raids on gay bars and homes of LGBTQ+ activists

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 14:25:56 GMT

Police in Turkey have detained 47 people in a series of raids on gay bars and the homes of LGBTQ+ activists, officials say.

Raids took place in 12 provinces over the weekend as part of a campaign dubbed "My Family is Safe" that the Turkish government says has been designed to protect family values.

One of the targets of the operation was LGBTQ+ association Kaos GL.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised in Turkey, with growing pressure on gay couples. Human rights groups in Turkey have accused the government of using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community.

Officers detained 26 people and seized drugs, digital equipment, smuggled alcohol and a firearm during the raids, according to the Istanbul chief prosecutor's office.

In a separate statement, the Ankara chief prosecutor's office said another 21 people had been detained as part of an investigation into Kaos GL.

The organisation said 50 activists had been detained, more than 10 taken after police raids on their homes.

It said that authorities had blocked several websites and social media accounts linked to LGBTQ+ organisations.

According to the group, authorities have accused Kaos GL of making "obscenity" in online posts that are available to children and had demanded the shutting down of the Kaos GL X account, as well as those of around 15 other LGBTQ+ organisations.

Same-sex relations are not an offence in Turkey but homophobia is common, with President Recep Tayyip Erdogan describing LGBTQ people as "perverts" responsible for the falling birth rate.

As part of "My Family is Safe", Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek says legal proceedings have been started against more than 160 people and a number of organisations and companies across the country.

Gurlek did not say how many people had been taken into custody, but said the raids came in the context of the "Decade of the Family" campaign.

However, the Turkish Human Rights Association says the Turkish government has been using the campaign to target the LGBTQ+ community in recent years.

"The real name of this operation is not 'My Family is Safe'; it is state-led discrimination, politics of fear and the dismantling of civil society," the organisation said on X.

There is only a "slim chance" the government will meet its target of building 1.5 million homes in England by the next election, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has told the BBC.

"The prime minister wants us to make sure we're building council houses. He's made that absolutely, fundamentally clear," she said.

"We're seeing home starts up by 15% last year, so we are making a difference."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised "the biggest council house building programme since the post-war period" - although he has not provided details on exactly what this will entail.

BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.

Rayner's predecessor in the role, Steve Reed, last year admitted a sharp surge in construction would be needed to reach the goal - but said he expected it would just about be met once the impact of planning reforms took hold.

Analysts have said reforms introduced by Sir Keir Starmer's government should help increase construction in the long term, including changing the rules on green belt development to increase the area in which homes can be built.

But some argue that construction is being held back by factors including high house prices relative to average incomes, higher costs due to global conflict and labour shortages since Brexit.

BBC Verify has been tracking performance against the target using government data on Energy Performance Certificates (EPC). Each newly created dwelling must have an EPC by law, making it the most timely indicator of new homes being built.

Data for the 12 months to June 2026 suggested about 203,000 new homes were delivered in England that year, far short of the 300,000 needed to meet the target.

Some dentists say more young people are grinding their teeth - are you one of them?

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 05:55:19 GMT

Ella can't remember when she first started grinding her teeth at night, but she can vividly recall the excruciating jaw ache, the headaches, and being told her molars were disappearing.

"I was in so much pain," Ella says. "My face was changing shape and my teeth were at risk of breaking - I knew I had to do something about it."

The 31-year-old has bruxism, a condition which can cause regular and often intense teeth grinding, but says the treatment she's recently had has "without a doubt" changed her life.

Bruxism affects millions like Ella across the UK. Some studies suggest nearly one in four people experience the condition, although many may be unaware until symptoms appear.

According to the British Dental Association there is some anecdotal evidence that bruxism is becoming more common, but no specific figures. However, some dentists have told the BBC they are worried about the increasing number of young people they're seeing with dental problems caused by incessant gnashing.

"It is definitely on the rise," Dr Aditi Desai, president of the British Society of Dental Sleep Medicine (BSDSM), says. "And it's no surprise given that life itself nowadays can be so stressful."

Studies suggest many of us Bruxers do it because of stress - but why do our jaws carry the burden of our everyday lives? What can we do about it? And can it actually be a good thing in some cases?

Bruxism is an umbrella term which groups together four different jaw movements - clenching, grinding, bracing and thrusting.

Some people grind at night, others through the day. Some barely notice they're doing it, while others can gnash through mouthguards and wake even the deepest sleeping bed partners.

So how can you tell if you do it? Here are the signs to look out for:

Teeth grinding is also mentioned more frequently in therapy according to the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy, which says people nowadays are more aware of how their mental health impacts their body.

Psychotherapist Rahi Popat says more of his clients - particularly younger ones - say they or someone else have noticed they've been grinding their teeth, "and they can often link that to a really stressful time in their lives and realise that's when their teeth grinding either increased or even started".

Trauma and stress can put you in "fight or flight" mode, where your heart rate increases, you release adrenaline, and your muscles tense, preparing the body for an external threat, he says. And because the jaw and the nervous system are so closely linked through the major cranial nerves, our muscles are triggered and we clench and grind our teeth.

"If we do it overnight, it's a way of our bodies releasing some of the stress and tension we might have felt through the day," Popat explains.

For Ella, nocturnal teeth grinding in her sleep became a way to release tension that had built up while she was awake.

"I know it's to do with my stress levels," Ella says. "I have high functioning anxiety - you wouldn't think it if you met me.

"I'm busy, and I go out a lot to mask it."

In her 20s, she says she just "put up" with the pain. But a few years later, when her dentist told her that her teeth were at risk, Ella decided to get treatment.

Even though it's not routinely offered on the NHS, Ella decided to pay her dentist to inject Botox into her masseter muscles - the ones that control her jaw. The procedure relaxed them and reduced the tension in her face, and should last 3 to 4 months.

"Over the past few months I've been able to sleep properly," she says. "I've got so much more energy in the mornings, the pain has reduced and my face is not as square."

Dr Simon Cove, a dentist who treats both private and NHS patients, says the physical impact of grinding on our teeth can be huge.

He uses a 3D scanner to assess his patients' teeth, and can see the wear over time.

"Often people are not even aware they are doing it, but then we get to see the damage," he says. "If the teeth have been worn down to such an extent, treatment can be extremely complex and can cost thousands of pounds."

But he says such cases are relatively uncommon and can take years to develop.

While you can treat the symptoms - by wearing a mouthguard, for example - getting to the source of what's causing your teeth grinding is just as important, says dental sleep specialist, Dr Aditi Desai.

"Too often," she says, "dentists give out mouthguards without checking why it is happening."

It's vital that serious, underlying conditions like obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) are considered, she says. OSA is caused by a blocked airway, so a patient may grind their teeth to move the blockage in order to be able to breathe again.

"That's a very good example of why bruxism can keep you alive," says Prof Frank Lobbezoo, a leading researcher on the condition.

And even though bruxism has its negatives (tooth damage, sleep disruption, jaw ache, to name but a few), it's not always the "bad guy", he explains.

"Bruxism is also important for the production of saliva," Lobbezoo says. "Moving the jaw muscles activates the big salivary glands. It cleans the mouth, it protects the teeth and it's vital for digestion."

Some studies also suggest that chewing can help with cognition.

"We know this in animals, and our preliminary research is showing it in humans," he says. "By working our jaw muscles we are stimulating blood flow to the brain."

But teeth grinding can also cause chronic pain, which can have a huge impact on your daily life.

Dentist Riaz Yar, a specialist in prosthodontics, treats patients struggling with the effects of severe bruxism - worn, cracked and fractured teeth, and dental work that keeps failing. Many also arrive with chronic jaw or facial pain and report poor sleep, all of which need assessing in their own right, he says, rather than simply being blamed on the grinding.

In the past, Yar says, teeth grinding was considered simply a mechanical problem of the jaw, but now there is strong evidence that it is much more complex. It's a "biopsychosocial issue", he says, driven by the brain and nervous system and shaped by the whole person.

"We take into account their sleep patterns, their diet, their weight, the amount they exercise, what medication they might be taking and we assess for signs of sleep disorders," he says. "Many factors can contribute to a patient grinding their teeth, so addressing the condition requires a multidisciplinary approach."

How best to tackle it? These things might help:

Along with muscle-relaxing injections, Ella says she is also meditating to try to reduce her anxiety and free herself from the tension she regularly carries.

"Having treatment has transformed my life," Ella says, "now I want to try and figure out the root cause."

They lost their jobs after posting about Charlie Kirk, but some have no regrets

BBC News Sun, 13 Sep 2026 00:49:08 GMT

In September 2025, Gerald Bourguet felt he was finally living his dream life: he and his wife had bought a house with a pool, they had just welcomed a baby boy, and he was writing about professional men's basketball as his full-time job.

But all of that changed after he made a series of online posts critical of the late conservative activist Charlie Kirk hours after he was fatally shot on 10 September, while speaking on the campus of Utah Valley University.

In the posts, Bourguet described Kirk as an "evil man" and suggested he had dedicated his life to hateful causes. He also criticised Kirk's supporters saying they had not been vocal about school shootings.

"I had seen the way that people were talking about this person - kind of eulogising him and lionising him and it bothered me based on a lot of the things that he had said," Bourguet told the BBC.

Kirk, who founded Christian youth organisation Turning Point USA, was a divisive figure in US politics. For many on the political right, he was charismatic and had a unique skill in making conservative ideas appeal to young people. But for his opponents, his comments on a large swathe of issues from race to immigration, gun control and gender identity were deeply offensive.

Screenshots of Bourguet's critical posts went viral quickly. He was fired from his job, his address was exposed online, and he began receiving threatening text messages, he said. Concerned for their safety, the family fled the state with their four-month-old. They returned months later to sell the house and permanently relocated.

A year later, he says he doesn't regret what he said, but acknowledged: "My life will never be the same after this".

"At age 35, I am having to start over in a lot of respects… I wouldn't wish this on my worst enemy," Bourguet said from his new location, which the BBC agreed not to disclose.

PHNX Sports, Bourguet's former employer, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Bourguet was one of hundreds fired or disciplined over critical comments of Kirk after his death. While some of those who have lost their jobs have been reinstated or received restitution - sometimes in the millions - others like Bourguet have had to rebuild from scratch.

In the aftermath of Kirk's assassination, most people kept their feelings to themselves, or shared them with close friends.

But on polarised social media, people rushed to laud, or denounce, the controversial activist. Some called the criticisms, posted hours after his death, tasteless. But others called for swift action, arguing they were callous, mocking, and could even incite further violence.

Laura Loomer, an influential right-wing commentator with nearly 2 million followers on X, warned Kirk's critics to "prepare to have your whole future professional aspirations ruined".

The push for punishment also came from the highest levels of US government.

"When you see someone celebrating Charlie's murder, call them out," Vice-President JD Vance said days after the assassination. "And hell, call their employer," he added.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle told the BBC: "Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible."

Critics on the left said there was a difference between criticism of Kirk and celebrating his death. Some accused these conservative leaders of hypocrisy, as many had previously bemoaned the rise of "cancel culture" – where people who voice controversial opinions face severe consequences at work and socially.

"Cancel culture can be good, it's bad when it's applied in the wrong ways," Jordan Pace, a Republican member of the South Carolina House of Representatives, told the BBC. "If you are someone who celebrates political assassinations and the murder of an innocent man with two young children in a way that many people did, then yeah, that's an appropriate way for society to function, to shame those people."

Pace had previously called for defunding universities in his state if they didn't take actions against employees who made comments about Kirk. One of his posts was re-shared by US President Donald Trump.

Across the nation, some employers – private and public – acted swiftly to the pressure campaign. Reliable figures on the number of people fired or disciplined are hard to come by, but a Reuters tally last November found more than 600 instances. It is likely an under-count because not all cases received national or local press attention.

The specific actions that led to these disciplinary decisions run the gamut. In Tennessee, anthropology professor Tamar Shirinian was suspended and later fired for a Facebook comment saying "the world is better off" without Kirk.

A Delta Air Lines flight attendant was fired after posting "good riddance" in response to Kirk's killing. Office Depot supply store fired an employee for refusing to serve a customer who had wanted to print flyers for a Kirk vigil. Delta Air Lines declined to comment. Office Depot did not respond to a request for comment.

Others were disciplined even if they did not make any direct comments about Kirk or his death. Darren Michael, a theatre professor in Tennessee, was fired after he posted a screenshot of a news article from 2023, that covered Kirk's controversial speech on gun control. In the article, Kirk is quoted saying protecting citizens' rights to own guns was worth it even if it led to some gun deaths every year.

Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission fired biologist Brittney Brown after she reposted a meme that also satirised Kirk's position on gun violence in light of his own shooting.

"I was absolutely gutted," Brown said about her firing to the BBC. "It was like the entire world just completely flipped on its head in a moment."

In the year since Kirk's killing, dozens of lawsuits have been filed across the country by people fired for their comments about the activist, arguing their terminations violated their rights to free speech. The suits have led to substantial pay outs in some cases.

Brown agreed to a $485,000 (£355,000) financial settlement – about 12 times Brown's annual salary.

Darren Michael was reinstated by the Austin Peay State University and in January, the school agreed to pay him $500,000 to settle legal claims. The school did not respond to a request for comment.

In the largest settlement reviewed by the BBC, the University of Tennessee agreed to pay $1.9m to resolve a lawsuit brought by anthropologist Tamar Shirinian, over her "better off" comment. As part of the settlement, she will not be reinstated and has agreed not to reapply for future positions at the school.

Recently, an arbitrator ordered The Washington Post to rehire, with back pay, opinion journalist Karen Attiah, who was fired for her online posts that said in part she was not going to engage in "performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence".

Several other lawsuits remain pending, the BBC found.

Most of the legal actions have been pursued by employees of government institutions, or unionised workers, who have some free-speech protections.

But in the US, most private sector employees work under "at-will" contracts, which means they can be fired without reason.

Even those who have scored some victories don't see it as a win.

"All I wanted was my job back," biologist Brown said. "How much taxpayer money did they waste on this when I barely made $40,000 a year? So no, it does not feel like justice."

Shirinian told the BBC she too had wanted to return to her job but felt a legal case could be a lengthy affair.

"I took a settlement because this allows me to move on with my life," she told the BBC. "The one small regret that I have is that I will not see my day in court and justice will not be served in that way. But I think that the number of the settlement actually speaks to that anyway."

The University of Tennessee and Florida's Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

As an at-will employee at a private company, Bourguet is unlikely to prevail in a lawsuit challenging his dismissal. A year on, he said he has struggled to find work. The new state he lives in has a professional basketball team, but he believes the ordeal has made him unemployable in the small world of sports writers. Instead, he's started his own podcast, although he doubts he can earn enough through it to pay the bills.

"I have accepted that that life is over and that I need to start a new one." Leaving the country is now on the table, he said.

Despite the huge personal and professional costs, those who spoke to the BBC said after months of reflection, they did not regret their actions.

"I have a right to say what I want to say," Brown said. "They are the ones who should have the regrets, not me," she said referring to her former employer.

Shirinian apologised to the university days after her suspension. She told the BBC her comment was "an emotional outburst" that was not intended to be public and that she regretted the tone used.

"I don't regret the sentiment, however" she said, adding "the sentiment was that I am not sad. And I refuse to be made to feel like I have to be sad that someone who was so hateful was killed".

Bourguet also said he does not regret his comments although he has conflicting thoughts about its consequences.

"I don't regret that line of thinking because I think it's important to push back on things that are steeped in hatred," he said, referring to Kirk's political message.

"I don't regret what I said. I don't regret the way that I said it. I do regret the ripple effects that came from it and the way that they impacted me, my career, my family, and my son."

Drag Race co-creator warns of TV representation 'crisis' after BBC drops show

BBC News Sat, 12 Sep 2026 23:49:23 GMT

The executive producer of Drag Race has said there is a "crisis of representation" on TV, following the BBC's decision to axe the UK edition of the show.

Speaking exclusively to BBC News, Fenton Bailey said he did not believe there was a "hidden agenda" behind the decision, but feared "vulnerable communities are going to be even more vulnerable".

The move led viewers to raise concerns about the corporation's on-screen representation, after it also cancelled two LGBTQ+ dating shows.

A spokesperson for the BBC said the decision was down to "significant financial pressures", as it attempts to make £500m of savings.

Other shows being cancelled include Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank and Live at the Apollo, and more than 500 job losses have also been announced.

World of Wonder (WOW) announced future series of Drag Race UK, including a new All Stars version, will be broadcast exclusively on the company's own streamer, WOW Presents Plus.

BBC News spoke to Bailey, screenwriters, TV critics and former Drag Race contestants about the move and what it means for on-screen representation.

When Drag Race UK launched in 2019, co-creator Fenton Bailey, who was born in Portsmouth but now lives in Los Angeles, said working with the national broadcaster felt like a "very special homecoming" for his production company, WOW.

The US version of the show, created by RuPaul Charles and produced by WOW, had been on air for more than 10 years and was a runaway success, with dozens of Emmy awards and an international following.

Fans were eagerly awaiting a UK series to showcase the unique British style of drag. Now, eight series and three spin-offs later, the programme will stop broadcasting on the BBC after the current series ends.

"Even at the best of times, queer culture is vulnerable and you can't take anything for granted," Bailey told BBC News. "Just because a door opened yesterday doesn't mean it won't be slammed shut the next."

BBC News understands discussions to renew the BBC's deal with the show lasted months, with producers hopeful an agreement could be reached, but talks ultimately failed due to the scale of the savings the corporation is trying to make.

Bailey said it was a sign of the "horrible financial situations" broadcasters are currently facing.

"The team at the BBC are amazing and so passionate about the show, this is not an easy thing for any of the people I interacted with, or something they wanted to do," he added.

Drag Race UK was consistently one of BBC Three's most popular offerings, but according to Barb Audiences data, while average viewing figures for the series rose between 2022 and 2024, overall they've fallen around 15% over the past four years, against a backdrop of declining TV viewing figures across the board.

Bailey said the figures "haven't plummeted," but had instead fallen in line with other terrestrial TV shows, and said the number of viewers watching on social media had risen "because that's where the audience has gone."

Following the announcement, some viewers speculated the show could be acquired by another UK broadcaster, but Bailey suggested the show's creators may prefer to go it alone.

"We love partnerships, but in this particular moment, having the freedom to make the show the way we want may be preferable to getting into bed with another broadcaster and potentially be in the same situation a few more seasons down the road."

A BBC spokesperson said: "As the BBC continues to navigate significant financial pressures and deliver the savings required of us, we have had to make some very difficult choices, none of which have been taken lightly."

Scott Bryan, TV critic and author of Out Now: A Queer Journey Through Modern Television, says the move is indicative of just how severe the financial pressures facing broadcasters have become.

"I can imagine Drag Race is an expensive show to make," Bryan told the BBC, "I can see the pressures the BBC are under, but it's rather concerning in regards to queer storytelling.

"You see LGBTQ+ lives reflected on soaps and primetime dramas much more casually, but there still needs to be shows specifically catering to a queer audience, and it feels like very quickly the drawbridge is pulling up."

Earlier this year the BBC announced LGBTQ+ dating shows I Kissed a Boy and I Kissed a Girl were also being cancelled. The corporation said at the time that it was "exceptionally proud" of the shows, but they had to make "difficult choices in light of our funding challenges".

Author and screenwriter Juno Dawson says viewers have begun to notice a "pattern".

She said: "I think that's why perhaps eyebrows have been raised, because Drag Race hasn't been cancelled in isolation. A couple of other LGBTQ+ shows have gone as well.

"It's a shame this is happening at the BBC, because commercial channels don't necessarily have an obligation to represent all the communities in the UK, but the BBC does and it's supposed to represent all of us, including LGBTQ+ people."

The BBC recently announced Smoggie Queens, which features predominantly LGBTQ+ characters, would be renewed for a third series, and it represents the community elsewhere through storylines in shows including Mr Loverman, Amandaland, Vigil and EastEnders.

A recent report from GLAAD, an American advocacy organisation, found film representation had fallen for a third consecutive year and more than 200 LGBTQ+ TV characters would disappear from screens in 2026 because of cancellations, endings or limited-run series.

While similar figures for the UK aren't collated, Dawson fears a shrinking television industry in the UK will make it harder for commissioners to make LGBTQ+ stories.

"So many of my personal shows have gotten right up to green light, but for lots of different reasons, different commissioners - not just at the BBC - have decided to back away.

"Nobody is ever going to say to you 'it's because it was too niche', but all I can keep doing is writing television that feels true to me and represents me and my life."

While Drag Race is known for its camp humour and glamour, most episodes also tackled serious topics, with contestants opening up about everything from non-binary and trans identities to substance abuse and the realities of living with HIV.

"There's something very clever about Drag Race," Dawson said, "because you come for the sequins and the sparkles, but actually under its surface, you're dealing with really big, heavy and important topics."

Kate Butch, who competed on season five of Drag Race UK and on spin-off UK vs the World, told the BBC they fear a move away from a public service broadcaster could impact the show's ability to reach audiences with "important" messages.

"It's great the show is going to carry on and shine a spotlight on the amazing drag artistry the UK has to offer," they said, "but I do mourn the possibility of someone maybe just flicking through the channels and randomly finding it."

Butch told BBC News that the show coming off the BBC may also bring some positive changes to the programme - including the possibility of prize money and sponsorships.

"It's a lot of effort to go on Drag Race, a lot of investment and emotional labour," they added, "so I hope the audience follows and keeps supporting the queens."

Fenton Bailey says he's excited about the show's future on its own streaming platform.

"We may not have the resources that the BBC has, but the spirit of Drag and RuPaul's Drag Race is about making something out of nothing," he told the BBC.

"As a community we can survive and thrive in less than optimal conditions.

"We have. We can. We will."

Will the Thirlwall report change the debate about Lucy Letby?

BBC News Sat, 12 Sep 2026 23:15:54 GMT

Mention Lucy Letby and you're likely to get a strong reaction.

The nurse was sentenced to spend the rest of her life in prison for murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven more.

But though two juries have convicted her, and she has twice been denied permission to appeal, it seems everyone has an opinion on whether she really did it.

There's loud scepticism about her convictions from some, and vocal certainty about her guilt from others. She has become the centre of an information war.

The name Lady Justice Thirlwall, however, attracts less recognition.

She's the judge who's been tasked with examining how Letby was able to commit her crimes at the Countess of Chester Hospital in 2015-2016, and whether her managers should have responded differently when suspicions about her were raised.

After months of hearings, the findings of her inquiry will be published on Tuesday, almost a year later than originally anticipated.

So will the Thirlwall Report change the conversation about Lucy Letby? Will people who have entrenched views about her change their mind as a result?

The quick take is this. The report won't change the narrative about Letby's guilt or innocence because it didn't examine that subject at all. That wasn't its remit.

Lady Justice Thirlwall said she had "approached the inquiry on the basis that Lucy Letby is guilty of the crimes of which she has been convicted".

She emphasised that it was not her role "to set about reviewing the convictions", telling the inquiry: "The Court of Appeal has done that, with a very clear result."

But there is also a longer, more complex answer.

Whatever the report's conclusions, Letby's convictions will stand. However, the inquiry hasn't operated in a vacuum. There are other parts of the legal system which will have an eye on its findings.

And the chairwoman of the Criminal Cases Review Commission (CCRC) - the only organisation with the power to send Letby's case back to the Court of Appeal - has told the BBC the CCRC will be paying close attention to Thirlwall.

Dame Vera Baird said: "We will be looking at the report with interest to assess whether it has any bearing on our review of the case."

The CCRC has given no indication of when it will make its decision.

But while questions over Letby's convictions weren't within the scope of the Thirlwall Inquiry, it didn't stop the subject making itself felt within the hearing room.

Just as the inquiry was wrapping up, the hospital's former executives applied for it to be delayed until the CCRC has made its decision.

Letters pushing for a delay were also written to the inquiry by Letby's lawyers and Sir David Davis, an MP who has campaigned on her behalf.

Sir David argued that an inquiry "predicated on the presumption that Lucy Letby's conviction is safe, when there is now a wealth of authoritative voices questioning that conviction, will only undermine the conclusions arrived at by your inquiry and potentially lead to more babies dying unnecessarily".

Lady Justice Thirlwall refused the requests to pause the inquiry. She said that she was not scrutinising Letby's actions, but those of the officials and managers who were responsible for responding to the crisis.

The families of babies whom Letby has been convicted of murdering and attempting to murder did not want the inquiry to be paused.

Richard Scorer from Slater & Gordon Solicitors, who represents three of the families, told the BBC that the fact that Letby's convictions still stand is crucial.

"That's the legal reality," he said. "And the noise about her convictions doesn't change that."

But he added that, irrespective of Letby's convictions, "serious failures" at the hospital – and the way in which managers handled concerns as they emerged – must not be repeated elsewhere.

So, what is the Thirlwall report likely to tell us?

The most stark question it may answer is whether any babies might have lived, or avoided injury, if action had been taken earlier.

The inquiry released thousands of documents which shed new light on what was going on inside the hospital. When the hearings finished, we put together this timeline which illustrates how events unfolded.

Should alarm bells have started ringing as early as June 2015 when three babies died in quick succession – the same number of deaths within two weeks that the unit would normally expect in a year? What about in August 2015, when a baby was poisoned with insulin?

The results of his blood test didn't raise an alert. At the inquiry, hospital consultants accepted this had been a "collective failure".

Lawyers for the baby's family said the test results "provided the clearest opportunity to detect and stop Letby" and were "a bright line within the chronology after which no babies should have been harmed".

By early 2016, senior managers including medical director Ian Harvey and director of nursing Alison Kelly knew there was an unusually high death rate on the neonatal unit and that there were escalating concerns about a nurse. But it didn't lead to safeguarding action.

It was only after two triplet brothers died in June 2016 that Letby was taken off nursing duty.

After widespread concessions from managers and other witnesses, it's expected the Thirlwall Inquiry will find there was a total failure of processes to ensure patient safety at every level at the Countess of Chester Hospital.

In her report, Lady Justice Thirlwall will give her assessment of revelations including Lucy Letby's parents threatening executives, Letby failing her training assessment for lacking empathy, and the extent of her relationship with doctor Mark Deakin, who arranged for her to make visits to another hospital, despite her being under suspicion of murder.

The doctor, whom prosecutors at Letby's trial referred to as her "boyfriend", was identified for the first time this month following his death.

Thirlwall will also make recommendations for change. These could include new controls on the storage of insulin; compulsory procedures to be followed when deliberate harm is suspected; detail on the regulation of NHS managers and executives; and greater use of CCTV within neonatal units.

She will also expose the number of recommendations made by public inquiries into more than 30 previous NHS scandals, which have not been followed.

Analysis by the inquiry's legal team showed that, of more than 1,400 recommendations made by previous healthcare-related inquiries, the majority have not been clearly implemented.

Solicitor Richard Scorer refers to the failure to implement recommendations from public inquiries as "the British disease".

"It is a betrayal not just of the people who have suffered in these cases, families like those I represent, it's actually betrayal of the public," he said.

Dr Rosie Benneyworth, who gave evidence to the inquiry, also believes the report has the potential to make a difference across the NHS.

"We can't keep going on diagnosing the problem, and not making the change," said Benneyworth, who is chief executive of the Health Services Safety Investigations Body.

She said the inquiry had "a huge amount" to report on and that it needed to lead to cultural change to help keep patients safe.

Carla Duprey of Bond Turner solicitors, who represents two families at the inquiry, sees the length of time taken to produce the report as a positive sign that Lady Justice Thirlwall has left no stone unturned.

"I am optimistic that the report is going to be thorough, will raise criticisms, and will hopefully result in some real change," she said.

By making recommendations for the whole NHS, the Thirlwall report will undoubtedly aim its fire further than Chester. But what about the question we started with - will it make any difference to the conversation about Lucy Letby?

Though the former nurse is the reason behind the inquiry, she was not allowed to be part of it. Her lawyers applied for her to be represented at the hearings but were denied permission.

Her bid to overturn her convictions has been running at the same time as the inquiry but it's wholly separate to it. Her supporters have run a media campaign which included two well-publicised press conferences.

They backed her application to the CCRC which was made after a panel of experts assembled by Letby's legal team concluded "there was no medical evidence" to support the convictions.

Journalist David James Smith, who is a former CCRC Commissioner, says the commission will be paying attention to the Thirlwall report "for any evidence that supports or undermines the convictions and supports or undermines the submissions it has received on Letby's behalf".

Cheshire Police will also have a close eye on the Thirlwall report. A criminal investigation into three hospital executives is still underway. They were previously arrested on suspicion of gross negligence manslaughter, and one of them has since been rearrested on suspicion of perverting the course of justice.

It's likely that detectives will look closely at the inquiry's findings about those managers, which could be factored into their investigation.

And then there is the public debate.

As the legal wheels have been turning in the background, those campaigning to free Letby have redoubled their efforts, with protests and websites dedicated to her cause. But there are also strong feelings from those who believe she belongs in jail. Both sides have found energy online, within highly active forums on Facebook, Reddit, Tattle Life, and elsewhere.

How will Lady Justice Thirlwall's report go down with those communities?

David Wilson, emeritus professor of criminology at Birmingham City University, believes it's unlikely that the report will reverse hard-baked opinions.

"The 'noisier' Letby commentators are almost universally on the side that she is innocent," he says. "I have no doubt there will be aspects of the governance of the hospital where she killed within the report that will be harnessed to support that view."

Prof Wilson believes it will become "another component of the information war that's constantly being waged about her guilt or innocence" and he feels much of the conversation about Letby "seems to generate more heat than light".

One thing is certain. No matter what their point of view, everyone with a strong opinion about Letby will pay close attention to the report. Even those who wanted it to be delayed, or who didn't support it in the first place, will scour its findings.

But it's much less likely to take the heat out of the public debate or draw a line under the case. Those who say they're already sure about Lucy Letby may scrutinise the report, but take from it whatever supports those ready-formed views.

Best friends for decades - until a DNA test revealed they were sisters

BBC News Sat, 12 Sep 2026 22:00:28 GMT

Theirs is a story straight out of a Bollywood film.

Two Indian-born women in their 40s, adopted as babies by different families and raised near each other in the Netherlands, have now discovered they are biological sisters.

Meena Geltink and Minal Tijssen, born in the early 1980s, were adopted from two different orphanages in the western Indian city of Mumbai within months of their birth.

When they first met in their early teens at an event hosted by the adoption agency their parents had used, they were struck by the uncanny similarities in their appearance and mannerisms.

Meena, now 43, remembers the day clearly.

"All the adopted children were brought together to hang out and bond and have dinner."

Both Meena and Minal were with friends who noticed how similar they looked.

"They said, 'Look at yourselves in the mirror'.

"And I was like, 'Oh my God, she has my nose! We have the same laugh'.

"At dinner, I kept looking at her the whole time," Meena told the BBC from her home in the Netherlands.

The following day, the girls exchanged telephone numbers and addresses and promised to keep in touch.

Even though there was no indication they were related by blood, their connection was instant, and for years they wrote each other letters, often addressing each other as "Sis" because "we felt that way".

They wrote about school, friends, boys, going out and dancing. They told each other about the sports they played and discussed music, discovering they both loved Backstreet Boys.

Then 15 years ago, they lost contact. Minal had moved to France. And Meena had recently had her first child and got busy.

In 2017, Meena attended another meeting of adoptees from India where she heard about DNA testing and decided to take a test herself. But she never found any matches and earlier this year, deleted the app because her phone storage was full. Then on 20 May, Meena received a message from Minal on Facebook.

"'Remember me?' she asked.

Minal had taken a DNA test in April while visiting her parents in the Netherlands and attached a screengrab of her test result.

"I reinstalled the app. I was so nervous I entered wrong passwords 10 times before I was able to log in," Meena says.

The result couldn't have been clearer - the two women were "a 100% match".

"I had a 'full sister' which means we shared the same biological mother and father," Meena explains. "It was like I had an adrenalin shot. I cried. Minal was my missing puzzle piece I had waited so long for. We had called each other sister.

"This DNA match was the confirmation that all our intuition was right."

On a fine sunny day in August the old friends met for the first time since discovering they were sisters.

"It was amazing. It felt like homecoming," Meena, now a mother to three children, says. "For years, Minal and I had felt a big hole in our hearts. We feel like we've been completed. Everything now feels like it's supposed to be."

Reporting on their "emotional reunion", Reuters said "tears, hugs ​and laughter punctuated their ​meeting... followed by their first selfie together".

Minal, 44, who lives in France with her partner and two sons, told the agency that when her ⁠DNA results came in April, she had initially not realised her match was the same teenage girl who had clung to her when ​they first met 30 years ago.

It only sank in when she looked at her photos on social media. "'Meena: Sister.' I couldn't believe it. We were friends before we were sisters.

"We were sisters the whole time," she said, "but we didn't know."

Meena and Minal were adopted from different orphanages by two different Dutch couples.

Meena says she grew up in a small village in the Netherlands with parents who taught at a private school.

"They were also my teachers," she says. "They were very loving people, very trusting."

Her father died a few years ago, but her mother continues to live in the same village. "We talk every day. She's still my safe space," she adds.

In 2003, aged 19, Meena had visited the orphanage in Mumbai with her parents and her brother who was adopted from Goa.

They spent two weeks looking through records, trying to find out about Meena's biological parents "because for me it was important to know where I came from. But the orphanage would not reveal any details about them," she says.

Since May, Meena and Minal have been speaking every other day. They've met each other's spouses, children, brothers and parents.

"Everyone notices how we finish each other's sentences, how we move our heads or walk similar," Meena says.

The fact they are siblings is still sinking in, she says.

"Sometimes we talk for two hours and lose track of time, suddenly remembering that we have to do groceries or pick up children from school."

One thing she and her sister would "love to do", Meena says, is return to the place where it all began.

"We'd love to go to India together sometime, to walk through the streets of Mumbai together.

"There were times when we both felt very lonely, like when I lost my dad or went through a heartbreak," she says.

"I regret we couldn't be with each other - we could have shared happiness, helped each other in tough times."

Natural feedbacks will warm world an extra 20 per cent this century

New Scientist September 10, 2026

Feedbacks that cause ecosystems to emit more carbon will make the climate crisis more severe than expected, amplifying global warming by 20 to 30 per cent this century.

It isn’t just fossil fuel emissions that raise temperatures. Warming itself creates more warming. For instance, a hotter atmosphere absorbs more water vapour, which traps more heat in the atmosphere, which then holds more water vapour.

Climate models already incorporate most global feedback loops like this one, and they have started to include feedbacks that are disrupting carbon storage in particular ecosystems. But no single model includes all ecosystem feedbacks. Now, a study has shown that these natural feedbacks will heat the planet by an extra 0.2°C to 0.4°C by 2100, on top of at least 1°C to 2°C of global warming already expected between now and then.

Advertisement

Earth’s carbon sinks are being eroded by climate change feedback loops

“That suggests we’re going to go further over 1.5°C global warming than we thought, with all the extra risks that brings,” says Tim Lenton at the University of Exeter in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the new research.

Christina Schädel at Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts and her colleagues estimated the emissions from four major natural feedbacks. The first is mainly in the Arctic, in permafrost that once remained frozen year-round. As this ground thaws, microbes begin to decompose plant and animal remains that have been frozen for millennia, emitting carbon dioxide and methane.

A second feedback involves wetlands, which also release more methane as temperatures rise. This is because warmer water can hold less gas, and because microbes in the water decompose organic matter at a higher rate. The same processes lead to additional methane emissions from ponds and lakes, a third feedback.

Free newsletter

The fourth feedback kicks in as the air gets hotter, winters get shorter and soils get drier. All of this increases the frequency and intensity of wildfires, which results in greater CO2 and methane emissions.

“We need to fully account for all sources of emissions that contribute to warming, otherwise we plan for the wrong future,” says Schädel. “These emissions are left out of carbon budgets, and we adapt to the wrong targets.”

Much of this extra warming is already unavoidable, the modelling suggests. In a climate scenario in which human emissions decline after 2050, the natural feedbacks add an average of 0.4°C of warming by 2100.

The world’s biggest carbon sink may start emitting CO2 after net zero

But even in a scenario in which emissions start declining today, the feedbacks add 0.2°C of extra warming this century, prolonging global warming.

“This additional warming keeps rising through 2100… because there is a lag between when emissions occur and when the temperature impacts occur,” says Schädel.

Rather than instilling hopelessness, this should inspire governments to redouble their efforts to cut emissions, she adds. Currently, fossil fuel emissions are still increasing each year.

Earth has already heated up by almost 1.4°C compared with the pre-industrial era, and August was the joint hottest month ever observed. Unprecedented heatwaves killed at least 35,000 people in Europe and contributed to record wildfires near Bordeaux in France and Madrid in Spain. In Nepal and Tibet, a glacier collapse and flood killed more than 1300 people.

Scorching conditions this year have triggered wildfires in European countries that are normally considered to be damp and cool

A record super El Niño causing a surge of warm water across the Pacific Ocean is expected to make 2027 the hottest year ever.

The UN said last week that humanity would fail to meet the Paris Agreement goal of limiting global warming to 1.5°C. Now, it said, the world must focus on limiting this period of “overshoot” through carbon dioxide removal, which includes massive tree planting initiatives as well as the use of machines that filter CO2 from the air and interventions to boost carbon uptake by the ocean. But these approaches still face questions about their cost and environmental impacts.

The new findings mean governments will need to invest even more in measures like flood barriers, drought-resistant crops and early-warning systems for climate tipping points, says Lenton.

“The overshoot of 1.5°C may go higher than we hoped, and therefore we’ll need more adaptation action to cope with the consequences of that,” he says.

Environmental Research Letters DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/ae9e24

New Scientist September 10, 2026

What sets off labour when a baby is ready to be delivered has long been a mystery, but now it seems that the immune system pulls the trigger. The uterus appears to start contracting after immune cells transfer energy to its muscle cells via tiny tubes.

“By understanding all the steps along the road, we’re getting closer to identifying therapeutics for preventing preterm birth,” says Stephen Lye at Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto, Canada.

Childbirth for many primate species is even harder than for humans

Lye and his colleagues previously found that, towards the end of pregnancy, the human uterus releases signalling molecules called cytokines and chemokines into the bloodstream. These usher immune cells called monocytes from the blood into the uterus. The monocytes accumulate in the muscle tissue of the uterus and turn into other immune cells called macrophages.

Advertisement

In the latest study, the team investigated the role of these macrophages by incubating them with muscle cells from uterus biopsies collected from pregnant women undergoing Caesarean sections at full term. “Remarkably, we found that the macrophages made these little tube-like structures that attached to the muscle cells,” says Lye.

Even more remarkably, the researchers could see the macrophages sending mitochondria through these tiny tubes into the muscle cells. “In the images we took, you can see tons and tons of these mitochondria passing into the muscle cells,” says Lye.

Mitochondria are probably transferred to muscle cells in the uterus to give it enough energy to contract and push out the baby, says Lye. In line with this, the team found that levels of the energy-providing molecule adenosine triphosphate increased in the uterine muscle cells after the macrophages connected their mitochondria-delivering tubes to them.

Free newsletter

The influx of mitochondria also increased levels of an enzyme that breaks down progesterone. This probably signals for labour to begin, because we know a drop in this hormone turns on the genes required for labour.

“In virtually all species, in order to go into labour, you have to get rid of progesterone,” says Lye. “Most species do this by stopping the production of progesterone, but in humans, progesterone levels in the circulation don’t fall by the time of labour. So for decades, people have been saying: ‘Why is it that women actually go into labour?’” he says. The new results suggest that human labour is specifically activated by a drop of progesterone in the muscle cells of the uterus, not the whole body, he says.

The researchers hope to use their findings to develop more effective interventions for preventing preterm births, which occur before 37 weeks of gestation. Being born before this time, when organs haven’t fully developed, increases the likelihood of conditions such as cerebral palsy, learning difficulties, asthma and vision and hearing problems.

If you show signs of going into early labour, you can be given drugs called tocolytics that relax the uterus and stop contractions. However, these usually delay labour by only a few days.

A study of more than 10 million siblings suggests that firstborns are more likely to be autistic and have allergies, while conditions like migraine and shingles tend to affect their younger sibling

Lye and his colleagues have already investigated a different kind of drug called a broad-spectrum chemokine inhibitor for preventing preterm birth. This is designed to stop the initial recruitment of monocyte immune cells by the uterus that kicks off the series of events leading to labour. It blocked preterm birth in four macaques, but hasn’t yet been tested in people.

The researchers are also conducting a study looking at various immune cells in the blood of those who present with possible signs of early labour, to see if they can identify who is really at risk of delivering.

In the future, it may be possible to do a blood test to tell if someone at full term is likely to go into labour soon, says Lye. “I think all of these things will be possible if we can find a way to detect the activation of the monocytes.”

Gamma ray burst may have been two supernovae in one

New Scientist September 10, 2026

On New Year’s Day in 2022, the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory detected a massive burst of gamma rays from a distant galaxy. After four years of analysis, a group of astronomers has proposed a dramatic story for the burst of light – known as GRB 220101A – in which a collapsing star triggered the formation of both a pulsar and a black hole.

The event began, according to a team led by Remo Ruffini, an astronomer at the International Center for Relativistic Astrophysics Network in Italy, with the collapse of the core of a massive older star, which had earlier been transformed via nuclear reactions into a mix of carbon and oxygen.

When the carbon-oxygen core exploded, the researchers argue that an accelerating cloud of electrons and positrons was released in a hypothetical event that they call an “HB supernova” after the late physicist Homi Bhabha, who studied collisions of those particles. This cloud then ran into a nearby white dwarf, causing it to collapse and become a neutron star. The white dwarf’s collapse triggered a second supernova blast 3.5 seconds after the first.

Advertisement

Earliest ever supernova sheds light on the first stars

Then, this second blast hit a third nearby stellar object, another neutron star. As a consequence, the neutron star released a further dramatic burst of energy, the brightest of the entire event, before collapsing to become a black hole.

Meanwhile, fast-moving material continued to fall onto the new neutron star, causing it to spin faster and faster, until it was twirling around in a matter of milliseconds, becoming a pulsar, a star whose fast spin and magnetic field produce regular beams of light. “It’s the most complex system ever observed in astrophysics,” says Ruffini.

Other experts aren’t so sure, though.

“Ruffini et al., put forward a fascinating idea for the origin of GRB 220101A. However, as always, extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence,” says Ryan Ridden at the University of Canterbury in New Zealand. “Even with the fantastic data available for GRB 220101A, the observations don’t definitively support this novel model”, and could equally well fit a story that ends with a single black hole and no neutron star.
