Exquisite 66-million-year-old bird feather preserved in dinosaur dropping

New Scientist September 10, 2026

A bird that was eaten and partially excreted by a dinosaur 66 million years ago has left behind the best-preserved feathers ever recovered by scientists from dinosaur-age rock. This pushes the evolution of feathers, like the ones on modern birds, back by 10 million years and may tell us more about why most birds didn’t survive the post-asteroid mass extinction.

“This is the best feather we’ve ever seen in a Mesozoic [252 million to 66 million years ago] deposit,” says Jingmai O’Connor at the Field Museum in Chicago. “[It’s] like a feather you could pick up off the ground.”

These dinosaur fossils reveal that T. rex wasn’t the only king

Birds were the only dinosaurs to survive the mass extinction triggered by an asteroid strike 66 million years ago. But, puzzlingly, only one branch made it through: neornithes, the ancestors of every bird alive today.

Advertisement

In 2016, David DeMar, Jr at the University of Washington in Seattle was collecting fish fossils in north-eastern Montana’s Hell Creek Formation when he discovered a broken coprolite, a fossilised dropping, with a feather clearly visible along its fractured surface. “I couldn’t believe what I was seeing,” he says.

A few years later, he invited O’Connor to team up with him and his colleagues to analyse the coprolite using micro-CT scans and 3D surface scanning. Two leg-bone fragments, 18 and 12 millimetres long, resembled some previously found at Hell Creek and attributed to hesperornithiformes. These were flightless, short-winged diving birds, similar to modern loons (Gaviiformes) or grebes (Podicipediformes), and were related to Neornithes.

Free newsletter

Further analyses showed that the 9.3-millimetre-long primary feather had a water-repellent structure, similar to that of modern pelicans, says O’Connor. Both this and a second, smaller wing feather also had lightweight, spongy cores surrounded by a harder outer layer. This combination makes them both light and stiff, which is typical of modern feathers.

“What is exciting is to push the occurrence of modern feathers into non-modern birds,” says O’Connor. Differences in plumage are emerging as a major contributing factor as to why some birds survived while others didn’t, she says.

The team also found two fluffy body feathers with loosely arranged branches, echoing primitive feathers found in 100-million-year-old Myanmar amber in a lineage that didn’t survive the extinction event.

Combined, this suggests that the bird the feather belonged to – and hesperornithiformes in general – had a “middle ground” of primitive and modern plumage, says O’Connor. While the wing and tail feathers might have allowed for successful diving, for example, the less advanced body feathers would have been relatively poor insulators, making the animals more vulnerable to the “winter” that occurred after the asteroid impact.

“These are the feathers that are responsible for keeping the body warm, right?” says O’Connor. “So maybe these primitive feathers were good enough to keep them warm during the greenhouse world of the Mesozoic, but not good enough to keep them warm during this environmental catastrophe that was triggered by this impact event.”

Embark on an exhilarating and one-of-a-kind expedition to uncover dinosaur remains in the vast wilderness of the Gobi desert, one of the world’s most famous palaeontological hotspots.

The dropping – which probably came from a Nanotyrannus or a young Tyrannosaurus rex – also contained two rigid, diamond-shaped scales, 3 to 4 millimetres long. The researchers think this came from a gar (Lepisosteidae), a narrow-bodied fish that still exists today. This would have been too small for the dinosaur predator and thus was probably eaten by the bird.

“This discovery is really exciting,” says Frank Muzio at the University of Connecticut. “It opens up so many questions about how feathers evolved, what they were originally used for, and how they came to perform so many different functions in modern birds.”

The links among the different animals involved are also fascinating, says Muzio. “Discoveries like this really make the imagination run wild,” he says. “From a single coprolite, we are learning about at least three individual species – morphologically, ecologically and evolutionarily. What more can you ask for?”

Here is how to understand OpenAI’s major mathematical breakthrough

New Scientist September 10, 2026

One of the trickiest problems in mathematics has fallen at the hands of an advanced AI model. Following the announcement that OpenAI has resolved one tantalising aspect of the Navier-Stokes equations, researchers are now urgently trying to understand its implications.

The Navier-Stokes equations were first written down around 200 years ago and describe the behaviour of fluids. They have been instrumental in everything from building better airplane wings to creating effective artificial hearts.

Yet, our understanding of the equations is so limited that resolving a relatively simple question about them is one of the prestigious Millennium Prize Problems, where a solution means a $1 million reward. That question asks whether the Navier-Stokes equations always work or if they sometimes break down and no longer make sense.

Advertisement

“The equations themselves are so simple, but we understand so little,” says John Evans at the University of Colorado Boulder.

Terence Tao: AI companies are harming mathematics

The team at OpenAI has found that the equations do sometimes fall apart, finding situations known as “blow-ups”, where the speed of part of the fluid suddenly becomes infinity. It would be like an infinite whirlpool suddenly appearing in your bath. The OpenAI team found the answer thanks to more than 10,000 AI agents working together in different configurations. About 88 hours later, they had a solution.

“This progress happened so fast and condensed what could have been months or years of human-driven progress to a matter of days,” says Zaher Hani at the University of Michigan.

A long road led here. In 2014, Thomas Hou at the California Institute of Technology and his colleagues showed one way to create a blow-up for Euler equations, one of the stepping stones towards Navier-Stokes. However, their approach applied only when the fluid in question was walled in, and not more generally. Other teams tried to extend it, but without success. Researchers started to suspect that the Navier-Stokes equations really can blow up, but no one had definitively shown how to construct a specific fluid flow that does so.

What’s next for mathematics now that AI is upending the field?

A breakthrough came in 2021, when Luis Martínez-Zoroa at CUNEF University in Spain and Diego Córdoba at the Spanish National Research Council developed a new method for creating blow-ups that worked for both Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. Their key insight was to divide the fluid into thin layers and perform calculations for each. Adding up the layers resulted in a cascade of effects that can ultimately cause a blow-up.

“This is really the showstopper,” says Steven Brunton at the University of Washington. “AI [use] was absolutely pivotal, and the scale [of it] is interesting and useful, but the solution approach was developed by brilliant humans.”

The one problem was that Martínez-Zoroa and Córdoba’s work relied on an unrealistic force being used, which means it wouldn’t solve the Millennium problem.

Then, earlier this week, Tristan Buckmaster at New York University and Levent Alpöge at AI company Anthropic published a breakthrough removing that requirement for Euler equations and several related situations, paving a clear path to Navier-Stokes. A few hours afterwards, OpenAI published its full result. (The controversy surrounding this is described here.)

OpenAI’s agents used an approach like Martínez-Zoroa and Córdoba, working iteratively to build a blow-up. However, the AI’s trick was ultimately distinct, not just a more powerful repetition, says Evans.

The specific blow-up was a spinning whirlpool that becomes longer, thinner and more intense over time, before its swirling ultimately becomes infinite. The new proof showed that this happens in finite time and using only a finite amount of force on the fluid. “We were very surprised by the developments: both Diego and I were confident that the resolution was a matter of time, but we weren’t expecting it to be so soon,” says Martínez-Zoroa.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Evans says that it is exciting that, in the work from OpenAI, most of the key ideas the AI agents used are relatively simple ones that an undergraduate could have learned in class. “Even though it’s 166 pages of complicated math, you can actually draw it down to a couple of simpler physical mechanisms,” he says. In his view, AI agents could help make better models of fluid flow in the future.

Brunton says that the Navier-Stokes equations will continue to be useful. “Every equation is an approximation. Navier-Stokes is a great approximation for a very big range of fluids, but at the point it starts to blow up to infinity, it’s not a good model of the world anymore,” he says.

The Navier-Stokes equations model fluids as continuous entities rather than made of individual atoms, so at very small scales a different mathematical model is necessary. However, for engineers, that level of precision won’t be needed, says Brunton. “Nothing changes for us,” he says.

Nevertheless, many of his mathematician colleagues have been reaching out to him about how to fully understand the AI’s process and gain deeper mathematical insights.

Because AI proofs are coming so thick and fast, there are concerns that mathematicians will continue to get more answers to conundrums, but without sufficient explanations. “It’s not clear if we will get the same long-term benefits to the scientific process, or our mathematical understanding,” says Hani.

The world’s biggest carbon sink may start emitting CO2 after net zero

New Scientist September 10, 2026

The Southern Ocean draws down more carbon than any other single region, absorbing about 10 per cent of human emissions. But if the world reaches net-zero emissions and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentrations fall, the ocean will start releasing CO2 into the air.

This massive release of carbon will prolong global warming for centuries, even if humanity artificially removes gigantic amounts of CO2 from the atmosphere, a study has found. The results show how difficult it will be to reverse climate change, even as countries place ever-larger hopes on carbon dioxide removal.

“That impact can sustain much, much longer than we expected,” says Yechul Shin at Seoul National University in South Korea. “Let’s say we try to reduce the CO2… this sink-to-source transition in the Southern Ocean still acts as an obstacle to reduce the atmospheric CO2 concentration.”

Advertisement

One of Earth’s most vital carbon sinks is faltering. Can we save it?

The notoriously strong winds around the “roaring forties” and “furious fifties” latitudes of the southern hemisphere stir up waves and encourage the water to absorb CO2. Through exposure to the cold Antarctic air, the water cools and sinks, storing that carbon away in the deep ocean for centuries or millennia.

This carbon uptake has been increasing as humanity pumps ever more greenhouse gas into the atmosphere, creating a higher concentration of CO2 in the air than in the surface water. But if the atmospheric CO2 concentration begins falling, that ratio will flip, and the Southern Ocean will start releasing rather than absorbing CO2.

“It’s like you’re constantly pressing a piston into the ocean,” says Nicolas Gruber at ETH Zurich in Switzerland, who wasn’t involved in the study. “If you pull the piston up again, then the CO2 comes back out.”

Free newsletter

Shin and his colleagues modelled a scenario in which the world reaches net zero in 2125 and the concentration of atmospheric CO2 starts to gradually decline from 700 parts per million as Earth’s natural carbon sinks remove some of the gas from the atmosphere. They also modelled one in which humanity drastically decreases atmospheric CO2 after net zero – again reached in 2025 – through carbon dioxide removal, a range of approaches ranging from widespread tree planting to machines that filter CO2 out of the air.

In both scenarios, the Southern Ocean goes from absorbing about 3 grams of carbon per square metre per year now to emitting 8 to 9 grams of carbon per square metre by the year 2400. Under both scenarios, atmospheric CO2 is projected to fall, but this decline gradually levels off after 2200 as the Southern Ocean emits more CO2.

In the carbon-removal scenario, atmospheric CO2 actually rises again for 50 years before levelling off at 425 parts per million – roughly the current concentration. Without carbon removal, it levels off at 590 ppm.

Collapse of AMOC ocean current may already be locked in

The scenarios aren’t necessarily realistic, though. Many countries, including the UK and members of the European Union, aim to reach net zero as soon as 2050. Moreover, the amount of carbon dioxide removal remains minuscule compared with emissions, which are still increasing.

But regardless of when humanity reaches net zero, the ocean as a whole is likely to become a net source of CO2 as it begins releasing all the carbon that major sinks like the Southern Ocean stored, according to Alberto Naveira Garabato at the University of Southampton, UK.

“Anything that changes in terms of the way the ocean interacts with the atmosphere could be like adding a massive country to the world’s carbon budget,” he says.

While scientists largely expect the Southern Ocean to begin emitting CO2 at some point, the new research finds that two major feedbacks may amplify this release, says Gruber. The first is driven by the enormous amount of heat that the Southern Ocean transfers to the depths alongside the carbon. Warm water can hold less gas. So, as that stored heat gradually returns to the surface, the Southern Ocean will lose more CO2, just like a glass of warm soda loses its fizz more rapidly than a glass of cold soda.

A global survey of microplastics in oceans reveals that tiny particles of plastic are prevalent throughout the water column, which could harm marine ecosystems and affect carbon storage in the deep sea

The second feedback is essentially an increase in ocean acidification. Many of the plankton in the Southern Ocean form alkaline shells of calcium carbonate. When they die and sink, they transfer alkalinity to the deep ocean. But as the surface water warms, it will become less dense. As a result, it will mix less with cold, dense and more-alkaline deep water. With less alkalinity returning to the surface, there is less potential for the water to react with slightly acidic CO2 in a process that increases the water’s capacity to pull more CO2 from the air.

The sooner humanity reaches net zero and stops heating the Southern Ocean, the less CO2 these waters will ultimately emit, says Shin.

This month, the UN said the world will fail to meet the Paris Agreement goal of keeping global warming below 1.5°C and should instead focus on ways to reduce global temperatures later on, including through carbon removal. But the new study shows this may be harder to do than we expect, says Gruber.

“It’s like crashing a car into the wall, and then you back up the car. It’s not the same car any more,” he says. “We can’t just simply take out CO2. There are consequences, and some of these consequences are long-lasting.”

Science DOI: 10.1126/sciadv. aee9228

Normally, emissions of NOx and other air pollutants from gas power plants are controlled using catalytic converters, but most of the temporary turbines powering the Colossus 2 plant don’t have them fitted.

NOx gases can inflame the airways and exacerbate the symptoms of people already suffering from lung or heart conditions. They also react with other air pollutants to form ozone and particulate matter, both key components of urban smog.

Kevin Gauld at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his colleagues used observations from NASA’s TEMPO satellite – launched in 2023 to monitor air pollution over North America – to assess the impact of the Colossus 2 plant on local air quality.

The satellite observations show a “strong increase” in local NOx concentrations from late 2025 onwards, according to the study by Gauld’s team, which is when SpaceXAI began deploying the temporary turbines to Colossus 2.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers then used the TEMPO satellite to calculate two-week-average NOx source rates from August 2025 to mid-August 2026. They first detected NOx emissions in December 2025, and emissions increased throughout the study period. The number of turbines on the site rose during the study period, from 27 in December 2025 to 69 by August 2026.

The satellite analysis suggests that emissions averaged about 730 kilograms per hour between February and August 2026, peaking at 1180 kg per hour in August 2026. By comparison, the monthly emissions from a nearby gas power plant in Mississippi averaged just 21 kilograms per hour of NOx emissions, the paper reports.

Martyn Chipperfield at the University of Leeds in the UK, who wasn’t involved in the study, says the pollution levels observed by the satellite are significant. “The values they report in the vicinity of the [temporary turbines] are values that we have seen over central London,” he says.

Can floating data centres meet AI’s huge energy demand?

Ronald Cohen at the University of California, Berkeley, says the paper is “solid” science. “It’s very clear that there’s a huge number of uncontrolled generators on this site, generators without emissions controls on them,” he says. “There’s a lot of electricity being created, and they are putting a lot of NO2 [the most commonly regulated NOx gas] into the atmosphere.”

Peter Zoogman at Minerva University, California, who worked on the development of the TEMPO satellite, says the NOx emissions, as calculated in the paper, would mean each turbine was producing roughly the same level of emissions each year as 50,000 cars. He called for further work to quantify the health impacts of the emissions, including measuring any change in the local levels of ozone pollution since the opening of the site.

In July 2026, SpaceXAI promised to remove all 69 temporary turbines by July 2027 and replace them with 41 permanent gas turbines. The company was granted permission to construct the permanent gas turbines in March 2026 by the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality (MDEQ). SpaceXAI also promised that all of the mobile turbines it uses – which it is starting to manufacture in-house – will be fitted with pollution-control technology.

Data centres could store information in glass for thousands of years

“Making sure these converters are fitted to these power generation systems is very important,” says Zoogman. “It does make a very large difference.”

However, the satellite study concludes that the current average emissions rate from the temporary turbines is about 16 times higher than it is expected to be once the permanent turbines are installed.

Responding to queries from New Scientist, SpaceXAI sent a court submission from a third-party air-quality expert, which claims local air-quality monitoring stations haven’t observed notable increases in pollution concentrations since the mobile generators began operating. It said the emissions from the site fall within the relevant regulatory requirements.

A statement from MDEQ in response to questions from New Scientist said: “MDEQ does not comment on third-party reports or matters involved in pending litigation. MDEQ recognizes the public interest in this facility and remains committed to carrying out its responsibility to protect public health and the environment through implementation and enforcement of applicable state and federal environmental laws and regulations.”

From massive solar panels to the difficulty of staying cool – not to mention high-energy radiation – there are a lot of engineering problems that need to be solved before we can build data centres in space

The satellite analysis comes as concern grows over the rapid rollout of new gas power to run the massive new data centres that underpin the booming AI sector. US gas-fired power under development jumped by 50 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to Global Energy Monitor, an independent non-profit.

Meanwhile, almost half of the proposals for powering data centres with gas involve using gas turbines and engines. These are less efficient and more polluting than combined cycle plants – which reuse waste heat from one turbine to power another – but are quicker to deploy. Experts warn this new gas build-out will lock in decades of additional carbon emissions and worsen air quality. Many data centres also rely on diesel generators for back-up power, which emit high levels of NOx and other pollutants.

Data centres may also need close monitoring to check that the new dedicated power plants supporting the facilities are meeting regulatory requirements. “That’s why having this public attention on it is really valuable,” says Zoogman. “I think it’s important to have this technology to do the monitoring and the assessment and figure out where the pollution is coming from.”

Rapid advances in satellite technology mean they are increasingly being used to spot unreported emissions across a whole range of sectors, including oil and gas infrastructure, landfills and manufacturing facilities.

Earliest alligator flourished in the wake of the dinosaur extinction

New Scientist September 11, 2026

A 2-metre-long reptile that flourished in North American waterways shortly after an asteroid wiped out most dinosaurs 66 million years ago has been identified as the oldest known representative of the alligator group.

Scientists have uncovered bones from about 15 individuals of the previously unknown species, which probably ambush-hunted near freshwater channels and may have sheltered in burrows.

The newly named Mandrasuchus milleri looked like a smaller version of a modern alligator, with pointed front teeth for seizing prey and rounded, molar-like back teeth that could crush shellfish and other hard-bodied prey.

Advertisement

Spectacular fossil preserves internal organs of ancient marine reptile

Combined, these characteristics may help explain its success in a dying world. This success may then have paved the way for the widespread expansion of alligators, says Sadie Sherman at the Denver Museum of Nature & Science in Colorado.

“We have a bunch of these specimens, so they were quite abundant,” she says. “And so to have a large-bodied apex predator not just living, but actually thriving, so soon after such an apocalyptic event is really telling.”

The asteroid strike at the end of the Cretaceous Period led to the extinction of all non-avian dinosaurs. Crocodilians, however, fared considerably better: multiple lineages, including the “true crocodiles” and the gharials, survived. The alligatorids survived, too. They are divided into two subfamilies. The “alligatorines” include the two living species of alligator – the Chinese and American. The other subfamily is the “caimaninae”, which includes the six known species of caimans.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Freshwater habitats may have offered some protection from the devastation, giving semiaquatic crocodilians a safer refuge, while their ability to eat a wide range of foods meant they could cope when particular prey disappeared, says Sherman. “If you’re not picky, you have a much better chance of surviving an extinction event, right?”

Even so, exactly when and how the alligatorids branched off from other crocodilians, and then split into today’s variety of alligators and caimans, has remained muddy.

A team from the Denver Museum, including Sherman, may have uncovered an important piece of the puzzle. Around a decade ago, they began finding well-preserved fossils of an unknown crocodilian at Corral Bluffs, a fossil site in central Colorado. The team has since recovered hundreds of bones, teeth and bony skin plates, or osteoderms, says team member Emily Lessner.

Dinosaur found with a crocodile in its jaws named as new species

Close examination and micro-CT scans of selected fossils suggested they belonged to a crocodilian with a short, broad, alligator-like snout and pointed front teeth that gave way to bulbous back “button” teeth. “It was probably just eating anything it could get its mouth on,” Sherman says.

After looking at 330 anatomical features – including tooth numbers, skull proportions and the shapes and positions of individual bones – and comparing them with the same features in nearly 150 living and extinct crocodilians, the researchers argue that M. milleri was an alligatorine. Analyses of fossil pollen and radiometrically dated volcanic ash revealed that the oldest skulls date to a mere 350,000 years after the asteroid strike, making M. milleri the oldest known member of its subfamily.

Several M. milleri skeletons were found with bones still connected, including one inside what may have been a burrow. Burrowing could have sheltered the animals from harsh conditions after the asteroid strike, Sherman explains.

Palaeontologists have found new evidence that the early ancestors of amphibians, reptiles and mammals did not have a larval stage with external gills like modern frogs or salamanders

The name combines the Greek mandra, meaning an enclosed space or corral, in reference to Corral Bluffs, with Suchus, the Greek name for the crocodile-headed Egyptian god Sobek; milleri honours Ian Miller, who used to work at the museum, and who found many of the specimens.

“Mandrasuchus milleri provides a rare insight into how alligatorids diversified almost immediately after the end-Cretaceous extinction,” says Adam Cossette at New York Institute of Technology in Long Island. “The fossils are compelling.”

Pedro Godoy at the University of São Paulo, Brazil, agrees. “The fossils of Mandrasuchus are beautifully preserved, and that’s always exciting,” he says. “They improve our understanding of the group’s morphology and, ultimately, its evolution.”

AI is both the best and worst thing to ever happen to mathematics

New Scientist September 11, 2026

Our best equations for describing the way fluids move were first written down 200 years ago. Ever since, we have been unable to answer a simple question about them: do they sometimes blow up? This explosive phrase has a precise mathematical meaning describing a situation where, apparently out of nowhere, part of the fluid starts to move infinitely fast. It would be like an infinite whirlpool forming in your bathtub in response to a flick of your toes.

Understanding the Navier-Stokes equations – named after the pair who discovered them – has been a long-running quest for mathematicians. So much so that the blow-up question sits on the list of prestigious Millennium Prize Problems, each of which comes with a $1 million reward for solving.

This week, OpenAI stunned the world of mathematics with its announcement that its AI agents have finally found the answer: the equations do sometimes blow up. The implication isn’t that fluids will start misbehaving, but instead that the equations aren’t perfect. This is good news for your bathtub. Mathematics, however, may never be the same again.

Advertisement

Terence Tao: AI companies are harming mathematics

The reason for this isn’t the result itself. The Navier-Stokes equations have already proven themselves to be incredibly useful many times over, in applications ranging from making better airplane wings to modelling the flow of fluids through artificial hearts. Mathematicians had a suspicion that blow-ups were possible; now they know for sure.

That isn’t to underplay the discovery – it is one of the biggest mathematical breakthroughs in decades. But the way it has happened, and the resulting fallout, is what will have the most dramatic effect on mathematics for years to come.

OpenAI began working on the problem after it got wind that a pair of mathematicians had made some progress on it, which hadn’t yet been published. Researchers at the tech company decided to set thousands of AI agents on solving the problem. Just 88 hours later, they were done.

OpenAI has solved the Navier-Stokes Millennium problem using $15m of AI effort

Over the past few months, AI has made breakthrough after breakthrough in mathematics, with this most recent development being by far the most impressive. It wasn’t that long ago that mathematics was a bit of an embarrassment for AI because it was so bad at it; now it is shockingly good. How many other long-standing mathematical conundrums will fall to AI is uncertain, but it will surely be many. OpenAI has already said it has made “substantial progress” on another of the Millennium Prize Problems.

But AI proofs aren’t a straight replacement for human ones. Mathematicians want to know the why; AIs not so much.

The great mathematician Paul Erdős believed that mathematical truth exists independently of humanity in a sort of celestial book, and it is the job of mathematicians to discover what is in it. Sometimes, a mathematician would discover a logical argument that was so insightful and so elegant that it would bring a fresh understanding or a completely new way of thinking. Erdős would declare that a proof like this was “straight from The Book”. It’s fair to say that OpenAI’s effort wouldn’t make the cut.

That is because AIs tend to produce hard-to-follow, convoluted arguments. For the sake of proving a theorem, this doesn’t really matter, thanks to the magic of a process called formalisation, where proofs can be turned into code that can be rigorously checked by computers. But for the sake of gaining insight, it is lacking.

Subscriber-only newsletter

So, where does this leave mathematics? Clearly, the AI mathematical revolution has arrived. It is a new era where we will have many more answers than explanations, and unpicking it all won’t be easy. It isn’t just the Navier-Stokes equations that AI has blown up, but mathematics itself.

These are unprecedented times, and yet mathematics has gone through upheaval before. When René Descartes made the link between geometry and algebra in the 17th century, showing that shapes could be written as equations, he completely transformed the toolkit available to mathematicians.

Geometry, however, had been the darling of mathematics since the ancient Greeks. It was trusted and considered pure. Mathematicians worried that the job would make them drones who simply manipulated symbols and came up with no new insights. Philosopher Thomas Hobbes described the approach as a “scab of symbols”.

But 300 years later, it is indisputable that making this link between algebra and geometry was a good thing. Without it, there would be no calculus or relativity – in fact, modern science would be completely unrecognisable. Perhaps AI will have a similar effect.

Mathematicians now have an imperfect truth machine that spits out mathematical answers. There are big challenges ahead regarding how to use it, who gets access and what role AI companies should play, but it is a tool that has the potential to allow mathematicians to make progress much faster than before. AI may end up being the best and worst thing to have ever happened to mathematics.

How to build powerful microhabits for your wellbeing – and keep them

New Scientist September 11, 2026

Like many people, I have the intention of practising self-care. I know that meditating each day will help break me out of stressful thought spirals, but it has never become a part of my regular routine. With tight deadlines and family commitments, there just doesn’t seem to be the time.

Slow breathing can calm the mind without any need for mindfulness

A new book – Micropractice: a science-backed approach for calm, clarity and joy in 30 seconds or less by US psychologist Eli Susman – might just offer the solution to my problem. Drawing on a growing body of research, he argues that we can glean many of the benefits of mindfulness from extremely brief exercises, lasting just 30 seconds or less.

If you’re sceptical, I can understand why. I would have been, too, if I hadn’t previously written about some of Susman’s research for New Scientist. A few years ago, he investigated the benefits of a very short self-compassion meditation, which encouraged participants to “send kindness and warmth” to themselves “by bringing one hand to your belly and the other to your chest, with the energy of giving yourself a hug”. The aim, according to Susman and his colleagues, was for participants to treat themselves like they would treat a friend.

Advertisement

That was it – 20 seconds of deliberate effort to treat themselves kindly. They were then asked to practise it daily for a month. Those who followed the instructions showed considerably less stress, and better overall mental health at the follow-up compared with participants who had instead practised a short sequence of finger-tapping exercises in place of the meditation.

In his new book, Susman describes similarly optimistic results for many other lifestyle interventions. “Study after study pointed to the same overlooked pattern – one that almost no one talks about: It’s not how long you practice, but how often,” he writes. “Consistency, not duration, is what drives change. And yet, it’s rarely acknowledged.”

Consider “breathwork”, which typically revolves around slowing our inhalations and exhalations, has proven benefits for our mental health. The length of the interventions varies widely, but a large meta-analysis suggests that the duration is largely unimportant. “Although slow breathing exercises significantly reduced stress, depression, and anxiety, the size of the effects didn’t change based on how long participants practiced,” writes Susman. “Whether brief or extended, the benefits held steady, defying the typical ‘more is better’ wellness mantra.”

The same goes for stretching and yoga poses. Even a short period of bodily movement can bring enormous benefits for our mental state. As evidence, Susman points to a study of surgeons, who were asked to perform stretches for 90 seconds every 40 to 60 minutes of the working day. The minimal adjustment to their routine improved their mental focus and reduced the physical pain that normally accompanies their work.

Susman has many suggestions for the kinds of stretches you might attempt at your desk. In “seated cat-cow”, for example, you sit with both feet flat on the ground and your spine straight. As you inhale, you lift your head, draw your shoulders together and arch your back, while letting you belly soften and expand forward. On an exhale, you then allow your spine to round as your chin drops to your chest.

The sheer brevity of these exercises should make them easier to fit into our busy lives, but that is no guarantee that we will build them into our routine. Flossing our teeth, after all, takes only a couple of minutes, but many of us either forget or refuse to do it every day. For this reason, Susman has analysed the available literature on behavioural change to build a brief course on habit formation. His conclusions largely echo those of Charles Duhigg’s The Power of Habit and Katy Milkman’s How to Change – but they bear repeating.

The trick, he says, is to first find a cue that anchors the habit in a specific event. Ideally, the cue should be something conspicuous that occurs very regularly. As a coffee addict, I might practise the self-compassion meditation while I wait for my espresso to pour, for instance. I might decide to practise the seated cat-cow whenever I reach for my phone. And to relax before bed, I might choose to practice a few moments of slow breathing as soon as I’ve put my pyjamas on.

Too busy to meditate? Microdosing mindfulness has big health benefits

According to Susman, you should enhance the sense of reward by articulating why you want to change your behaviour in the first place and savouring those benefits afterwards. As you get started, you should also keep track of your progress, which can help to enhance your sense of accountability.

Most counterintuitively of all, Susman suggests allowing yourself two “emergency skip days” each week, during which you can cut yourself some slack if you fail to meet your goal. “When people give themselves permission to be human, they’re far more likely to keep going,” advises Susman. “Because what derails progress isn’t missing a day – it’s the shame spiral that follows.”

In a forthcoming study, Susman found that teaching these simple tips in a brief 15-minute video vastly increased the chances that someone would practise the self-compassion meditation over the following six months. And that, in turn, determined the size of the benefits for their mental health.

Susman’s argument is strong enough that I have started incorporating a few of these suggestions into my life, and I am already appreciating the moments of calm that they bring. I can only hope that this continues in my most hectic periods, too.

“At first, micropractices might just feel like something you do,” writes Susman. With time, however, “it stops feeling separate from your life and starts becoming the way you move through it”.

David Robson’s latest book is The Laws of Connection: 13 social strategies that will transform your life. If you have a question that you would like answered in his column, please send him a message at davidrobson. me/contact

Country Life: Would you drink milk from a vending machine?

New Zealand Herald September 13, 2026

Tammy Acton-Adams runs The Good Cow with her husband, Andrew McKenzie. Photo / RNZ, Anisha Satya

By Anisha Satya of RNZ

When it comes to milk, Tammy Acton-Adams is pretty particular.

“There are certain brands, and very popular brands, that we just don’t even buy,” she told RNZ’s Country Life.

“If we’re away and we need milk, we won’t even try them.”

It needs to be creamy, but not so creamy it’s no longer milk.

Lucky for her, that’s exactly the stuff she’s milking from her small herd of dairy cows.

Acton-Adams shares the taste of raw milk with her community through The Good Cow, a 24/7 milk vending station on her North Canterbury farm near the Ashley River.

“Nothing’s taken away. It’s got all the goodies,” she said.

“It’s got all the vitamins, all the minerals, prebiotics, probiotics. Everything’s in there. It’s 4.8% fat.

“And the taste is unbelievable; it’s very rich. Even in your coffee, you can tell; it just makes it that wee bit creamier.”

The beef, calving and contracting farmer first tried her hand at dairying to help out a former client.

“We had baled their hay for 20 years.

“Their grandson needed help, so he asked us to come over one afternoon to help milk the cows.

“I hadn’t been in a cow shed since I was 15 – within 10 days he had gone, and so they asked us to take over.”

Four years milking 120 cows – a sixth-generation Friesian pedigree herd – taught Acton-Adams a lot about the business.

“When we finished farming [there], we had two cows left over.

“And we just thought, you know – we loved the taste of the milk.

“We just didn’t like the idea of going back to supermarket milk.”

Enter The Good Cow – a raw milk business supplied by Acton-Adams’ 35-strong, mostly Friesian herd, which sells its milk on the farm.

Cows are milked in a 9-aside herringbone shed.

Just a few steps beyond the shed, the milk is stored in small vats and transferred to a vending machine.

Customers bring their empty milk bottles and pay $3.50 a litre for the unpasteurised milk.

As Acton-Adams’ cows are all high producers, she also supplies some milk to Fonterra.

The Good Cow’s raw milk gets tested every 10 days to meet MPI standards for cell count and pathogens, like E. coli.

“For raw milk, your [cell count] has to be under 160, not allowed to sell anything over 320.

“We’re quite lucky, we’ve got a good herd, and so it sits around that 60.”

There are machine cleanliness standards and other requirements Acton-Adams has to meet to ensure the milk is safe for selling – but it’s worth it to her.

“Other people do it for health reasons, and they’re very passionate about the fact that it hasn’t been pasteurised.

“Our passion is the taste.”

A coroner has issued a “critical” warning about the life-threatening effects of excessive alcohol consumption after a 20-year-old Otago University student died after becoming heavily intoxicated at a party in 2023.

Associate Coroner Emma Van Son ruled that the first-year student died from asphyxia after aspirating gastric contents while unconscious.

Toxicology results showed a blood alcohol level of 319 milligrams per 100 millilitres, more than six times New Zealand’s legal driving limit for adults.

Contact our Christchurch newsroom.

In her findings, Associate Coroner Van Son described the death as “senseless” and a “woeful illustration of the prevalent youth drinking culture in New Zealand”, warning that unconscious drinkers should never be left to “sleep it off” and should instead receive immediate medical attention.

“It is critical that young drinkers, particularly, appreciate the seriousness of the dangers of binge drinking, and know what to do if someone becomes unresponsive after drinking,” she said.

The student – whose name has been permanently suppressed – attended a birthday celebration at a Dunedin flat on September 30, 2023, arriving about 6.40pm.

He went on to consume an unknown quantity of alcohol before becoming heavily intoxicated.

Associate Coroner Van Son heard that the 20-year-old was later found passed out and “pretty much unresponsive” in the kitchen. He then started vomiting.

They decided to carry him to a bedroom and put him to bed. He continued to throw up, and one of the young people present checked for a pulse in his throat.

It was unclear from the evidence whether the student was left alone or whether someone remained with him.

A witness described “a big group of people” clearing vomit from the student’s throat before he became pulseless and blue in the face.

Emergency services were contacted at about 11.25pm. The student was carried into the hallway of the flat and was described as looking very pale. His face was starting to turn purple; he was not breathing, and CPR was commenced by partygoers before being continued by paramedics.

Despite extensive efforts to revive him, he was pronounced dead at 12.16am on October 1, 2023.

Following a post-mortem examination, a pathologist found the student’s death was consistent with asphyxia due to the aspiration of gastric contents while intoxicated.

The pathologist advised that “the key mechanism in alcohol related aspiration deaths is depressed consciousness and blunted protective airway reflexes (cough and gag reflex) from intoxication”.

“This allows vomitus to enter the airway rather than be expelled or swallowed normally,” he said.

Ambulance staff described finding “large chunks” of food in the student’s upper airways.

The inhalation of vomit was also confirmed during the post-mortem examination, which found vomit in the student’s trachea, bronchi and bronchioles.

A toxicologist told the coroner that alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that exerts its effects in a manner similar to general anaesthetics.

Where alcohol is concerned, there is a “fine line” between anaesthesia and death, the toxicologist advised, warning that if a person becomes unconscious as a result of heavy alcohol consumption, there is always a risk that the person could die.

“Fatalities are more commonly attributed to alcohol when the post-mortem blood alcohol concentrations are in the range from 300 to 500 milligrams per 100 millilitres,” the toxicologist said.

Witnesses told the voroner it was unusual for the student to “get that drunk”.

While there was no evidence of the type or quantity of alcohol consumed, nor the period over which he drank, Associate Coroner Van Son said it was obvious from the toxicology results that he had consumed a very significant quantity of alcohol before his death.

Police found no suspicious circumstances and no evidence to indicate the involvement of any other person in the student’s death.

“The student’s death was the tragic consequence of excessive alcohol consumption by a young person,” Associate Coroner Van Son said.

“His death was senseless and is a woeful illustration of the prevalent youth drinking culture in New Zealand.

“Sadly, the student’s death is not an isolated incident.”

The University of Otago today welcomed and endorsed the coroner’s recommendations and comments.

“Our thoughts remain with our student’s family, whānau and friends following this tragic loss,” a spokeswoman said.

“The safety and wellbeing of our students remain our top priorities, and we will continue to communicate regularly with students about responsible consumption of alcohol.

“As well as proactive communications, the University has a range of services available dedicated to supporting students’ safety, health and wellbeing, including clinicians with specialist drug and alcohol harm expertise.”

Associate Coroner Van Son said she hoped greater public awareness of the risks associated with binge drinking would reduce the chance of similar deaths.

“At very high levels, alcohol can cause a person to become unconscious,” she said.

“As a result, that person has less control of breathing and is in danger of their airway becoming blocked, particularly if they vomit and aspirate on their gastric contents.

“While your first instinct may be to let a friend who has passed out ‘sleep it off’, it is important to know that things can go from bad to worse quickly when someone drinks enough to lose consciousness.”

Coroner Van Son said visible signs of acute alcohol intoxication included confusion, vomiting, seizures, blue-looking or pale skin, being unco-ordinated and stumbling, passing out and being unable to be woken, and slow or irregular breathing.

“If a person becomes unconscious due to the effects of alcohol, the safest first aid treatment is to call for an ambulance and let properly trained medical professionals assess that person,” she urged.

She also highlighted advice from Hato Hone St John Ambulance and Health New Zealand.

“Do not leave them alone. Treat this as an emergency. Call 111. You will not get into trouble for taking action,” she assured.

The coroner imposed suppression orders prohibiting the publication of the student’s name at the request of his family.

“The Coroner’s Court is a therapeutic jurisdiction, which strives to operate in a people-centric manner,” she said.

“For those closest to the deceased, the matters the court deals with will often be some of the most traumatic and difficult periods in their lives.”

She said publicity surrounding a loved one’s death, sometimes years after the event, had the potential to have “a retraumatising effect”.

The family had highlighted the significant impact the student’s death had had, and continued to have, on them.

Associate Coroner Van Son said “there is a real and appreciable risk that the publication of the student’s name would cause harm” to one family member in particular.

She extended her “deepest condolences” to the student’s family, friends and loved ones for their “very sad loss”.

The coroner’s findings came soon after the release of Stats NZ data showing alcohol consumption per capita has fallen to 5.98 litres of pure alcohol, down roughly a third since 2011, with New Zealand’s consumption now among the lowest OECD countries.

Vanuatu ferry disaster: ‘It’s a miracle anyone survived,’ rescuer says

New Zealand Herald September 13, 2026

Tui's Shipping owns the MV Matui. Photo / Facebook

By RNZ Pacific Reporters

An Australian pilot who helped locate survivors after a ferry disaster in Vanuatu says “it is a miracle anyone survived”.

The MV Matui sank in rough seas on Friday morning, and more than 30 people remain missing.

The ferry departed from Santo at 6am on Friday for Ambae, about 96km away. However, it capsized in large waves. Luganville MP Matai Seremaiah said the vessel sank around 9.30am.

Tragically, confusion around the vessel’s status, and misinformation, meant that it was over 30 hours before help arrived. Reports suggest 15 people survived the sinking.

Although the current confirmed death toll stands at two, more than 30 people remain missing. One body was recovered over the weekend but another could not be brought back due to bad weather.

Mark Turnbull, a pilot and doctor based on Gaua Island, in Torba Province, was one of the first people in the air looking for survivors. Turnbull said he was contacted by an individual to help start the search..

“The government is pretty slow, even the shipowner was very slow, but there was one individual who was particularly motivated to help,” he said.

“The weather was rough and it wasn’t possible for very small boats to go out, and so they had to send fairly substantial-looking ‘smallish’ ships.”

Turnbull would conduct an aerial search, return to refuel, and then resume the search.

From the air, he was able to see debris and objects floating, which had obviously come out of the vessel.

“We saw drums of fuel, we saw flotation stuff, lots of these lifejackets that had been separated from the people somehow, then this big tank they were hanging on to, and some wheels [and] inner tubes some people had been holding on to as well.”

He told RNZ Pacific about the “big black tank”, a 1000-litre agricultural tank that had fallen off the ferry.

Turnbull said that a group of survivors told him that they had been clinging to the tank, and during the first night five people had died. Apparently, the second day they were in the water, the survivors let go of the tank and went separate ways to seek rescue.

The survivors Turnbull spoke to were weak and extremely dehydrated from their ordeal. Almost all of them had swollen eyes from exposure. One of the survivors had very swollen lips and had been attacked by fish; “he was feeling wounded and weak”.

Turnbull said that one of the survivors had swum from where the ferry sank to Santo to raise the alarm that the vessel had sunk. Until then, it was believed that it was merely adrift. This raised the urgency level of search and rescue efforts.

He said that the terrible weather conditions would have made survival in the water very difficult.

“It was a dire situation, terrible weather, hard to do search and rescue because the wind was so horrific, up to 30 knots and sometimes gusting to even higher than that.”

After talking to survivors, Turnbull said that the vessel was probably hit broadside by a large wave.

This had happened very suddenly, so there was no time to evacuate properly before the passengers and crew found themselves in the water – without proper survival gear.

He said without a working liferaft, people were scrambling for “little bits and pieces” to hold on to to stay afloat.

“It’s amazing that anybody survived that, for them to travel such a long distance was incredible, it was truly incredible, the distance they travelled was massive, it was huge.

“Those conditions through the night, with the waves pounding at them, it’s really amazing that anybody survived.”

Turnbull said he hopes this will be a turning point for search and rescue procedures in Vanuatu because the initial effort to locate and rescue survivors in this instance was very poorly co-ordinated. Private citizens had to step forward and co-ordinate the rescue attempts before official rescue efforts were organised.

“I hope this is an opportunity for the leadership of that area of maritime search and rescue. That they will come up with a much more co-ordinated plan. We were not sure exactly who reported the ferry’s GPS coordinates, as things were poorly organised.”

Turnbull, who operates the Wings of Hope Flying Doctor Service, said most of the search and rescues have since been called off, but he was aware of some still happening.

The City Rail Link feels like Auckland’s version of the new Christchurch stadium and will make things “much more dynamic” and bolster public transport by 50%, the Prime Minister says.

Christopher Luxon has told Newstalk ZB’s Mike Hosking Breakfast that it was expected the CRL would boost rail patronage by 50% on top of existing travellers, though he didn’t have a timeframe.

Luxon was at Ōrākei station on the weekend, and met people coming from “all over the place” including a group of seniors doing a CRL ale tour. Other passengers told him it would save 15 minutes on their travel time each morning.

“It’s a real opportunity now. Look, yep, it took 10 years, it’s probably cost more than it should have. Now we’ve got to make the thing work.”

International cities showed that a big piece of infrastructure like the CRL meant more apartments and more businesses, he said.

The CRL opened to passengers on Sunday, with National pledging a new Auckland transport police team if re-elected in November, to keep train, bus and ferry passengers safe.

While the launch of the long-awaited underground rail network dominated weekend headlines, parties have continued to release other election promises.

Labour yesterday revealed its KiwiSaver policy, pledging to make employer contributions compulsory even if employees pause or reduce their own contributions. It would also lift the rate to 6% by 2032 if re-elected in November, and ban new total remuneration contracts which include KiwiSaver contributions in salaries.

New Zealand First announced a raft of immigration policies it will take to the election, including more powers to deport criminal non-citizens, making it harder to become a New Zealand citizen, and holding a referendum on capping resident visas at 20,000. The party also would demand the immigration portfolio if re-elected to Government.

Luxon this morning dismissed NZ First’s new hardline immigration platform, saying New Zealand didn’t have an immigration problem, with net migration dropping from 65,000 to 25,000.

And he agreed with Hosking’s assertion that NZ First leader Winston Peters was “playing the Hanson-Farage card” - referring to Australia’s Pauline Hanson and the UK’s Nigel Farage.

New Zealand was different to other countries because immigration was strongly linked to employment and economic conditions, he said.

“It’s a dynamic system, but it is smart and it is fair and it is linked to our economics and also to infrastructure. And if you do that, then that’s good.

“It’s when you end up in situations like the US, UK, Germany, France even, where you’ve actually got massive influx of illegal immigration, which we don’t have, and that’s not linked to infrastructure or public services and causes massive resentment and becomes an issue.”

Meanwhile, Act has unveiled its election list, ranking former broadcaster Paul Henry in the fourth spot after party leader David Seymour, deputy Nicole McKee, and Biosecurity Minister Andrew Hoggard. That puts Henry ahead of Children’s Minister Karen Chhour and MP Todd Stephenson.

Last week’s Herald-Motu Research Poll of Polls put Act on 7.5%, which would give the party nine seats, down from the 11 it currently holds.

The model – which runs thousands of simulations based on recent polls – has National on 30.3%, Labour on 27.9%, New Zealand First on 11.8%, the Greens on 11.1%, the Opportunity Party on 8.1%, Act on 7.5%, and Te Pāti Māori on 2.2%.

If Te Pāti Māori were to win one seat and there was no overhang, that would see a hung Parliament of 60 seats each.

Petone Beach’s leopard seal dies

New Zealand Herald September 13, 2026

A leopard seal on Petone Beach garners keen public interest. Photo / Sam McGee

By RNZ

A leopard seal which drew hundreds of spectators has died, a Hutt City councillor says.

The female leopard seal was spotted two weeks ago lounging on Petone Beach, with some concerns that members of the public were harassing the animal.

Councillor Brady Dyer said the seal died on Sunday night, and will be removed by the Department of Conservation (DoC) today.

Conservationists echoed the news on social media, saying they suspected the seal looked unwell.

DoC has been approached for comment. Staff had previously expected the seal to return to the water when it was ready.

“[In] the last few years, this is probably the third one that I’ve seen. We had a massive, huge leopard seal in Oriental Parade by the boat sheds for a time,” DoC ranger Melody McLaughlin told RNZ a week ago.

“He’s perfectly happy having the snooze on the beach here, and he will go when he’s good and ready to go back into the water.”

‘An error of judgement’: Pro Ref admits mistake in awarding Haaland’s derby winner

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 21:31:19 GMT

Officiating body announces it will review the incident

Unhappy Carrick says error was ‘as obvious as it gets’

Pro Ref admitted Erling Haaland’s winner in Sunday’s Manchester derby should not have been awarded, after the video assistant referee ruled Enzo Fernández was not interfering with play in the buildup. The elite officiating body will review the decision and has contacted Manchester United.

Haaland’s 60th minute strike for Manchester City at Old Trafford was initially ruled offside before the VAR’s intervention. It came after Josko Gvardiol’s cross hit Patrick Dorgu’s boot, passed Fernández and the United defender Lisandro Martínez, and was finished by the City No 9. VAR decided Fernández was not interfering despite Martínez marking the midfielder.

A Pro Ref statement said: “Following the incident in the 60th minute of Sunday’s Premier League fixture between Manchester United and Manchester City at Old Trafford, we can provide clarification regarding Erling Haaland’s awarded goal.

“The on-field decision was offside against Haaland – that was checked by VAR and he was found to be in an onside position.

“In the same attack, it was established that Fernández did not play the ball and therefore that makes any offside offence subjective, however, on this occasion, the VAR did not recognise the likely impact of his position and should have recommended an on-field review.

“Contact has been made with Manchester United this evening to acknowledge what we deem is an error of judgement. A review of the incident will take place.”

After the match but before the Pro Ref statement, an unhappy Michael Carrick expressed concern over Haaland’s winner.

“At the time I hadn’t totally seen it. But the explanation I got was he wasn’t interfering with play, so I just don’t get it,” the United manager said. “I can’t understand how they’re trying to help referees and putting so many layers behind them with so many people, screens, and so many whatever offices to try and come up with the right decisions.

“If that’s how the rules are interpreted, that you’re not interfering with play because you’ve thrown yourself at the ball six yards from goal and pretty much nearly touched it, which then Lisandro has to react from – it’s worrying if that’s really how the game’s seen by those who are officiating it.”

Carrick was asked if an apology from Pro Ref would be welcome. “Yeah, that’d be great, that. Yeah, I can’t wait for that one,” he said. “I don’t really know how you go and get another explanation on that one. I think we all understand what that rule means [regarding interfering with play], and it’s pretty obvious. It’s as obvious as it gets.”

Enzo Maresca, though, was adamant that Fernández was not interfering. “Yeah – and the fourth official said Erling is onside,” the City manager said.

The 199th Manchester derby’s other controversial decision was Phil Foden’s 23rd-minute red card. The forward kicked Bruno Fernandes in the stomach, but only after United’s captain had kicked him. Maresca backed Michael Oliver’s red card but suggested the referee should also have sent off Fernandes.

“Phil Foden red card is a red card, but I also think it is red card from Bruno,” City’s manager said. “Reviewing the action, it is a clear red card for Phil because it is a reaction but you can also see Bruno’s [action].”

Carrick was asked about the pre-game protest against the club’s move to eradicate ticket touts that some believe to be draconian. United said on Friday that 685 accounts had been subject to a ban and 464 supporters had received a reduced sanction or final warning.

‘Sweat the asset’: new development minister plots path to make UK aid count

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 21:30:14 GMT

Kirsty McNeill reaffirms Labour’s 0.7% of GDP pledge and promises value for money to allay voter concerns

The development minister, Kirsty McNeill, has declared herself “a huge believer in aid”, as she reaffirmed Labour’s manifesto pledge to return to a target of 0.7% of national income spending.

McNeill, a former adviser to Gordon Brown and senior executive at Save the Children, declined to give any timetable, repeating the formula that the government would work towards the target “when fiscal circumstances allow”.

But she made a full-throated argument for the benefits of aid – as well as promising to build new “agile partnerships” to work on development challenges.

“I’m a huge believer in aid; I’m a huge believer in the quality of British aid, and when you have more of it, you can have more impact. And I think it’s important that colleagues hear that underscored,” she said.

Repeating the manifesto pledge that Labour made before the 2024 general election to return to 0.7% – instead slashing aid the next year – McNeill insisted that in the Burnham government, “everyone from the prime minister down is a believer in the spirit that animated that manifesto”.

McNeill will be setting out her priorities in a speech to charities and campaigners at the New Economics Foundation thinktank on Monday.

She will announce that the government is making up to £15m available via its humanitarian crisis fund to support preventive action in countries most at risk from El Niño.

“It will just do very practical things like vaccinate livestock and get cash to farmers to provide supplies,” she said. The UN has warned that the climate phenomenon is likely to be the most severe in 1,000 years, exacerbating risks of wildfires and flooding.

The 0.7% aid target was adopted by the Blair government and became a cross-party consensus, until it was set aside by Rishi Sunak in the depths of the Covid pandemic, as the government rapidly stepped up domestic spending.

Charities have warned that Labour’s more recent aid cuts, taking spending to 0.3% of national income, are causing sharp reductions in bilateral UK support to some of the world’s poorest countries. McNeill’s predecessor, Jenny Chapman, took the job after Anneliese Dodds quit over the scale of the cuts.

At the time of Starmer’s decision, some Labour strategists were concerned about what they perceived as the unpopularity of aid spending among voters. But McNeill said Labour should not be afraid to make a straightforward argument for development.

“As we’ve lost our confidence, we started trying to make lots of different arguments for development that go beyond what I believe to be the core one, which is, if you have the capability to save people’s lives and to change people’s lives, you should deploy that capability ambitiously,” she said.

“I think aid is a really good instrument to save children’s lives. And the impacts of British aid, through immunisation, or by feeding children who would otherwise starve, is one that in every conversation with the public I’ve had, whether it’s with a constituent on the doorstep or in my previous job at Save the Children, when you’re saying, ‘Do you think if we can do that, we should do that?’ people say: ‘Yes, we should.’”

Voters’ concerns are more about the value for money and effectiveness of aid spending, she said, promising to “sweat the asset” when it came to getting the best out of the current straitened resources.

She said she saw her role as bringing all the expertise and leverage of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) to bear on what she called the “five securities” – “health security, climate security, food security, human security and economic security”.

“The focus on securities is an attempt to recast my job as being about global cooperation and how we get security through solidarity,” she added.

“That will mean pressing for reform of some of the international bodies that spend UK aid, as well as forming ‘bespoke partnerships’, to work on specific issues.”

A veteran of the Make Poverty History campaign in the mid-2000s, McNeill contrasted this approach with that of the Blair government, which used the UK chairing of the G8 group of industrialised countries in 2005 to secure significant debt relief for developing countries.

“Many of us came of age at a time when there were summits with big announcements, and a cheque from the UK government, and actually the thing that I want to be held to account for is have I done the grind, the diplomatic grind, to get the maximum we can out of our relationships?”

McNeill has been the MP for Midlothian, south of Edinburgh, since 2024, winning the constituency from the Scottish National party.

Her boss, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has signalled that he wants development to be a more prominent focus of the FCDO’s work, including by directly taking up the UK’s seat on the World Bank board.

“The foreign secretary’s been very clear that both development and climate are going to be at the heart of British policy: they’re not an addition, they’re right at the beating heart, which I’m obviously absolutely delighted about,” she said.

Andy Burnham to host entrepreneurs and local mayors at No 10 on Monday

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 21:30:13 GMT

Prime minister vows to ‘reindustrialise Britain’ through new partnership with business

The prime minister is to host business leaders, entrepreneurs and local mayors at Downing Street on Monday to pitch his government as a “partner for growth” that can offer a stable platform for investment and jobs in the UK.

Ahead of the event, Andy Burnham said the country had “everything it needs to succeed”, including talented people and world-class universities, but requires “a culture shift in how Britain does business” if it is to unlock its full potential.

The new prime minister vowed to “reindustrialise Britain” through a new partnership with business. “That means putting government firmly on the side of the people who take risks, start companies, create jobs and bring new ideas to life,” he said.

“It means ensuring ambition is rewarded, making it easier to start and grow a business and giving people the confidence that if they have a great idea, they’ll get all the support they need to bring it to life.”

Burnham will host a roundtable with entrepreneurs – including the founders of Octopus Energy, Revolut and Starling Bank and quantum computing companies including Oxford Quantum Circuits – before welcoming chief executives from some of Britain’s largest businesses for a reception in No 10 along with regional mayors.

They include the bosses of financial companies HSBC, Aviva and Standard Chartered, supermarkets Morrisons and Sainsbury’s, telecoms groups BT and Vodafone, oil companies BP and Shell and manufacturers Rolls-Royce and BAE Systems.

Monday’s round of meetings come as Burnham and John Healey, the chancellor, prepare for their first budget on 28 October.

Burnham has vowed to deliver growth across the country and to devolve power and resources away from Westminster to do so. But Healey faces a tough task, presenting his budget amid rising borrowing costs and the impact of the Iran war on the global economy.

Although the economy unexpectedly grew by 0.4% in July, boosted by AI and cloud computing, economists have warned rising energy costs may have held back growth in August and September.

Suren Thiru, chief economist for the Institute of Chartered Accountants England and Wales, said the chancellor could be left with a “budget headache” if economic growth starts to dwindle, as more muted growth and surging borrowing costs erode his fiscal headroom, raising the prospect of further tax rises.

Both Burnham and Healey have stressed their commitment to the fiscal rules laid down by former chancellor Rachel Reeves, which require day-to-day spending to be covered by taxes and government debt to fall as a share of the economy by 2029/30. They are also bound by Labour’s manifesto commitment not to raise income tax, national insurance or VAT.

In his first major speech as chancellor last week, Healey said boosting economic growth would be his defining mission as chancellor but also warned Labour had to “be honest” about the need to control public spending at next month’s budget.

He talked of putting more power and resources into the hands of local leaders, reducing the cost of doing business and using public investment to attract private capital.

Apocalypse review – the stupidity of these people will make you scream yourself hoarse

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 21:15:13 GMT

This ‘radical social experiment’, in which 14 strangers have to see if they could survive the end times, will make you fear for the future of both TV and humanity

I have always assumed that my main use in the event of an apocalypse would be as protein. Ideally, I’d have a few weeks of peace first, eating whatever was in my now defunct fridge and reading a few last books, before tough, athletic, practically skilled survivors found me and chopped me up for parts. I’ve always been aware that I am built for mod cons, not dystopia.

But the new Channel 4 reality show – sorry, “radical social experiment” (give it UP, Channel 4, you’re racing as fast to the bottom as every other broadcaster) – Apocalypse has made me rethink my chances. All I need to do, I now realise, is find an Australian cattle farmer and I’m golden.

To explain: 14 people are split into rival camps (East and West). Two teams of seven comprising two or three TV archetypes apiece – each team unaware of the other’s existence – have been plonked in a 1,000-acre abandoned town deep in rural Indiana that is now used only by the US military for urban warfare practice. There they must survive for 28 days and eight episodes using only what they can scavenge or create from what they find. According to the surrounding publicity, the participants received three days’ training for how to do so before they were turned loose. This is not mentioned in the programme itself. Probably because no one would believe it.

For the first hour the teams do almost nothing but stand, sit or lie around, unless you count choosing the two biggest, draughtiest buildings available in which to make their base camps. Can they rebuild society from scratch, asks the voiceover. To which the short and honest answer from the available evidence is – no, mate.

At least 13 of them seem to be pretty useless. Two of the women in the West team are immediately at each other’s throats, alternately scoffing and raging about “setting boundaries” and being “disrespected” instead of “gathering firewood” or “finding tins”. The next day, a pair of Westerners find the town’s massive supermarket. But it’s boarded up. Oh well. They go back to base, where the emergent leader – Welsh sheep farmer Ioan – suggests they tidy up the place rather than go back to the big building that likely contains plentiful supplies of food and other vital items and see if they can break in. For absolutely unfathomable reasons, the famished team complies.

In the East, content creator Steven is insisting that nobody so much as scratches their arse without a collective decision to do so. Psychologist Kiera (“I’m a bit of a princess. I own it”) lets Steven go to the toilet before her to do a poo, which is among the top three stupidest things you can do even with modern plumbing – and these guys have a bucket. “We’re fucked on quite a few fronts,” says theatre director Bertie, not inaccurately. Bertie cries a lot, which is heart-rending but not an awful lot of use.

The only thing that is a bit of use involves Scott, the aforementioned Australian cattle farmer. When Steven insists that their first move should be foraging in the forest, Scott calls him “as much use as tits on a bull” and heads off to raid buildings, taking Bertie – who is enjoying a brief dry-eyed period – with him. They find the supermarket, break in and return with food while the foragers are still peering at berries and trying to decide which ones look most like a McDonald’s. Scott institutes immediate rationing of the food (“I want rice!” “No”) until they all decide – I don’t know … that the Spam tins are like the magic porridge pot in the fairytale? That the emptied supermarket will be refilled by producers overnight? – and demolish most of it. They leave just enough for the Westerners to swing by the next day and steal it, because the two people left to guard it do not guard it.

The stupidity that dominates the opening episodes is deeply boring. You can only scream for so long before you give up, especially as you know they are not in any true danger of starving to death. Things get more interesting by the third episode (only three were available for review) as a group’s engineer starts cobbling helpful machines together from the junkyard, someone finds a hunting rifle and Nigerian-born politician Celia turns out to be God’s forthright gift to television (“Men think with their dicks. Women think with their brains. So do not ever think men are making the best decisions.”)

But, fundamentally, the venality and impenetrable individualism that mean no one is willing to concede to an expert, prioritise sensibly or follow orders, and which thus hamper every endeavour, is depressing. I fear for the future – of programming mostly but, sure, humanity too.

Apocalypse is on Channel 4 now

Caleb Williams threw for 269 yards and two touchdowns and ran for 65 yards and two more scores as the Chicago Bears defeated the Carolina Panthers in the highest-scoring season opener in NFL history. Chicago and Carolina scored eight more points than the previous record of 88 set in Tampa Bay’s 48-40 win over New Orleans in 2018. Coach Ben Johnson’s prolific Bears also broke a franchise record for points in an opener, a mark that had stood since 1948, when Chicago hung 45 points on Green Bay at Wrigley Field. The Texans led 31-30 when Allen split two defenders to find Palmer. The two-point conversion failed.
