Arteta embraces perfect storm to play the victim in game of his own making

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 20:35:23 GMT

Refereeing is now an impossible job owing to the culture of micro-analysis the Arsenal manager has helped to create

A gentleman is never rude unintentionally, only by design. Nobody really knows who said this first. But it could easily be a line from the Elite Football Manager’s Guide to Press Conferences (Premier League edition). Because nothing happens by accident in these spaces.

Every word spoken in front of the board covered in adverts is metered and planned. A manager is never angry, or concerned, or even charming unintentionally. The game is the game, but so are all the other bits spilling out either side of it.

It was hard not to think about this while listening to Mikel Arteta talk about the penalty awarded to Sunderland at the Stadium of Light for a perceived act of grappling on Dan Ballard by Ezri Konsa. This is said with genuine professional respect. As everyone who has ever done a podcast knows – and this is, let’s be clear, everyone – there are lost Amazonian tribes discussing Girls season three in their own dark corner of Spotify – there are moments when you just have to flip the switch, up the energy and turn on full clip‑this‑bit‑up‑please‑Dave sincerity mode.

Arteta did this beautifully in the moment, appearing genuinely struck by what he was saying, radiating wounded integrity, like a disappointed junior headmaster appealing for the return of the school minibus keys.

Let’s be clear though. Arteta is not “very worried” about all this. He’s not “sad” or indeed, as he later emphasised for good measure, “really sad”. He’s not concerned solely with “protecting the game”, speaking here for all of us, just a fan of football.

Come off it. This is a manager we know to be obsessed with the most marginal of gains, to micro-plan the micro-details. As is all elite sport now. There has been talk of rowing coaches installing fibreglass toilet seats at their training hubs having calculated the average athlete spends 20 minutes in there and this is all key glute management time. Arteta loves this stuff. There’s no way Ben White isn’t sat fiddling with his phone at the training ground on a gold-standard Easy‑Cup Mega-Soft Evacu-Throne.

So it is with his public statements. This will have all been gamed and contingency‑planned in advance. And for hard, rational, tactical reasons, because this is how the game is played and run now. So what does it mean?

There are three things we know for sure. First, Arteta was right. This was a bad refereeing decision. Most obviously it was factually wrong. Ballard very skilfully pulled Konsa down on top of him, while simultaneously feigning shock that such a thing could happen.

It was doubly bad because the referee’s response was pre-planned, flagged by the early-season chat about refereeing in a more interventionist fashion. Go into any situation with a voice in your head, a vaguely worded mission to fulfil: this will skew your judgment.

The second thing is that referees are not biased. They’re just not very good. Two things have happened to them. First, the barrage of information to be absorbed in real time during a game is now utterly mind-boggling.

Most referees are not from a high-pressure data-processing background. These are not military pilots or traders on a currency floor. Less than a quarter have an academic degree. The task is beyond them. This is not a slur or an insult. It’s a simple description of what is happening, as supported by the evidence.

This is doubly annoying because referees have become fundamentally confused about their role. Referees are not ringmasters, or curators of the spectacle. They don’t get to decide what our sport should look like. Pro Ref is a private company with no locus standi to rule on the aesthetics of football. A referee should exist at the very edge of the spectacle. You’re not a local government planning officer with a mandate to decide which double-glazed French doors are or aren’t in character with the neighbourhood. Stop getting football not just wrong, but wrong.

But Arteta was also ready for this. Arsenal’s coaches will have known this would happen at some point. That press conference response was already in the chamber. Arteta may even have practised his sad-not-angry face, his key lines.

And this would be the correct thing to do. None of this is breaking the rules, just as Arsenal are not a dirty team or a bunch of cheats. They play the game that is being presented to us, a sport that is being made to operate at the edge of its own ludicrously micro‑analysed rules on small issues of physical contact.

Arteta’s Arsenal have been masterful at finding advantages in this. Defenders are very good at playing with the ball at their feet now. Defenders are not selected for their ability to resist physical challenges. It is logical to exploit this, just as it is logical to seek to protect your ability to do so by speaking in public about how the rules are applied. This is why Arteta is good, and why he wins.

It is also true that this has created a strange environment. The tone of the wider Arsenal fanbase is another element here. There is no one type of football fan. All human life is here. But the fact remains, the loudest voices in the online Arsenal hive mind, even the atmosphere in the stadium is unique in its absolute conviction of victimhood, of conspiracy, of a galvanising sense of adversity.

There is no other ground where every single refereeing decision, even the who-knows 50-50s, is so violently and eloquently disputed. There are supporters who seem to spend most of the game up on their feet in a state of performative, weaponised indignation, whose entire interaction with the spectacle is an attitude of aggrieved injustice.

This makes sense, too. It speaks directly to the game we have created. Aggrieved middle-aged rule pedantry. This is the new cauldron of hate.

Is it based in reality? Not perhaps on the outline numbers. Arsenal have been awarded more fouls than any other team this season. Only six teams last season had more fouls awarded against them, and the same the year before. They had the fewest yellow cards last season. They haven’t had a single red since they had six of them in 2024‑25.

Still, certain key incidents continue to grate and fester. There was the incorrectly denied penalty claim for Bruno Guimarães at Aston Villa. The balls-up with VAR lines against Brentford in 2023, which, if it really was deliberate conspiracy-cheating, was the worst, most public attempt at deliberate conspiracy-cheating ever conceived.

There is discontent at the way some rules seem to be applied more severely to Arsenal, the silly little stuff like delaying or fiddling about with restarts. But then again, if you make the game about that, if you plan to play on the margins, and successfully so, more stuff might happen in that place while you’re doing it.

Arteta has also played the role of arms-length rage conjurer expertly, has gone from rarely commenting on referees to heartfelt and carefully targeted critic. The Sunderland penalty award was a first opportunity to unload on the refereeing backlash to Arsenal’s tactics, to launch his pre-prepared defence; and to point out something demonstrably true. Referees have lost control of this, because the game has got beyond them.

In many ways this was a perfect storm for Arteta. Not just a decision that didn’t matter, because the penalty was saved. But a decision that was clearly incorrect too, a chance to get your lobbying in while very obviously in the right.

There will be more of this as the season plays out, as Arsenal work to preserve the advantages they have made for themselves in close quarters, tactical attack and defence. Factor in that masterful turn at a press conference j’accuse, and Saturday was a significant win in more ways than one.

Josh Kerr bags $150,000 for 1500m win at World Athletics Ultimate Championship

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 20:21:07 GMT

Scot wins with ease ahead of Nuguse and Myers

Henrich’s final leg earns Britain silver in mixed relay

Throughout Josh Kerr’s perfect ­season, he has made the sublime look routine. So when the bell rang for the final lap of the men’s Ultimate 1500m final, with the Scot in third and ­closing on the leader, Yared Nuguse, the next 53 seconds felt preordained.

So it proved. First Kerr sauntered past Robert Farken into ­second. Then with 250m ­remaining, he ­scootered past Nuguse. The 20‑year‑old ­Australian star Cam Myers chased valiantly but Kerr smoothly nursed a three-metre lead to the finish.

As Kerr crossed the line in 3min 29.35sec, with Myers 0.33 back, he cupped his hand to his ear. The sound he was hearing? The adoration of the crowd, and the kerching of the $150,000 (£111,000) first prize. “To be honest, I didn’t feel amazing in the warmup,” Kerr said. “But these are the things you have to overcome.”

Asked about Myers, who won the Diamond League final last week, Kerr replied: “He’s an awesome athlete but I was able to peek over the screen. I pressed again at 120m, and then the gap didn’t change, and I knew that at that point I had it.”

The only shame was that Jakob Ingebrigtsen, who won a brilliant 5,000m victory on Friday, decided to skip what would have been a mouthwatering clash. But Kerr was generous to his great rival afterwards, describing Ingebrigtsen’s victory as “very impressive” and praising his decision to rest up to protect the ­longevity of his career.

Kerr will now take a holiday ­having ended his season ­having shattered the world mile record and walked away with three major prizes: world indoor championship gold over 3,000m, Commonwealth Games gold over the mile, and now the ­Ultimate Championship trophy. But the 28-year-old continues to have big plans for the future – including an attempt on the world 1500m record next year. “I want to roll this into 2027 and 2028,” he said.

“These are the peak years, and we’re really starting to get some offensive going. But I’m a human being, and I understand the highs of the sport are sometimes followed by a lot of real lows. I had that in 2025. I’m not taking it for granted.”

Elsewhere the American Melissa Jefferson-Wooden had plenty of jaws crashing to the floor in the 200m. Against the Olympic champion Gabby Thomas, Jefferson-Wooden ran 21:47 – the fourth ­fastest time in history. It was 0.13sec off Florence Griffith Joyner’s world record, despite a -0.6m/s headwind.

Thomas was second in an impressive 21.77, while Britain’s Amy Hunt was fourth in a season’s best 22.10 in what was her 47th race of the year.

“My coach has given us eight weeks off,” Hunt said. “I’m not an early-morning person and so I’m ­looking forward to being on the beach, ­spending time with my family, and try to pack it with fun stuff – art galleries, museums, and the cinema.”

Earlier, the new 400m ­hurdles world record-holder, Alison Dos ­Santos, again proved he was top dog in his event by running the third fastest time in history, 45.98, against the world champion, Rai Benjamin, and the former world champion Karsten Warholm. “What we are doing is so important and so impressive that people sometimes take it for granted,” Benjamin said, which seemed an entirely fair comment given the trio now hold the 38 best times in history.

In the men’s javelin, Rumesh ­Pathirage capped a brilliant breakthrough season by throwing 91.09m to take first prize – and said later that cricket had helped him to become the best in the world. “I inputted almost all my technique from cricket into the javelin throw because there are some similarities,” he said.

In the men’s 800m, Marco Arop’s brave frontrunning tactics came just short of sealing victory as he was overtaken by the Algerian Djamel Sedjati, who won in 1:41.91.

There were two other spectacular performances on the night. In the high jump, the Italian Gianmarco Tamberi jumped a world-leading 2.37m to take first, while in the men’s 200m Kenny Bednarek ran a world lead 19.52 sec to comfortably beat the Olympic champion, Letsile Tebogo, who ran 19.76 in second.

WSL roundup: Arsenal rue misses in Palace draw, Manchester City crush Villa

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 19:58:52 GMT

Gunners held at Emirates despite 30 attempts on goal

City win 4-1 at Aston Villa to extend perfect start

Arsenal were left to rue 30 missed chances after dropping points in a 0-0 draw against Crystal Palace at the Emirates Stadium.

The Gunners hit the target nine times and had almost 80% possession but could not convert their superiority into goals. Promoted Palace put on a resilient performance, with the goalkeeper Pauline Peyraud-Magnin batting away attempts from Alessia Russo, Chloe Kelly and Mariona Caldentey to earn another clean sheet.

The reigning champions, Manchester City, continued their winning start to the campaign with a dominant 4-1 victory against Aston Villa. Jade Rose broke the deadlock for City in the early stages, tapping home after Akane Okuma failed to claim a corner. Assisted by Khadija Shaw, Mary Fowler doubled the advantage with a low-driven strike into the bottom-right of the net.

Amalie Vangsgaard gave Andrée Jeglertz and his players a fright after converting Chasity Grant’s pass in the 42nd minute, but Shaw returned to the scoresheet after half-time to restore the two-goal cushion. City wrapped up the victory in added time when Lauren Hemp’s strike was deflected in by Mathilde Harviken.

Brighton came from two goals down to snatch a last-minute equaliser at Birmingham City. The promoted hosts took an early lead through Oceane Hurtre, who capitalised on a lapse in concentration from Caitlin Hayes before running into the box and slotting past Chiamaka Nnadozie.

Lily Crosthwaite made it two in the second half with a low driven shot across the goalkeeper, but Brighton gathered momentum when Olivia García came off the bench to close the gap in the 77th minute. As Birmingham attempted to hold on for the win, Kiko Seike raced into the box with just a few seconds remaining and made the most of a small gap between Sophie Baggaley and the near post to score.

At Goodison Park, Charlton fell to a 1-0 defeat by Everton following an own goal and two red cards. After a goalless first half, things quickly went downhill for the promoted side when Ashleigh Neville saw red for a high boot which caught Ruby Mace. With 13 minutes of normal time to play, the visitors found themselves behind when Holly McNamara’s cross deflected off the leg of Leighanne Robe and into the net. In the latter stages, Charlton went down to nine players after the substitute Hawa Cissoko received two yellow cards in quick succession.

Enric Mas reigns supreme at last in Vuelta a España to delight Spanish fans

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 19:30:04 GMT

Mas wins title after three second-place finishes

Tobias Johannessen takes final stage in Granada

Spain’s Enric Mas secured his first Vuelta a España title on Sunday as Tobias Johannessen won the 21st and final stage in Granada, bringing the three-week Grand Tour to a close.

The 31-year-old, who took the red jersey after Tadej Pogacar abandoned the race after a crash on stage eight, held off the four-time champion Primoz Roglic to become the first Spaniard to win the Vuelta since Alberto Contador in 2014.

Mas, a three-time Vuelta runner-up, finished 2min 15sec ahead of Roglic in the general classification, with Felix Gall third, a further half-minute behind.

Mas crossed the finish line arm-in-arm with his six Movistar teammates stretched out beside him. It was the Spaniard’s first Grand Tour triumph, which he effectively sealed by limiting his losses to Roglic in the individual time trial on Thursday and then expanding his lead on Saturday in the last mountain stage.

“I’ve dreamed of this and fought for it,” said Mas. “I felt some nerves, it was a day with a mix of emotions, all of them positive.

“We have to keep on doing what we’re doing, we’re sportsmen and it’s like this – we’re thinking about the next objectives and we have no time to enjoy our victories.”

The Norwegian Johannessen prevailed in the 112km final stage, which started in a supermarket and featured a series of loops through Granada and around the Alhambra palace. The Uno-X Mobility rider held off Alessandro Romele and Ramses Debruyne in a sprint finish.

The last 9.8km of the race was neutralised earlier on Sunday in agreement with the governing body, the UCI, after riders raised safety concerns, so for the general classification contenders it was a procession to the finish line.

Mas inherited the red jersey from Pogacar after the Slovene, who was the overwhelming favourite to triumph at the Vuelta for the first time, suffered a severe crash which ended his season. Five-time Tour de France winner Pogacar was hoping to become only the fourth rider to claim a Tour-Vuelta double in the same season.

A runner-up in 2018, 2021 and 2022, Mas fended off attacks from Roglic and Gall along the way and proved a worthy winner, rising to every challenge. It was Team Movistar’s first Vuelta win since Colombia’s Nairo Quintana claimed victory in 2016.

“The reality is that the team needed a victory like this, and now we have it,” said Mas.

‘No stopping him’: Hamilton admits defeat as Antonelli charges towards F1 world title

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 19:17:07 GMT

Retirement in Madrid leaves Hamilton 101 points back

Antonelli leads way by 81 points after Spanish GP win

Lewis Hamilton has conceded his Formula One world title hopes are over as he praised the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, saying there was no stopping the Italian after his victory at the Spanish Grand Prix.

Hamilton, in third place in the championship, had to retire from the race at the Madring with a brake problem on lap six. After Antonelli’s victory it leaves the seven-time world champion 101 points behind the 20-year-old Italian, who took over his seat at Mercedes when Hamilton joined Ferrari.

“There’s no stopping him and Mercedes this year,” Hamilton said. “They’ve done a phenomenal job and they deserve it.”

George Russell, Antonelli’s Mercedes teammate, is in second place 81 points behind with nine meetings remaining, a chasm. But Hamilton, who won his first race for Ferrari at Barcelona this season, insisted he felt there was still more to come from the team, even if Antonelli could not be caught.

“I think we have a good [car]. We’ve had a pretty decent car, a good car this weekend and we will continue to try and improve it and we have better results coming in the future.”

Antonelli’s win came after Lando Norris was unlucky with the timing of a virtual safety car, called just after the McLaren driver had passed the pit entry. Antonelli, behind Norris on track, was able to dive into the pits under the VSC and subsequently Norris lost track position. He was unable to make it back with overtaking all but impossible at the circuit and finished third.

Trade unions, MPs and donors urge Burnham to revisit party funding rules

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 17:50:08 GMT

PM has so far declined to insert curbs on UK-based donors, despite £72m donations from billionaires to Reform UK

Trade unions, MPs and donors have urged the government to look again at party funding rules, after Reform UK insisted £72m in donations from two crypto billionaires was within the law.

Andy Burnham, a previous backer of caps on domestic donations, has so far declined to insert any curbs in the elections bill that would apply to UK-based donors.

Labour MPs have voiced anger on internal WhatsApp groups that the government did not act last week when the elections bill was in the Commons to restrict domestic donations after two donors – Christopher Harborne and Ben Delo – gave Reform UK a total of £72m over the weekend.

The bill returns to the House of Lords next week where peers told the Guardian they would ask the government to look again at the issue.

The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, suggested on Sunday that the donations could be caught in a new bill which would apply retrospectively on donors from outside the UK.

The two donors who gave Reform £36m each have both previously been based outside the UK. Harborne is a citizen of the UK and Thailand, while Delo recently moved back to Britain from Hong Kong. It is unclear when Delo returned to live in the UK and whether Harborne remains a resident of Thailand. Reform said both donations were within the rules.

Senior government sources indicated the government was prepared to look again at the issue of domestic donations once it receives advice from a newly commissioned taskforce and from the Electoral Commission.

One No 10 source said they did not want to delay the elections bill – which gives votes to 16-year-olds and puts new curbs on foreign donors – but said the bill was “not the right vehicle but this is not the end of the story”.

Several Labour MPs said they had been assured by ministers that further legislation could still come before the general election. Trade unions are also understood to be wavering on the issue and a possible donations cap is expected to be part of discussions at the TUC congress next week, where Rayner and Burnham will speak.

Unions have been central to the decision not to impose a domestic donations cap after several, especially GMB, argued it would be a slippery slope towards future rightwing governments curbing union donations.

On Sunday the Unite trade union said it was in favour of a cap – and the largest trade union, Unison, said it would fight attempts by billionaires to influence politics.

“For individual donors there must be a cap,” said Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary. “I think at some point it gets beyond what people think as normal.”

Andrea Egan, Unison’s general secretary, said: “As his support dwindles in this country, Farage is turning to crypto billionaires in an attempt to undermine our democracy. The trade union movement will oppose him every step of the way.”

Stella Creasy, the Labour MP whose amendment on donations caps attracted support in the Commons, is liaising with peers about how they can raise the issue when the bill returns to the House of Lords this week.

The Labour peer Michael Wills said: “The government has already committed to urgently reviewing the questions of caps on donations. Now the bill is in the Lords, it offers an unmissable opportunity to say when that review will complete its work, and what its remit will be.”

Creasy said the Reform donations had “concentrated people’s minds about what is now happening in our politics and what it will do to the voices of working people if it’s not stopped – we have the chance with the Lords to amend this bill with a cap”.

Her amendment proposed an annual cap of £100,000 on most domestic donations. It was not put to a vote after the government said it would ask a taskforce to look at the proposal.

The former shadow chancellor John McDonnell said it was time for the government to move faster and for unions to get onboard. “It’s clear now to the trade unions meeting in congress this week that action is needed to protect our democracy and there’s a growing expectation the government will respond with urgency,” he said.

Two influential big party donors also called for a cap on Sunday. The billionaire businessman and Phones 4U founder, John Caudwell, who previously donated to the Conservative party in 2019, told BBC Radio 4’s Broadcasting House: “There should be a definite change in law. We should not have very wealthy people making undue influence.”

Dale Vince, the Ecotricity founder who has given donations to the Labour party, said it was “urgent” the government dealt with donations rules. “Ridiculous sums of money don’t level the playing field – they distort it.

“Our current system of funding is anti-democratic – those with big money have more say than the simple vote we all have. A cap on donations would be a step in the right direction – the end game should be publicly funded politics.”

The TUC general secretary, Paul Nowak, suggested he was sympathetic to further action. Speaking before the opening of the TUC congress, he said: “No one wants the UK to become a country for hire in the way Reform is clearly a party for hire. Without a doubt, we are going to need to restrict the ability of billionaires like Delo to buy and sell our politics. But we’ll have to do that in a way that doesn’t cut across workers having their voice heard politically.”

Reform has said it is confident that its two donors will not be caught in a retrospective cap on donations from Britons living abroad. “We are 100% confident both are legal and won’t ever have to be handed back,” a spokesperson said, suggesting both men would meet the criteria on residency even within the rules of the new bill.

As part of the new legislation, donations to political parties from Britons living abroad or those who have returned to the country within the past 12 months will be capped at £100,000 a year, with the rules backdated to March.

Rayner – the minister responsible for the bill – said it was not targeted at individual donors or parties. “We didn’t know that donors were going to be putting that money in, and this isn’t about individual donors to a political party. This is an issue that has been raised about protecting our democracy from foreign interference, and the government is taking action on that,” she told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme.

Reform’s economy spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, said the two donors were well aware of the law. He said: “It’s a breakthrough moment, really, for the party. It means that we will be battle ready if Andy Burnham calls an election, and we can compete now finally on a fair, even playing field with the two old parties.”

Train carrying Boris Johnson and ex-CIA chief may have been targeted in Russian strike, officials say

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 17:43:03 GMT

Ukrainian Railways says former British PM and David Petraeus crossed into Poland shortly before drone attack near border

A train carrying Boris Johnson and the former CIA chief David Petraeus may have been the target of a Russian drone strike that hit a train engine near the Poland-Ukraine border, according to Ukrainian Railways.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, described the attack as “Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato”.

Overnight attacks across Ukraine involving more than 450 Russian drones and missiles killed at least six people and injured more than 40. Ukraine’s air force said it had intercepted 405 drones and four missiles.

Western Ukraine, which is typically quieter than Kyiv or the eastern frontline zones, was particularly badly hit.

The strikes prompted air-raid warnings in Poland, which shares a border with western Ukraine.

Ukrainian and Polish authorities said a lorry less than 1km from the Dorohusk-Yahodyn border crossing between the two countries was also hit.

Katerina Sergatskova, the director of Daily Humanity, an organisation that provides training to people working in high-risk environments, was travelling on a Warsaw-bound train and witnessed the attack.

She said passengers were told to evacuate at about 9am as the train approached the Polish border having already been told to disembark for two hours in the middle of the night. “At this point, the mood was different, we were asked to move very fast,” she said. “Then I heard the first drone.

“Seeing and hearing Shahed [drones] just a few hundred metres from the border is a very unpleasant experience.”

No casualties were reported on the train.

A British economist who preferred not to be named, travelling on a night train from Kyiv towards Chelm in Poland, also witnessed the attack. “We spent 10 hours at the border and were evacuated three times. On the third evacuation a missile came over and totalled a locomotive in front of our train.”

Railway officials instructed the “grimly focused” passengers to hide in bushes by a lake, said the economist, calling the Ukrainian response “timely and disciplined”. They “gave us good warning of the evacuation and had a plan, which everyone followed”.

“The conductor said when we boarded that there was a high risk that we would be evacuated during the journey. The lady and her eight-year-old son who were in my compartment said they had been travelling back and forth every month to Kyiv from Warsaw since 2022 and they had never been evacuated, or the train attacked, while travelling the route. This is clearly an escalation by Putin and the Russians.”

Ukrainian Railways, which operates the line, said a train carrying several security advisers from European countries, as well as Johnson, the former British prime minister, and the former CIA chief Petraeus, had passed through the border crossing shortly before the drone strike.

“It is quite likely that the target of this Russian drone could also have been the diplomatic train, which departed from the station earlier than planned as part of the real-time review of train schedules due to the constant threat of Russian strikes,” the rail company said.

Johnson wrote on X: “I don’t know what warped logic drove Putin to blow up a stationary Ukrainian locomotive on the Polish border this morning. What we can say for sure is that this is the kind of random and senseless attack Ukrainians are enduring every day – even on civilian railways.”

Three people were killed in the eastern Donetsk region, and a 71-year-old woman was killed in the southern Mykolaiv region.

Sybiha said the Russian strikes were “not just a continuation of its attacks on our state borders”.

“This is Putin’s terror knocking directly on the doors of the EU and Nato. Russian barbarians are at your gate, dear partners,” he wrote on X.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote on Telegram: “Ukrainians are fighting every day to prevent these strikes from spreading further into Europe, giving their lives and preventing the aggression from expanding.”

The Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned on Sunday that intensifying Russian attacks in Ukraine in the coming weeks could affect Poland, as he chaired an emergency meeting after the Russian drone attacks near the border.

“The coming weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions on the Russian side,” he said, adding Poland “cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory”.

He added that Poland had been tipped off by its security services, and by intelligence agencies from allied countries, that an attack such as this was likely. “We knew that the Russian plan would include an attempt to disrupt, paralyse, and perhaps even destroy Ukrainian border crossings,” Tusk said.

Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, who visited Kyiv this week, said on X after Sunday morning’s attack: “Putin is escalating.”

The Polish interior minister, Marcin Kierwiński, said: “We treat these events with the utmost seriousness. The situation is being monitored continuously. Russia is the enemy of the free world.”

Russia claimed it struck “railway infrastructure” in western Ukraine used to “transport military cargo” from Europe.

“Strikes have continued on railway infrastructure in the western regions of Ukraine, which are used to transport military cargo from European countries,” Moscow’s defence ministry said in a statement.

Ukraine and Russia have increased attacks on critical infrastructure in each other’s countries as long-range drones and missiles take the war away from the frontlines.

The US president, Donald Trump, said on Sunday that Zelenskyy should “stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia” because it was causing shortages.

“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel,” Trump said, adding that shortages were caused by the Russia-Ukraine war rather than the US war in the Middle East.

The Plaid Cymru leader, Rhun ap Iorwerth, the Scottish National party leader, John Swinney, and the Sinn Féin vice-president, Michelle O’Neill, are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding at a landmark conference in Cardiff on Monday that will call on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”.

The three are meeting in their capacity as party leaders, rather than as officials in their respective governments, alongside the Sinn Féin president and leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald. They will also discuss Europe, international cooperation, the economy and energy issues.

Plaid Cymru’s victory in May’s Senedd elections ushered in a new era for the Celtic independence movements, with separatist parties in government in all three countries for the first time.

Burnham has made much of his support for regional devolution of power and resources in England since becoming prime minister in July, but his approach to the devolved administrations in Belfast, Cardiff and Edinburgh is less clear.

He wrote to Swinney last week to reiterate that a repeat of 2014’s Scottish independence referendum remains “off limits” after apparently misspeaking during prime minister’s questions.

Donald Trump also weighed in on a potential breakup of the UK during a weekend visit to Ireland, telling reporters at a press conference with the taoiseach, Micheál Martin, that he would love to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”. The unexpected intervention prompted a swift rebuttal from the UK government and the unionist power-sharing members of the Northern Ireland executive.

Asked about the diplomatic backlash, Trump said on Sunday: “I love my comments.” Shortly after reiterating his stance on Irish unity, the US president said he would save his opinion on Scottish independence for another day.

Ap Iorwerth told the Guardian this week that he has been encouraged by warm initial discussions with Burnham – a stark contrast to his interactions with Keir Starmer – but that he was wary about the new prime minister being captured by a consensus Westminster view against relinquishing further powers.

A Plaid Cymru source called Monday’s summit an opportunity for “a new partnership between our nations”.

“Following the historic Senedd election in Wales and the changing political landscape across these islands, there is a strong case for practical political cooperation on areas including energy, the economy and our relationship with Europe, as well as on the wider political and constitutional questions facing our nations and on the right to self-determination,” they said.

“Our parties have much to gain from working together, as partners and as equals, where we share common interests and where cooperation can improve the lives of the people we represent.”

Speaking before his visit to Cardiff, Swinney said: “We are at a pivotal moment of constitutional change, and our parties share the common belief that our interests will never be served by Westminster, and that the people of our respective nations must have a meaningful say over their future.

“This discussion comes the week after the prime minister accepted that a referendum should take place when there is majority support for independence in Scotland. That acknowledgment that the people of Scotland can and should determine their own constitutional future is long overdue.”

Latest polling suggests 47% of Scottish voters would opt for independence in a referendum held tomorrow, along with 36% in Northern Ireland and 32% in Wales. Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum, while data suggest it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland.

The Guardian view on the government’s corporate reforms: entrenching neoliberalism, not ending it

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:30:07 GMT

A recent consultation on corporate reporting prizes the interests of shareholders over society. It’s a step in the wrong direction

The question of what corporations are for is deeply political. In a 1970 article for the New York Times, Milton Friedman argued that the “social responsibility of business is to increase its profits”. The idea that CEOs should worry about providing good jobs was “pure and unadulterated socialism”, he wrote. Friedman and his fellow neoliberals saw companies as vehicles for enforcing their politics. Their ideas endured: UK bosses are now paid 130 times more than average workers.

Despite Andy Burnham’s pledge to end neoliberalism, a 12-week consultation recently launched by his government risks entrenching it. The consultation was first announced as part of the Starmer government’s crusade against “red tape”. The average annual report for some businesses now runs to 98,000 words, and no doubt there are areas that could be simplified. But the consultation proposes removing vital information and presumes that company reports primarily serve shareholders, rather than other stakeholders. Both are steps in the wrong direction.

The consultation proposes scrapping information about the ratio between CEO and worker pay, removing a vital benchmark for inequality. British CEOs already earn 95% more on average than their European equivalents, and opaque pay ratios only serve their interests. There is scant evidence that higher-paid CEOs create more productive firms. As one Harvard Law School paper observed, pay ratios show how much a company invests in its “human capital”, and matter to workers and investors alike. Consumers who are made aware of this information are more likely to choose products from firms where the ratio is lower, encouraging those firms to address glaring pay disparities.

The consultation reflects the idea that inequality within a company is immaterial, a perplexing stance for a government concerned with fairness. It suggests removing annual shareholder votes on director pay, on the basis that votes are still required every three years. Annual votes were a modest attempt from Theresa May’s Tory government to tame the “unacceptable face of capitalism”, and the GC100 lobby group of corporate leaders has called to scrap them. By giving way, Labour would be removing a Tory policy designed to rein in boardroom greed.

It also proposes allowing companies to shift towards fully virtual annual general meetings. Companies have been holding online AGMs since Covid, and the government suggests these can improve “accessibility”. This is misguided: such meetings tend to be shorter, and prevent shareholders from asking as many questions. In-person AGMs are an imperfect form of accountability, but confrontation is easier to avoid when people aren’t in the room. Earlier this year, more than 50% of BP shareholders voted against a resolution to replace in-person AGMs with online meetings. Shareholders and climate groups argued these were a threat to accountability.

If reporting is too onerous, it would be better to start afresh with a new regime that recognised the interests of workers and society at large. Some voluntary initiatives, such as B Corporations, already take a more holistic approach to the information they disclose. Even better would be a requirement to include workers on company boards and provide greater transparency on pay levels, including that of all executives and workers paid less than the living wage. As the legal professor Katharina Pistor observes, corporate law is a tool that creates inequality. If the government wants to end neoliberalism, it should scrap this consultation and start again.

The Guardian view on Russian parliamentary elections: glimpses of weakness behind the facade

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:25:07 GMT

The Kremlin’s clumsy efforts to engineer the outcome reveal growing anxiety about the public mood and a war that is failing

Vladimir Putin’s authoritarian powers are not constrained by elections, but he is alert to the danger that his rule would look illegitimate without them. That creates a tension, which is resolved through “managed democracy” – a euphemism for fraud and repression camouflaged with ritual ballots, held under a constitution that notionally guarantees political freedoms but in reality serves only the president.

Russians are invited to elect a new Duma, the lower chamber of parliament, later this week, but they know in advance that United Russia, the official party of Putinism, will win a majority.

Engineering that outcome is not without risk for the ruling regime. The mechanics of stealing an election are simple enough. Ballots can be stuffed, official media are pliant. But too blatant a theft can be counterproductive. If the results are wildly divergent from most people’s sense of the real public mood, an authoritarian leader risks advertising his fear of a genuine democratic consultation. It is a sign of weakness.

To an extent, this has happened already. Last month, the supreme court blocked Yabloko, an old and marginal liberal party, from appearing on Duma ballot papers. The case was spurious to the point of absurdity.

Yabloko is not one of the pseudo-opposition “system” parties that provide a pretence of pluralism in parliament, but nor does it pose a serious challenge to the regime. If it did, it wouldn’t have survived this long. It was last represented in the Duma in 2007, although it still sends deputies to local and municipal legislatures.

It is also opposed to the war in Ukraine. This Duma ballot is the first parliamentary poll since the full-scale invasion in 2022. Yabloko’s single-sentence manifesto calls for a ceasefire, diplomacy and peace. A decision not to let the bearers of that message participate even in a rigged ballot suggests nervousness about the popularity of a “special military operation” that was supposed to last weeks but is now well into its fifth year, with no end in sight.

Ukraine’s use of long-range missiles and drones to attack infrastructure deep inside Russia has made it hard for Moscow to downplay the scale of the war on their doorstep or shield civilians from its consequences. The reality of fuel shortages and inflation penetrates the wall of propaganda. So does loss of life.

The true number of Russian casualties is hard to know, but is thought to be about 1.5 million, with hundreds of thousands of fatalities. In the absence of volunteers, army recruiters are increasingly turning to coercion, press ganging or tricking people into signing up. There are rumours, denied by officials, that a mass mobilisation of reserves – unwilling cannon fodder – is coming once the election is out of the way.

So it is hardly surprising that the Kremlin has abandoned what was left of its flimsy pretence of permitting dissent. The machinery for delivering an election result to the president’s satisfaction is well oiled. There is no reason to think that it will fail this time. That doesn’t make the vote irrelevant. Mr Putin’s brutal record proves that he doesn’t care about the wellbeing of ordinary Russians, but he cares about the appearance of being supported by them. The harder the Kremlin is seen to work at constructing electoral proof of that support, the less confident it looks.

Nordqvist sounded unsure about elements of the Solheim Cup’s captains’ agreement before a ball was whacked in anger. The last laugh belongs to the Swede herself, who can sail off into the sunset having added a triumphant Solheim Cup captaincy to a career that had already returned three major wins.

What a rousing afternoon this soon became for women’s golf in Europe. The understated Nordqvist was on the podium once more.

The wait for a USA win on foreign soil, stretching back to 2015, goes on. Europe are due huge praise for their singles performance here, which had felt unlikely from a four-session ­position of an 8-8 tie. Nordqvist and her players, including four rookies, were underdogs. On day three, there was seldom any doubt they would upset the odds. The record books will show 15-13 as the margin of victory when, in essence, there was more between the teams on Sunday.

“I think there has just been so many emotions bottled up,” ­Nordqvist said. “It’s just been such a long road. It’s been a lot of hard work. It’s been really hard retiring weeks ago, then doing this and doing them both at the same time.

“I’ve been living my dream. I’m forever grateful for everything that’s happened. It doesn’t feel like I worked a day in my life. Having my family support from very far away, living in the US on my own, but to have them here at every single ­Solheim Cup, and now to share it with my nieces and nephews, seeing my brothers cry, my sister-in-law, it’s just always been a family affair for me.”

In fact, it feels inadequate that ­Nordqvist wants to step away from it all.

The defining moment belonged to Woad. Her tap-in to secure a 2up win against Auston Kim meant Europe reached 14 points. Carlota Ciganda was 3up on Jennifer Kupcho with the same number of holes to play, ­meaning the 14½ Europe needed to reclaim the trophy was inevitable. Ciganda made sure she won, which completed the formality of taking Europe to 15 points. “I am very happy to do this for Anna,” Ciganda said.

There was also an element of revenge for Ciganda, who was undone by two moments of brilliance by Kupcho in Saturday’s fourball session. On Saturday evening Ciganda received a message of encouragement from José María Olazábal, her Spanish compatriot and a Ryder Cup icon.

Europe flew out of the traps. Hull played like a golfer with a point to prove in seeing off Megan Khang 3&2 in the opening match. Hull justified her captain’s constant faith by winning the opening hole and staying ahead from that juncture. “It was a no-brainer to put Charley first,” Nordqvist said.

“We saw the stats yesterday, ­Charley and Lottie were actually in the top‑four players that made the most birdies for the week. They just played really tough matches. People don’t understand how good all these ­players are and how good the golf has been all day in the last three days.

“Lottie has been playing so good this week and not really getting anything off of it. But holing the winning putt, I don’t think that’s ever going to be hard to remember for her.” Hull was being force-fed champagne by her captain as victory sunk in.

Esther Henseleit rampaged to 4up on Alison Lee after seven and still that after 11. What happened next is the finest comeback in Solheim Cup history. Lee won on the final green.

Why English devolution is fraught with difficulty

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:00:36 GMT

Readers respond to an editorial that argued for more accountability from local authorities in return for greater power

Your editorial on Andy Burnham’s devolution plans rightly argues that greater local power must be accompanied by greater scrutiny (The Guardian view on Burnham’s devolution plans: power must be accompanied by scrutiny, 6 September).

I work as a bid manager in the third sector, applying for publicly procured contracts to deliver employment and support services. From that perspective, the increasing devolution of funding has real potential: decisions can be made closer to communities and, importantly, local organisations should have greater opportunities to deliver services.

Yet my experience is of an increasingly complicated and inconsistent commissioning landscape. Different local and combined authorities take markedly different approaches. Some have strong procurement practices, engage constructively with providers and appear well equipped to manage devolved funding. Elsewhere, processes can be fragmented, difficult to navigate and considerably less transparent. It is beginning to feel like a postcode lottery.

There is also a contradiction here. One stated benefit of devolution is the ability to engage more local suppliers, including smaller voluntary and community organisations with deep roots in the places they serve. Yet these are often the organisations least able to navigate multiple procurement portals, differing requirements and commissioning approaches. Large national organisations can resource this complexity; small local charities often cannot.

My concern is not with devolution itself. But transferring substantial sums of public money must be accompanied by investment in local commissioning expertise, procurement capacity and meaningful scrutiny.

As more funding moves away from Whitehall, we should ask not simply where power sits, but whether every place has the capacity to exercise it well. Haile ReedBirmingham

In your editorial, you focus rightly on accountability, but overlook something more fundamental: whether local authorities currently have the capability and capacity to deliver devolution at all.

England is already midway through reorganising local government, with 185 councils being reshaped across 21 areas into new unitary authorities, alongside six new mayoral authorities. Disruption is inevitable.

This is happening against a backdrop of serious financial strain. Eight councils have issued section 114 “bankruptcy” notices in the last six years, compared with almost none in the 18 years before that. In a 2024 survey, the Local Government Information Unit found 51% of councils thought it likely they would issue such a notice within five years.

Layering new devolved responsibilities on to institutions that are simultaneously being dismantled and rebuilt, and in many cases barely solvent, risks devolving responsibility faster than those institutions can actually deliver it. Devolution may well be the right destination, but the sequencing matters. Alan CoppinFormer Crown Representative, Cabinet Office

Lamenting the decline of local media, your editorial proposes “a tax on social media giants to fund local journalism”.

Yes please. The Hastings Independent Press (HIP), a professional-quality, bi-weekly, 24-page newspaper written by and for the community, has somehow survived 11 years and 310 issues. Edited by an all-volunteer editorial team, who mentor and support new writers as well as produce the paper, HIP has no premises, no equipment and no grant funding, relying on advertising from small businesses – a diminishing source of revenue as they battle falling income and rising costs.

Funding from “the socials” would make all the difference to our grassroots collective. To stop living hand to mouth, to plan issues, perhaps even find people to deliver 7,000 copies of the paper to shops instead of doing it ourselves. We can dream. David YoungSt Leonards-on-Sea, East Sussex

Not glamorous, but common: how to manage dandruff at home and when to get help

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Experts don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, but if you’re seeing light flakes on your scalp, over-the-counter products can help

You spy a scatter of white flakes on your collar. Or you’ve got an itch that won’t quit, no matter how much you wash your hair. Dandruff isn’t glamorous, but it’s common: about half the world’s population has it.

An itchy, flaking scalp is rarely dangerous, but it can be annoying. Here’s what you need to know about what might be causing your flakes, what you can do about it, and when it’s time to get help.

Dandruff is the mildest form of a condition called seborrheic dermatitis, a type of skin inflammation that usually affects the head, face or trunk. At its worst, this condition leads to patches of red skin covered in tiny, greasy scales. However, most people with dandruff have just minor scaliness and no redness, affecting only the scalp.

Experts still don’t know exactly what causes dandruff, and it’s likely there are various contributing factors. A yeast called Malassezia is a leading suspect, says James Pathoulas, an assistant professor of dermatology at the University of Minnesota medical school who specializes in hair and scalp disorders. Malassezia usually lives harmlessly on the scalp, but overgrowth has been linked with scalp inflammation.

It’s better to think about seborrheic dermatitis as a system in dysfunction rather than one organism causing trouble, according to Natasha Mesinkovska, an associate professor of dermatology at the University of California, Irvine. Scalp health comes down to a “trifecta” of factors, she says: the scalp’s microorganisms, its ability to keep those organisms out of deeper skin layers, and the skin’s immune response to them.

It’s not clear why some people get dandruff and others don’t. Genetics may play a role – at least 11 gene variants have been linked to the condition – as can hot, humid weather or a supercharged workout routine.

Hormones that drive oil production can also ramp symptoms up or down, beginning around puberty and changing during pregnancy or menopause.

If you’re seeing occasional light scale on your scalp with no significant redness or itch, over-the-counter dandruff shampoo can help. Zinc pyrithione, selenium sulfide and ketoconazole are the three most common active ingredients. They’re all equally good at lowering Malassezia populations, tamping down inflammation, and stopping the flakes.

Pathoulas recommends massaging the shampoo into your scalp, not just your hair, and leaving it on for a few minutes before rinsing. Use it three times a week; either your regular conditioner or a dandruff-specific product is fine. If you want to wash your hair on in-between days, your regular shampoo and conditioner are fine.

Ketoconazole and selenium sulfide can dry out hair and cause breakage, especially for dry, highly textured or coily hair, Pathoulas says. If that occurs, or you already rely on hair oils or leave-in conditioner, look for a gentler, sulfate-free zinc pyrithione formulation made for textured hair.

Go fragrance-free where you can, says Pathoulas. Fragrance is a common cause of scalp contact allergy, and it doesn’t have to be synthetic to cause a reaction: natural botanical fragrances can also wreak havoc.

Sign up to Well Actually

Practical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good life

after newsletter promotion

Once symptoms clear, most people can taper dandruff shampoo use to once a week. If a shampoo that’s worked for months suddenly stops being effective, the yeast may have grown resistant to it, Pathoulas says. Switching to a different active ingredient for a while, then back again, can restore control.

If your scalp clears up with a medicated shampoo but flaking resumes within days of stopping, that’s a signal the underlying problem needs more attention, says Mesinkovska.

Thick, red, sharply defined plaques with silvery-white scale point toward psoriasis rather than dandruff, especially if you also have them on the elbows and knees. If the redness or scaly skin shows up elsewhere on your body, it could indicate an allergic reaction, depending on its location and your exposures, says Mesinkovska. Dandruff shampoo won’t have any effect on scalp flakes resulting from either of these conditions.

Hair loss or a burning or stinging sensation accompanying flakes is never normal, says Pathoulas. If you have these symptoms, a clinician should evaluate you for scarring alopecia.

If an evaluation shows that you just have ordinary dandruff but it isn’t responding to the basics, there are prescription options. The experts suggest ciclopirox shampoo, an antifungal with some antibacterial activity built in, and prescription-strength ketoconazole. Roflumilast is a newer option that you apply to your dry scalp as a foam.

Some researchers are trying to understand if manipulating the scalp’s bacterial populations might help – that is, adding good germs to outcompete any bad ones that might be causing problems. But that research is still in its early stages, so for now, experts aren’t recommending approaches like applying yoghurt or kombucha.

The far right’s rise is a wake-up call for Europe

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:58:00 GMT

Rafael Behr is right to warn that far-right parties, Maga ideology and Kremlin influence threaten Europe’s liberal democracies (European democracies are running out of time to turn away from the abyss, 9 September). But he overlooks the role of the liberal centre itself in creating the conditions for their rise.

While Thatcher, Reagan and their successors weakened trade unions and workers’ bargaining power, subsequent centre-left governments largely accepted these changes rather than reversing them. Under the banner of the “third way”, they expanded labour market insecurity, embraced financialisation and allowed private interests to penetrate ever deeper into public services. Social and economic inequality soared.

From the anti-globalisation movement and post-2008 anti-austerity protests to more recent pro-Palestinian mobilisations, the liberal centre has relied increasingly on policing, surveillance and legal restrictions to contain political opposition.

Decades of economic insecurity, shrinking democratic participation and declining faith in established institutions have created fertile ground for the far right. Kremlin money and Maga-style politics can only thrive because the centre has hollowed out the social and political foundations of liberal democracy. The Alternative für Deutschland’s success should be a wake-up call. History suggests the centre will hit the snooze button. Benjamin SelwynProfessor of international relations and international development, University of Sussex

Jörg Lau rightly identifies the shattering of Germany’s postwar consensus in Saxony-Anhalt, but framing this as a sudden rupture obliterates decades of the political establishment’s structural rot (Friedrich Merz is now on borrowed time. But that’s not why the AfD’s triumph is seismic, theguardian. com, 8 September).

Germany’s crisis began with suppressing authentic reckoning. In the immediate postwar era, former Nazi party members were allowed to dominate state institutions. This continued until the 1970s. Willy Brandt, the “Historikerstreit”, the countrywide discussion of the series Holocaust and Goldhagen’s book Hitler’s Willing Executioners were short glimmers of real change. Then the institutionalised remembrance culture emerged. It was top-down – a state-directed ritual to appease European partners that reinforced the German “nanny state” mentality.

In eastern states like Saxony-Anhalt, this top-down moral framework was forced on a population thrust into the post-1989 market shock. Now, with an ageing demographic and economic stagnation straining the social safety net, this abandonment is coming due. The AfD feeds on these unhealed wounds, exploiting anger over stale ritualised politics and, once again, channelling economic angst into xenophobic nationalism.

Merz is a product of decades of missed opportunities. But the AfD is not an alien shock to the system. Mainstream parties built the void the far right now occupies. If mainstream political Berlin continues to ignore their systemic neglect, the collapse will be complete. Dr Michael EsserLos Angeles, California, US

The Public Order Act 1936 put a stop to the quasi-military demonstrations by Oswald Mosley’s blackshirts. Is there any reason why it cannot be used to put an end to thuggish demonstrations by intimidating, black-clothed and balaclava-wearing protesters on the streets of Dover and Portsmouth?William WardLondon

And what did the Tories get in return? A gift of about £12k. You’d have hoped the lesson Honest Bob had learned from that was not to sell his soul – if he has one – so cheaply.

“Everything was totally above board,” he insisted. Though forgive us all for asking the question. Reform is currently the subject of at least two – or is it three? it’s so easy to lose count – police investigations into alleged financial wrongdoing, and the party has acquired a reputation for being at the sleazier end of British politics. A place where Dicky Tice shuffles money from Posh George into and out of his accounts and Nige is so blase he can’t even be bothered to listen when two potential donors talk at length on how they are planning to break the law. Remarkable stuff. Nige can even not listen while maintaining a conversation.

Laura did suggest that Reform might have to give some of the money back if the government were to retrospectively implement the findings of the Rycroft review into party funding. But Honest Bob wasn’t having any of it. There was no way he would be handing back a penny. Finders keepers. Possession nine-tenths of the law. You’d be amazed how Reform can make money disappear when it feels like it. Though, of course, everything would be done in a totally legitimate way.

What we all had to understand was that this was a huge vote of confidence in Reform. Far from being an indication that the party’s funding had become exponentially more murky, this was proof that it was being totally transparent. Think of it this way. When he had been a Conservative MP, Honest Bob had been more than happy for his party to shower peerages on donors. Some only had to hand over less than £100k to end up in the Lords. But Delo and Harborne weren’t asking for anything like that. All they wanted was for the laws around crypto currencies to be relaxed a little. Where was the conflict of interest in that?

after newsletter promotion

Ben and Christopher were just regular guys who just happened to be billionaires. And yes, it was unfortunate that Ben had been convicted in the US for failing to comply with anti-money-laundering legislation – somehow the fact he had been pardoned by Donald Trump made him sound doubly guilty – but this had just been an oversight. He was a very busy man and it had been the sort of mistake anyone could make.

“They are both just patriots,” Honest Bob continued. So patriotic that Delo had spent much of the last few years based in Hong Kong while Harborne lived in Thailand. We should try to feel their pain. They were both just run-of-the-mill billionaires who happened to have been priced out of Mayfair. Rather than indulge in the politics of envy, we should applaud them for their philanthropy. Two guys just trying to make a difference. Making Britain better.

Now and again, Honest Bob found himself getting a little confused. For example, when he came to think about it, Delo and Harborne giving £72m from their crypto empires was much the same as tens of thousands of ordinary workers donating to Labour through their union subscriptions. Because what Ben and Chris wanted most was for the income tax threshold to be raised to £15k. That £500 they would get back could make the difference between them remaining tax exiles and returning to this country.

The money would be spent on the professionalisation of Reform. When all welfare payments – those that were left – would be paid in crypto. When Reform would rise above the ashes of sleaze. When all bus sites and billboards would be covered with adverts for Reform. When all TV stations promoted Reform without question. It wasn’t enough to have GB News doing that for nothing. There would be no rest until the BBC had also been captured. Make no mistake. This £72m was only the start.

Pregnant woman among more than 10 killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:51:33 GMT

Woman’s family says she died of injuries after being shot in the head while sitting inside a tent near Khan Younis

A pregnant Palestinian woman died on Saturday from injuries sustained after being shot in the head by Israeli forces south of Khan Younis, according to her family and medical workers, as strikes across Gaza killed at least 10 people in 48 hours.

The woman, named as Iman Shalouf, 27, who was nearly eight months pregnant, was sitting inside her family’s tent in the al-Mawasi area when Israeli gunfire struck her, according to paramedics and witnesses.

‘‘We heard the sound of gunfire while I was praying,’’ Wathfa abu Mashi, Shalouf’s mother-in-law, said in a video interview with Anadolu. “My daughter asked me, ‘Where is Iman?’ I told her she was in her tent. She went to check on her and found her covered in blood after she was hit by a bullet.”

Shalouf’s husband, Ismail abu Mashi, said “Where is the ceasefire they keep talking about? There is no such thing. There is killing every day. People are dying here every day.”

Shalouf was rushed to Nasser hospital, where doctors initially detected her unborn baby’s heartbeat, but she and her unborn baby died a few hours later.

According to relatives, Shalouf had already chosen the name Ayoub for the baby, who was due in November.

Relatives and community members gathered at the hospital to hold funeral prayers for Shalouf and her child before carrying their bodies for burial in Khan Younis. They were buried side by side.

Contacted by the Guardian, the Israel Defense Forces said they were looking into the incident.

Despite the ceasefire agreement reached in October 2025, violence and the killing of Palestinians continue on a daily basis.

The health ministry in Gaza said 10 Palestinians had been killed and 56 wounded in Israeli attacks over the previous 48 hours, amid artillery shelling and gunfire in several areas of northern, central and southern Gaza.

Four members of the same family – Momen Ahmed, his wife, Haneen Saleh, and their daughters Lana, 12, and Bana, eight – were killed when their home in Beit Lahiya was struck on Thursday night, according to the ministry. Six other Palestinians were reported killed in Khan Younis and Gaza City on Friday, including a man who died of wounds sustained in an earlier attack.

Several other Palestinians were injured in attacks across Gaza. On Friday, two people were reportedly seriously injured in an attack in Beit Lahiya, while three people including a woman six months pregnant and a child were wounded by gunfire in the same city. On Saturday, nine people were injured when a displaced people’s tent in al-Mawasi was shelled, according to the Palestinian Red Crescent.

On Sunday, two Palestinians were killed and several others injured when a vehicle was struck in Tel al-Hawa in Gaza City, according to the health ministry. The attack also injured people on a passing bus carrying women and children.

On 28 August, Unicef said at least four children had been reported killed in the preceding five days and many others wounded, including children who sustained life-changing injuries. On 2 September, it said three other children had reportedly been killed and at least five others injured in the preceding 24 hours, bringing the number of children reportedly killed between 23 August and 2 September to seven.

“Airstrikes by Israeli forces continue killing and wounding Palestinians,” Médecins Sans Frontières said. “Between September 6 and 9, Israeli forces issued 18 so-called evacuation orders and struck a building less than 250ft from an MSF clinic.”

The humanitarian situation remains severe. According to the UN’s humanitarian office, “most of Gaza’s 2.1 million are approaching the rainy season in overcrowded displacement sites, at risk of flooding and disease, while efforts to help them prepare are constrained by funding shortfalls and access restrictions”.

On 31 August, a temporary halt to desalination in Israel reduced the water available to about a million people in Gaza who rely on the Israeli grid.

Several electricity generators at hospitals across the Gaza Strip have stopped working because of shortages of spare parts and fuel, the territory’s health ministry has said.

According to the ministry, 1,369 Palestinians have been killed and 4,627 wounded since the fragile ceasefire took effect on 11 October 2025. Since Israel’s war in Gaza began on 7 October 2023, at least 73,783 Palestinians have been killed and 174,738 wounded, according to the ministry.

Police have released images of six men they would like to speak to after violent disorder in Portsmouth last week that left seven officers injured.

About 200 people gathered at Eastney Marina on Sunday night after a small boat carrying asylum seekers arrived on the south coast having crossed the Channel. The activists dispersed the following day in the early hours.

Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said seven police officers were injured and treated at the scene, while vehicles belonging to the Coastguard and Border Force were damaged.

The force said it reviewed “hundreds of hours’ worth” of footage from the disorder and released images of six men it believes “can assist our investigation”.

The first person charged in connection with the demonstration in the city appeared in court on Saturday morning.

Del Leon Somerville, 42, from Paulsgrove, Portsmouth, appeared at the city’s magistrates court charged with violent disorder and assaulting a police constable.

A 16-year-old boy from Waterlooville was also arrested on suspicion of violent disorder in connection with last Sunday’s events. He has been released on bail until 12 December.

Anti-immigration activists returned to the streets of Portsmouth on Saturday afternoon, where they faced counter-protests from anti-racism groups.

Tony Rowlinson, assistant chief constable, said the scenes at Eastney Marina had gone beyond peaceful protest. “Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest,” he said. “Clearly events on Sunday evening were not peaceful protest, rather violent public disorder.”

Rowlinson said officers had worked to protect people in the area and warned that police would pursue those responsible after reviewing footage.

“The reality of public order policing is that arrests at the time are not always possible, especially where evidence may need to be reviewed to clearly identify who is responsible for offences,” he said.

He added that none of the seven injured officers had been seriously hurt, but said they “did not deserve to be assaulted” while policing the demonstration.

Police also said they were investigating online threats and abuse directed at officers and staff from partner agencies after the disorder.

The force has appealed to anyone who recognises the six men to contact police on 101 or report information online, quoting reference 44260435943.

Rowlinson said: “If you break the law we will take action against you and where it is feasible to do so seek a prosecution.”

Stephen Fleming inherits intriguing squad after England’s unsettling summer

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:23:00 GMT

New Test head coach’s arrival and Root’s calming influence as captain add to promising signs in the post-Stokes era

As Joe Root calmly ran the rule over the Test summer and reeled off the ways in which it had been “chaos”, “unusual” and “unsettling” for England, it felt telling that first among them was Ben Stokes calling time on his international career during a match and a series that were both still live at the time.

Cricketers announcing their retirement mid-game is nothing new. Heather Knight went on to do the same during the women’s Test at Lord’s two weeks later. Root is also too loyal to Stokes to question openly whether that scene-stealing exit before New Zealand’s win at Trent Bridge was entirely in keeping with his call for “selfless cricketers” four years earlier.

But even with two drink-related incidents either side, it was the week when England bottomed out: their first home defeat for 14 years in a series of three or more Tests, and one that had the Black Caps quite literally laughing in their faces during the final throes.

Since becoming unhooked from the emotions of Stokes, and realising they would never shake the stigma of Bazball without Brendon McCullum’s removal as Test head coach, things have settled down a touch for England (the sight of Brydon Carse in handcuffs in Derby, Stokes lurking in the shadows, notwithstanding).

They also got a taste of how New Zealand felt in June, or Australia during the Ashes last winter, claiming the win but seeing the losers hog much of the focus. For all that the 21‑year‑old Razaullah deserved the headlines at Edgbaston, with his jaw-dropping 81 in keeping with south Birmingham’s love for unexpected fireworks, Pakistan were a reminder that there are different levels of dysfunction.

Scraps with Saracens players? A curfew that may or may not have been spelled out correctly? I’ll raise you seven players sent home, a head coach and bowling coach likewise, mobile phones seized, and a light shone on a government-run board that would sooner no one thought about the plight of the country’s greatest captain. As Saj Sadiq, the editor of PakPassion. net and someone who has seen it all over the years, neatly put it: “As an entire series, this has been the most embarrassing and difficult to watch. On and off the field Pakistan have been an absolute shambles.”

For all that Pakistan were easy-beats, it would be wrong to call this a wasted summer for England. Stephen Fleming may not be arriving in the UK until this week (Root is itching to finally meet his new head coach in person after a long-distance courtship) but he will have learned a fair bit about the team he inherits while catching up with the highlights over his cornflakes in Canterbury.

For one, a promising stable of fast bowlers is emerging. Ollie Robinson has returned to devastating effect, Jofra Archer’s appetite for Test cricket lives on beyond Stokes, while Josh Tongue has hardened up physically and is becoming a significant weapon. Gus Atkinson’s returns dipped after the Rex Rooms and a change of role, but it was also the quickest that England’s quiet man has bowled across a season.

There are caveats, of course. The ball dominated the bat – a wicket every 41 deliveries led to the lowest strike-rate in England since the 1880s – and Pakistan’s batters were a wet paper bag in terms of resistance. The one time conditions eased – a good Edgbaston pitch, plus a ball that went soft after getting damp the previous evening – England lacked a bit of bite and struggled for breakthroughs.

Root also had a couple of familiar nightmares against the tail; Razaullah’s assault and when standing in for Stokes at the Oval in June. Marcus Trescothick, the interim head coach against Pakistan but unsure of his future place in the Test setup, fancies Fleming will be a good fit for Root here, as a tactically astute captain and the most decorated coach in the hothouse of the Indian Premier League.

What lies beneath the four first‑choice quicks is a question mark as thoughts turn to South Africa in December. A personal view is that Olly Stone’s late‑summer county form with Nottinghamshire should help him leapfrog the kids on the cab rank. And clearly the lack of a frontline spinner continues. One wonders if Fleming will want a Daniel Vettori-type – multifunctional – with Liam Patterson-White one such candidate.

Fleming’s own experiences as a player may also be relevant to a batting lineup that racked up 23 half-centuries this summer, with only Ben Duckett going past three figures. Fleming scored 10 before his first Test century, so may be able to ease the pressure that Dan Lawrence, for example, keeps putting on himself.

Every team strives for a settled lineup but Fleming may like the current tension for spots that will require a tricky call when Jacob Bethell is fit. Emilio Gay, likely to tour but already seeing his ceiling questioned, looks most vulnerable in terms of the XI. But this will mean manufacturing an opener to partner Duckett, who aside from his 113 at Trent Bridge has seemed caught in two minds post-Bazball.

Jordan Cox may be the one pushed up which, given the ninth over was the latest the No 3 appeared against Pakistan, is not a huge change of role. While like Lawrence he fell short of a defining score, settling for three half-centuries, Cox made an impression through his presence at the crease; almost cocksure, with Root admitting: “I didn’t really know what to make of him when I first met him.”

Cox has said on record that he has been trying to outdo Root which, while made easier by one of the captain’s quieter summers, is a pretty high bar of 14,000‑plus Test runs. But it’s probably also the template for this team post‑Stokes: to look to their captain not for inspirational moments or residual aura but as the quieter embodiment of what is required to thrive at Test level.
