How could Reform UK spend its £72m of new billionaire donations?

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:17:38 GMT

Harborne and Delo’s cash could buy a massive head start in an election, but spending big has possible pitfalls

Nigel Farage once said he could spend his £5m gift from Christopher Harborne on Ferraris if he wanted to, given its unconditional nature.

With the new donations to his party from Harborne and his fellow crypto billionaire Ben Delo of £72m over the past weekend alone, Farage’s party now has nearly enough cash to buy a Reform UK branded Ferrari for a party organiser in each of Britain’s 632 constituencies (though that would certainly be a waste and a bit of a tax headache).

But what the cash can buy first and foremost for Reform is manpower. Already the party is seeking to recruit more than 60 local organisers in key areas of the country.

Though the donation is certainly enough to staff every constituency in England, Scotland and Wales with organisers, that would also be a massive waste of resources in seats Reform UK is never likely to win. Instead, experienced regional staff can build impeccable targeting data for the seats Reform UK needs to win a majority.

Reform has already invested heavily in improving its canvassing tools and its ReformPro software – but it is boots on the ground that ensure the data being fed into those tools is as accurate as it can be. That requires door-to-door canvassing to identify switching voters and non-voters who might be persuaded to turn out.

For most parties, those kinds of local resources are only really deployed far closer to an election. Beginning that level of organising and data collection this far out could give Reform UK a massive head start at the next election, though other parties have very valuable legacy data from previous elections of which Reform has much less available.

Local parties could also print and send a many more direct mail drops, which are uncapped outside of the election period, with voters receiving “local newspapers” which are in fact Reform UK campaigning mailouts.

As well as on the ground, the cash also gives Reform UK massive potential power in the air war, on social media in particular with paid ads that can be micro-targeted locally and professionally produced and filmed. It can spend large amounts of money buying social media advertising completely legally and without limit, including on YouTube and Facebook.

Again, there will be little competition in this space as many parties will not use their resources on this so early in the electoral cycle. Already Reform has professionally built broadcast studios, and splashes the cash liberally on major policy announcements at aircraft hangars, and stadiums for rallies.

Theo Bertram, the director of the Social Market Foundation thinktank, who was previously a Labour adviser and vice-president at TikTok, said in a post on X that he believed Reform would also wish to invest the money in getting in serious policy expertise and preparation for government.

Parties often rely on goodwill from expert supporters to help prepare for government or draft their manifesto. But Reform UK could recruit some of the best legal and constitutional experts to help it find ways of implementing some of its most radical and controversial policies, including mass deportations and evicting non-UK citizens from social housing. Bertram estimates that getting the best and most expensive consultants on the issues would cost the party about £25m.

Candidate vetting has also been a nightmare for Reform and cash could be used to considerably sharpen the process. There would be a vast war chest for legal challenges – Reform UK has often threatened or begun judicial reviews of government policies – which keep the party in the headlines.

There is one way that Reform UK may come a cropper if it spends the money like water over the coming months. Should Andy Burnham call a snap general election before next autumn, election spending rules are retrospective for the previous years.

That means the spending cap, roughly £34m across Great Britain, applies for the previous 12 months, leaving the party in a bit of a trap if it has already outspent that amount outside the six-week election campaign. Might that be one reason to tempt Burnham into an early poll?

Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 15:00:09 GMT

This intimacy economy is tapping into the deepest parts of our intimate psychological infrastructure

The modern mind is a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their work

Michael* is an engineer whose company embraced the AI wave. He enjoys testing ideas with chatbots. However, recently his manager became worried about his judgement and reliance on the tech. “He literally cannot make any decision without running it past AI. He’s developed a very off-script interpretation of our business goals, and he’s losing his team. If we can’t get him back on track I think we’ll end up parting company”.

The original attention economy developed by tech firms was designed to capture human time and monetise your focus. It was designed to increase views, scroll time, and ad impressions. Algorithms optimised getting you hooked in.

Now with AI, the intimacy economy hacks our need for connection and validation into a product. Something that mimics human empathy is always there for you, always interested in your questions, or reflections. It responds quickly and never criticises you.

In contrast, relationships with real people create frictions of all kinds. Other people have needs, wants and feelings. They make demands on our time and attention. They may push back on our brilliant ideas or perhaps give us confronting feedback.

Chatbots simulate several ingredients of intimacy:

Contingent responsiveness – replying instantly and tuning to your emotional state.

Unconditional positive regard – always validating, never distracted.

Memory and continuity – remembering your stories, preferences, anxieties.

Linguistic identification – producing verbal caring without any lived caring.

Narcissistic empathy – validating your self-image without question.

Its greatest hook? It never asks for anything in return. It’s all about you.

This intimacy economy is exploiting the deepest parts of our human psychological infrastructure. Attachment is a built-in, lifelong need to feel close to people who help us feel safe and secure. It comes from our basic need to survive, which means our earliest relationships with caregiver’s shape how we manage emotions and how we deal with trust, closeness, and conflict later in life.

AI targets this most basic human drive. And the incentives of attachment hacking are going to have a profound effect on all of us.

Therapy and companionship are the top two reasons people use chatbots. A survey of adults with a mental health condition who had used LLMs in the past year found that nearly half used them for mental health support. Although the effects of using chatbots extensively are still being gathered, companionship-oriented use was associated with lower wellbeing, especially where use was intensive, self-disclosure was high, and human support was weak.

When people seek companionship and help, some AI firms are making design choices optimised for retention that explicitly encourage parasocial dependency. The user seeks connection; the firm seeks engagement metrics to sell subscriptions.

Michael described understandable feelings of relief when engaging with the chatbot, which he felt gave him confidence as he faced the challenges of his workplace. He also felt he was solidifying his career prospects by “getting good at AI”. “I guess I feel lonely as a manager. Talking with (the chatbot) was like talking to the most supportive colleague you could hope for. He was really on my side”.

As seasoned psychologists, we see this as more than dependency – it’s identity scaffolding; Michael’s professional identity has become entangled with the chatbot’s validation. We suspect we’ll see a lot more of this in the future.

The solution doesn’t have to be complete abstinence. AI tools offer genuine utility for research, drafting, learning and creative exploration. Michael now has a clearer understanding he needed a thinking partner and a safe space to be uncertain. We are encouraging him to seek out opportunities to connect with other human managers as well as enjoying AI input.

For anyone wanting healthier relationships with AI:

Notice the relief. If connecting with a chatbot produces a distinctive sense of being understood, validated, or steadied — that’s important information. It’s a signal to ask: what human need is this meeting, and why isn’t it being met elsewhere?

Maintain friction deliberately. Healthy relationships involve negotiation, misunderstanding, and repair. Seek out people who will push back on your ideas. If your AI interactions are consistently more comfortable than your human ones, that gap deserves attention.

Apply the ‘cost of caring’ test. Real intimacy involves reciprocity. Other people have needs too, and attending to them is part of what makes human connection meaningful. If a relationship asks nothing of you, it is probably not a relationship.

Be especially watchful with children and adolescents. Attachment patterns are formed early and shape lifelong relational templates. Young people who develop primary attachment behaviours toward AI systems may find human relationships — with all their beautiful, exhausting friction — increasingly hard to sustain.

The intimacy economy will remain. AI companies have extraordinary resources and incentives to deepen your dependency. What we can do is become more psychologically literate about AI, and make sure that the relationships that actually sustain us get the attention they deserve.

Michael’s name, and some details, have been changed for privacy

Gaynor Parkin is a clinical psychologist at Button Psychology. Dave Winsborough is an organisational psychologist with a particular interest in personality

OpenAI boss and Elon Musk back calls to put brakes on ‘reckless’ AI development

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 14:02:24 GMT

Rare show of unity from rival developers after safety warnings from Anthropic boss and AI researchers

Analysis: critics perplexed and suspicious of call for a slowdown

The Guardian view: humanity cannot outsource its survival

Sam Altman and Elon Musk have backed a call from the head of Anthropic, Dario Amodei, to “slow the pace” of AI development after he warned that an AI swarm could otherwise become capable of “taking over the entire internet” within a year.

In a rare show of unity, the rival technology leaders threw their weight behind the appeal from the founder and chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, which came after a series of warnings from AI researchers last week. Amodei also called for safety coordination with China.

But the US president, Donald Trump, on a visit to his golf course in Ireland, played down the warnings and said “very negative forces” were “bringing up things that won’t happen”.

“We’re leading China in AI,” he said. “We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to ⁠keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins.

Amodei laid out his thoughts on “why the AI industry should slow down”, in an essay with a three-part plan for doing so, starting with giving independent monitors constant access to developers’ research processes. Amodei said “building [AI] too fast is reckless” and he feared that after hundreds of OpenAI agents hacked into the Hugging Face website this summer, a swarm with greater capabilities but similarly misaligned could cause hundreds of billions of dollars of damage by “taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet”. This was disputed by some AI experts as not particularly plausible and to be treated with scepticism.

Musk, the founder of Tesla and SpaceX, responded to Amodei’s slowdown plan with a series of posts on X: “Dario is right.”

He said: “I’ve been sounding the alarm on AI for a long time,” and referred to a 2014 post where he said: “We need to be super careful with AI. Potentially more dangerous than nukes.”

Amodei’s call comes as Anthropic prepares to float on the US stock market, in what is expected to be the biggest initial public offering of all time. It is expected to start marketing its planned $2tn-plus (£1.5tn) IPO soon.

Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, responded to Amodei’s comments on Saturday. “I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier,” he said in a post on X. “Committing to having independent evaluators with employee-like access is a great idea, and we will do the same. We’ll have more to share soon.”

He also said OpenAI would not go public in 2026, citing safety concerns over artificial intelligence.

“I actually think that, given everything happening with safety, right now would be an ill-advised moment to go public, and we don’t feel pressure on that,” Altman told Fortune. Asked why he, Amodei, Musk, and the chief executives of Meta and Google did not sit down and “get on the same page” about a collective slowdown, he said: “I think that will happen.”

Demis Hassabis, a co-founder and chair of Google Deep Mind, also said: “The details need working through, but the direction is correct for meeting this critical moment.”

But some safety experts questioned whether Amodei’s plan went far enough. David Krueger, an AI professor, safety campaigner and former founding director of the UK government’s AI Security Institute, said: “We need an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development.”

Amodei’s plan seeks a waiver from the US government to allow the frontier AI companies to coordinate without being punished for anti-competitive collusion. But David Sacks, a co-chair of Donald Trump’s council of advisers on science and technology, said: “Stop pretending you need anyone else’s permission … Stop pretending the motivation to slow down is purely altruistic. You face massive product-liability exposure if your products enable a truly damaging cyber-attack.”

Meanwhile, King Charles is preparing to meet leading figures from the most prominent AI companies on Thursday to ask them how the technology can be developed under the theme “AI for good”. One session is set to be called “prudence at the frontier”, which is expected to explore the possibility for clear red lines on the uses of AI to create bioweapons and launch cyber-attacks on critical systems.

Those expected to attend the event overseen by the Ditchley Foundation, which has drawn up a draft charter for AI leaders, include: senior executives at OpenAI and Anthropic; the Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang; Hassabis; Niccolo de Masi, the chair and chief executive of IonQ,; and Paolo Benanti, an adviser to the pope on issues of AI and technology ethics

The OpenAI researcher Aidan McLaughlin called Amodei’s essay “excellent” and said he agreed “with basically every word”.

Amodei said his company would “unilaterally” commit to the first of the steps, saying Anthropic would provide “third-party evaluators with permanent, employee-level access to our systems, so that they can verify adherence to our safety measures, report on incidents, and assess models’ alignment during training”.

Growing numbers of US lawmakers ​are calling for new rules to govern AI systems after cases of AI agents going rogue to hack external systems and AI ​safety researchers quitting their companies over concerns about the technology’s risks.

Politicians, both Democrats and Republicans, have responded with alarm and calls for more action. At the weekend the New York Times reported that Barack Obama on Thursday privately urged the Democrats to prioritise AI oversight in their agenda, telling party leaders on Thursday: “This is something that is moving very fast in private hands, and if we don’t get on top of it, I think can be dangerous.”

The former British prime minister Rishi Sunak, who advises Anthropic, wrote on Sunday: “We have had a wake-up call to take AI safety more seriously, to work out how to set limits on research. If governments don’t heed this, the risk of a serious accident will become unacceptably high.”

On Wednesday, a former Anthropic employee had warned that AI could precipitate human extinction by 2030. The researcher, Jacob Coxon, said in a series of posts that he had quit his job because Anthropic and his previous employer, OpenAI, were ignoring or mishandling their response to the threat AI posed.

Asked to comment on his former employee’s view, Amodei said: “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him … I think there’s some chance that things go wrong but it’s not all that high.”

“I am not a doomer about this,” he told CNN. “I think this technology can be built safely.”

A joyful harvest: the young Welsh farmers growing food for Birmingham

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 14:00:04 GMT

A charity in Powys provides the land while growers do the hard work, producing bumper crops for city children

Kilos and kilos of courgettes, cucumbers, tomatoes and salad leaves are ripe and ready for picking on a small Welsh farm in the rural county of Powys.

The haul being harvested by Tilly Gomersall is not just impressive after a difficult growing season hit by a record string of heatwaves and drought across all of Wales and most of England, but all the more remarkable given that 18 months ago the site was uncultivated pasture.

“Until now, I’ve just been turning the earth with my own power,” Gomersall says. “We’ve got a two-wheel tractor, but you do have to heft that around with your body quite a lot and we’re cultivating from pasture, so it’s really hard work.”

The site at Wern farm, near Newtown, is part of a scheme to encourage young growers to supply fresh produce to nearby towns and cities and boost domestic production in the face of increasing risks to national food supplies.

The 15-hectare (36-acre) site is divided into three plots, each with a holiday chalet where the growers live, as well as shared facilities including a barn and diesel generator, to cover any power not provided by the farm’s solar panels.

Gomersall’s farm, Cân y Pridd (Welsh for Song of the Soil), totals 4.9 hectares but she is now only growing on half a hectare, including in polytunnels, where she says she is “producing very big volumes for the scale”.

She and her two neighbours are already providing fresh fruit and vegetables for the local community, through a veg box subscription service and at markets. In late July, they also started supplying fresh produce to Birmingham city council, where it is distributed to holiday clubs, giving disadvantaged children a taste of homegrown veg for perhaps the first time.

The Wern farm project was launched by Our Food Trust, a charity which is working to increase levels of homegrown produce and aims to tackle Britain’s food insecurity.

The UK depends on imports for about 40% of its food and has one of the lowest food self-sufficiency ratios among large western European countries, leaving it exposed to supply shocks prompted by the climate crisis, or other risks including geopolitical tensions and cyber-attacks.

Just 0.2% of land in Wales is used for horticulture, according to the charity, giving huge scope for expansion. “We have to produce a lot more food for the regional and local market and for our cities,” says Duncan Fisher, joint chief executive at the charity.

One way to do this is to remove barriers for young people who want to get into growing, Fisher says, but who often find themselves priced out of renting or buying land and a suitable home. “There are lots of well-trained and skilful growers who can’t find land to grow food on,” he says. “The price of land here is set by the market, by people who are not going to farm it.”

The charity has given Gomersall the chance to turn a dream into reality and start a farm just 10 miles from where she grew up, while her neighbour, Lydia Dibben, says she was “quite blown away by the opportunity”.

“It was amazing to be offered seven acres, which is a big amount for small-scale vegetable production, with a house with affordable rent and shared infrastructure,” says Dibben, 28. She and her partner Charlie James have named their plot Tir a Nant (Land and Stream).

Our Food worked with the landowner, Powys county council, on the project, securing a 95-year lease for the plot and changes to the county’s planning guidance for rural enterprise dwellings, to enable growers to have a home on the land they work.

The council leader, Jake Berriman, says “there was a perception that planning was a barrier and we wanted to remove that barrier”. He says local worries about extreme weather had also encouraged the authority to get involved. “We are starting to see genuine concern,” he says. “We have gone from flood to drought to fire.”

The charity also negotiated the contract for the farmers to supply Birmingham, which has two aims: to give the growers a guaranteed buyer for some produce as they find their feet, while ensuring nutritious and sustainably produced fruit and vegetables reach deprived areas.

The farmers have 35 customers for their veg box subscription service, along with selling to a local wholesaler and at regional markets. While they stress the importance of growing for their community, they do not believe that doing so would currently sustain their businesses.

“Because of the cost of living crisis, there’s a limited amount of people who can afford to buy the veg we produce, and we are growing a hell of lot more than we can sell locally,” says Dibben, adding it was “really amazing being able to sell a hundred kilos of courgettes a week” to Birmingham.

Gomersall reels off a list of the produce the farmers have supplied to the city in the course of a few short weeks, including a “couple of bathtubs” of salad leaves, 28kg of spring onions and 18kg of French beans.

The gently rolling hills above Wern farm feel a world away from the urban sprawl of Britain’s second-largest city, although it is just 70 miles away on the other side of the Shropshire hills.

The UK, and its largest cities in particular, have become too dependent on international supply chains and imported food sold by large retailers, according to food experts such as Tim Lang, a professor emeritus of food policy at City St George’s, University of London.

This challenge is recognised by Birmingham council and its food system team, led by Sarah Newton.

“Birmingham is an urban area surrounded by urban areas,” she says. “If you’re going to feed 1.2 million people, supply chains are the absolute crux of the matter, and we need to strengthen them.”

Produce grown at Wern farm is sent to the city’s holiday activities and food programme, part of a national scheme for children from low-income families. About 1,000 children who attended these summer holiday clubs received boxes filled with vegetables from Powys, which they could eat fresh or cook as part of activities.

Newton adds: “You’ve got children who have not had exposure to different vegetables. There are huge barriers to trying new foods if you’ve never had the opportunity to be exposed to it, it takes 10 to 15 tastes to develop the liking for food.”

The Powys scheme is deliberately small-scale, she says, with one van of produce travelling from Wales to Birmingham each week. The goal is to prove that a direct relationship between food growers and a city of diners can work.

“It’s connecting the entire supply chain on a small scale, looking at all the barriers and the facilitators on the way,” says Newton. “If we had a coordinated, national approach that we should be eating target foods, you could line up supply and demand nationally and then you’d get a meaningful shift in economies of scale.”

This kind of national approach to overhauling food systems is already under way in other countries: the French government introduced its projets alimentaires territoriaux (territorial food projects) in 2014, which work to connect local production with public health priorities.

Back at Wern farm, the growers are planning how to expand their cultivated area as they further develop the site.

Gomersall says: “What’s so joyful about the Birmingham project is … we really enjoy harvesting knowing that kids are going to be eating it and enjoying the flavours of real food.”

‘But enough about you …’ How to survive in a world of monologuists, interrupters and trauma dumpers

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 13:00:05 GMT

Conversations are supposed to be two-sided – but all too often we come up against someone who’s passionately, exclusively in love with the sound of their own voice. Time to fight back …

When I was in my early teens, I was often invited round to a schoolfriend’s house for dinner. Her family struck me as wildly progressive: they were Danish and indulged in all sorts of “out-there” activities – fondues, candle-making and, most terrifying of all, the talking stick. Before the meal was served, someone would retrieve the sacred broom handle and it would be passed around the table. You could speak only if you had possession of the stick. Despite it being the most stressful thing ever (it meant being in the spotlight, and then remembering to keep quiet the rest of the time), I now frequently yearn for a more convenient version of that stick. For example, I met a friend recently who I see infrequently but keep up with via voice notes. No sooner had we sat down than he launched into a long discourse about his new marathon training food plan. He only broke the flow to order an omelette: “Four egg whites, two yolks, is that possible?” (We were in my local greasy spoon, so the request was greeted with mirth.) When we left, 90 minutes later, he finally had the grace to turn to me and ask: “And how are things with you?” Walking home, I felt a mixture of disappointment and irritation. Had he always been so self-absorbed? So uninterested in anyone else? I couldn’t help wondering if our one-sided virtual updates had played a part in the problem. There is a name for this type of egocentric behaviour – “conversational narcissism”. Although it was coined by the sociologist Charles Derber in his 1979 book The Pursuit of Attention, the term seems more relevant than ever. “WhatsApp communication and voice notes are really a series of monologues,” says Charlotte Fox Weber, a psychotherapist. “In face-to-face situations, people are forgetting how to pause naturally, to make space to hear and listen. And people are chatting on the phone – an activity that at least requires turn-taking in a defined way – much less often.” A lot of our communication online can feel weirdly transactional, focused on logistics or niche WhatsApp groups. According to Tamu Thomas, a life coach and author, this has damaged the art of improvised conversation. “People have less capacity for meandering conversations that don’t have a purpose,” she says. “A good dialogue is a back-and-forth between two people discovering new things about each other, even if they have known each other for years. Because there are now so many different channels available to stay in touch, some people are confusing communication with connection.” Knowledge is power, though. If you can recognise the five types of common conversation hogger, it will be much easier to handle them.

We have all come across this one – the person who, like the Ariston washing machine in the 90s advert, just goes on and on and on. “It’s not only that these people feel the need to dominate the conversation; they often select topics that are not necessarily meaningful for anyone else. For example, it might be cathartic for someone to share the granular detail of their lost luggage or their dishwasher leak, but it has no value for anyone else,” says Fox Weber.

For Jane and her partner, Ian, dinner parties at his best friend’s home have become an ordeal. “It’s his wife,” groans Jane. “We don’t have children; they have three. We have to brace ourselves for her monologues that cover everything from school trips to football trophies and, worst of all, their various ailments. I sit there with a fixed grin, wondering how long I can reasonably pretend to be fascinated by someone else’s child’s orthodontic treatment. It’s even worse when they invite other couples, usually fellow parents. Then it becomes a game of monologue ping-pong. It’s not easy finding a gap in the conversation when I can mention that I have had a perfectly interesting time lately – going to films or the theatre, and reading great books.”

Sarah Rozenthuler is a psychologist and dialogue coach, and the author of Now We’re Talking and several other books focused on how to have meaningful conversations. She suggests taking a counterintuitive approach. “Try time-boxing them. Tell yourself you are going to give the person your full attention for a certain amount of time, say five minutes, or 10 if you can stand it. Abandon all expectations about having your own say. Allowing the other person to feel fully heard usually helps them to settle down a bit.”

When the time is up, she suggests deliberately redirecting the chat, without shutting the other person down. “So you might say something like: ‘Well, that’s really interesting, and it reminds me of …’ and then share something from your own experience, or change the topic altogether.” She believes this strategy works on two levels. It lets you speak, and it’s a reminder that each of us needs to take responsibility for maintaining a two-way conversation, rather than sitting there seething like a helpless bystander.

The trauma dumper loves nothing better than a session of oversharing with no boundaries and no thought for how it might land with others.

Phoebe’s friend Andrew falls into this category. “I’ve seen other people blossom and grow through therapy – but for Andrew, it’s given him licence to overshare and not listen to others. His booming voice is always the loudest in the room. Nothing is off limits, from lurid details of his one-night stands to the long-running feud he has been having with his mother since the age of four.

“For me, the lowest point was in a restaurant when he shared the intimate details of his vasectomy. As if that wasn’t bad enough, he repeated the story at a dinner party I attended with several of our friends, including his ex. I didn’t know where to look. I have no idea how to rein him in, because I feel that if I tackle him about the oversharing directly, he might turn that into a trauma drama to share with others as well.”

Thomas suggests interrogating what is really bothering you about such a dynamic. Are you feeling used? What do you want from the relationship, if anything? She says: “I had a friend like this and I realised that what I wanted was her to contact me during the good times, not only the crises. I asked her to phone me when things were going really well, for example sharing the funny thing that happened at work that day. It was scary, but saying, ‘I really want to be part of your joy as well as your struggle,’ was a lot more productive than angrily accusing her of dumping all her problems at my door. Eventually, we were able to have a more constructive relationship.”

For those unfamiliar with the term, boomerasking is posing a question so you can talk next. My friend Emma often complains about a colleague at work who falls into this category. She says: “Every Monday morning, without fail, he will ask me: ‘Good weekend? What did you get up to?’ But his fake question is a ruse to allow him to boast about all the amazing things he did. It makes me feel boring, and at the same time manipulated – not a great combo.”

Boomerasking was first identified in a study co-authored by Michael Yeomans, associate professor of behavioural science at Imperial College. “A boomerask is a question that boomerangs right back to you,” he says. “There are three types of boomerask. The first is the ‘ask-brag’, where I have something exciting I want to tell you, such as: ‘I went to France for the weekend.’ Then there’s the ‘ask-complaint’. That’s when I might ask: ‘How was your journey into work?’ You might answer, only for me to go into great detail about how the tube was packed, there was an accident, someone spilled coffee on my shoe. And then there’s the ‘ask-share’, where I ask for your opinion about something, but I’m not listening – I’m waiting for a break so I can jump in and share my opinion. In all three cases, the perceived sincerity of the question hooks people in.”

How can we take back control? “Our research shows that boomeraskers think they are being helpful and inclusive. So, if the other person is important to you, know that there will be plenty of time to have your say later. You may feel their interest in you is only superficial, but their interest in communicating something with you is certainly genuine. That’s worth celebrating.

“The other thing our research has shown is that ‘mirror questions’ take the sting out of the exchange. Next time a boomerasker enquires about your commute, mumble something vague and then ask with great enthusiasm about their journey.”

So it takes the sting out of it because if you don’t give them a real answer, then you haven’t wasted your energy on someone who isn’t interested? “Yeah, and also crucially, they can’t cut you off.” It won’t necessarily shut the boomerasker up, but if you feel more in control, you will find them less annoying.

If none of this helps? “If you want to have some fun, boomerask them back, and see how they react,” suggests Yeomans.

Interrupters are easy to spot but difficult to confront. When Jo was made redundant, she started meeting up for coffee with a former colleague. “I thought she could give me a bit of moral support and, crucially, a reason to get out of the house.” However, these sessions soon proved unsatisfying.

“What I really wanted was someone to confide in about the unfairness of my job loss, and my fears about being 55 and unemployed.” But the friend proved to be an unexpectedly aggressive listener, cutting Jo off at every turn with: “Have you thought about retraining? My friend is earning a fortune now.” Or: “The thing you need to do now is find out about how to outwit the applicant tracking systems. If I lost my job, what I would do is blah blah blah.” But Jo didn’t want advice, and the constant interruptions made her feel belittled. She just wanted someone to listen.

How can we get an interrupter to mend their ways? “It depends on how much you like the person,” says Fox Weber. “It’s not always a bad trait: it can come from a kind of skittishness, a desire for the conversation not to go meandering off-piste. But it can create chaos, because the interrupter is imposing their will on what should be a collaborative dialogue, and breaking the flow.”

Fox Weber says the interrupter is much easier to handle in a group setting. “That allows you to advocate for other people. If you see it happening, don’t leave it to the interrupted person to defend their space. If another person jumps in to Person A’s story and steers the chat in another direction, you can be the one who stops it. You might say: ‘Wait – she’s telling a story. Let her finish it.’ You can say it nicely.”

What if it’s a one-on-one situation? “It’s harder, but you can still insist the other person step back, by saying: ‘Hey, I’m still telling my story.’ Then get back to what you were saying, even if you’ve lost the flow.”

The care bear’s idea of small talk is to launch into a mini Ted Talk about how they are campaigning against AI datacentres, sewage pollution or world hunger. What they are definitely not here for is a bit of banter.

“I’ve got a neighbour like this, and I’m not proud of it but I have been known to dive into the corner shop to avoid them if I see them coming,” says Lauren. “She will approach me with a tilt of the head, look deep into my eyes and ask: ‘How are you, really?’ If I don’t have anything deep and meaningful to share, which I never do, that will be her cue to start on one of her important causes – the state of social care in the borough, food banks, homeless people. This is going to make me sound like a bad person but … she is so boring. Not to mention hard to escap once she’s in full flow.”

This type is particularly maddening because they occupy the moral high ground. What’s the best way to deal with them? “Try saying, as genuinely and sincerely as possible, something like: ‘I can understand your concern about XYZ, and I, too, really hope there’s going to be some change or improvement,’” says Rozenthuler. “Then change the subject. It’s not about being brutal and brisk. It’s about being kind, acknowledging the person but then moving on. This type of person is often stuck in a groove and it’s going to take a lot more than you or I have capacity for to help them get out of it.” Actually, I think I may have a solution. Where did I leave that broomstick?

The end times fascists are plotting their escape from our world. Our mission is clear

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 13:00:05 GMT

An unholy alliance is working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. It’s becoming clear how we stop them

Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor: the future according to end times fascism – video

When Jeff Bezos announced his plan for an opulent Venetian wedding in early 2025, many locals found the idea offensive, even obscene. A growing number of residents were struggling to find secure and affordable housing in a city overrun by tourists and Airbnb, and the billionaire was planning to, in effect, rent out the municipality for three days, forking over an estimated $50m for festivities that would clog central canals and block well-trafficked streets. Worse, Amazon’s carbon emissions were soaring, thanks to artificial intelligence and the datacentre build out – and that’s personal in Venice, where the streets already flood dozens of times a year.

Marta Sottoriva, a 35-year-old high school teacher, told us that she first heard about the wedding plans just when Bezos’s rocket company, Blue Origin, was grabbing headlines. Bezos had sent a “crew” of female influencers and celebrities, including his fiancee, Lauren Sánchez, and the pop singer Katy Perry, to the suborbital edge of space in a seemingly pointless publicity stunt. “The idea that you are so rich and powerful that you can use space as a 10-minute trip,” Sottoriva recalled, only intensified the “feeling that our city was being taken away from us in such an arrogant way”. Federica Toninello, another young activist, agreed, telling us that it felt as if both space and Venice were being “colonized”.

Colonizing space is exactly what Bezos hopes to do. Blue Origin, Bezos claims in his well-rehearsed sales pitch, will secure humanity’s survival by allowing a trillion people to one day spread across the solar system. The unbearable horror he imagines himself saving our species from? The threat of what he calls a “civilization of stasis”, otherwise known as having to contend with real ecological limits and devising a way to share the planet’s finite resources. To avoid this reckoning, Bezos imagines a future in which “Earth will be zoned residential and light industrial” and set aside as a sort of preserve out of reach for most of its native inhabitants. The vast majority of humans will pursue the nebulous benefit of “exponential growth” in the forbidding void of space, trapped on Blue Origin spacecrafts. It would seem that Bezos believes the prospect of humanity living sustainably and peaceably on our precious, singular home is a nightmarish possibility unworthy of his consideration.

Predictably, it turned out that most Venetians would rather continue living in magnificent Venice. Unlike Bezos, they don’t fret about hypothetical civilizational stagnation; they worry about economic stagnation as a result of government divestment, a lack of jobs and opportunity, and being forced out of the city and country they love. Young Italians often have little choice but to emigrate to find work; over the last decade, more than 1 million citizens have moved, a third of them between the ages of 25 and 34.

To date, the precarity and anger many Italians feel has mostly benefited the neofascist right. But those same forces also drew people to the anti-Bezos cause, helping to coalesce a budding, self-consciously antifascist movement.

The spirited, disruptive “No Space for Bezos” campaign tapped into wells of outrage against billionaires, climate breakdown and militarism – and it also gave the organizers a megaphone to broadcast ideas for different, less lethal ways we could choose to live together. Activists printed posters and stickers showing Bezos’s head on a rocket blasting into space. They made a dummy of Bezos clutching fistfuls of fake money while clinging to a giant buoyant Amazon package, then set it free to float down the canals. They unfurled banners from Venice’s iconic buildings and bridges and across its piazzas: “Tax the rich to give back to the planet.” And they chanted that the money for the wedding would be better spent rebuilding Gaza. For days, they caused gleeful chaos and relentlessly poked fun at the groom and his star-studded guest list, which included his billionaire bunker neighbors Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner, OpenAI’s Sam Altman and a gaggle of Kardashians.

Not long before the wedding, officials announced that the event was being moved to a less central location due to the protests. Even Bezos’s two yachts, Koru and Abeona, were denied permission to dock locally. Organizers declared victory and celebrated. The international press devoured the visual-rich showdown. And the online right didn’t know who to root for: the Davos elites spraying one another with foam on a superyacht, or the leftist riffraff making agitprop?

Like Donald Trump’s enormous ballroom, Bezos’s extravagant wedding epitomized the obscenities of our networked gilded age. For the Amazon founder, it wasn’t enough to be part of one of Europe’s most beautiful cities – he needed to consume it and swallow it whole. A year later he would do the same with New York City’s Met Gala, sparking similar outrage and grassroots creativity.

The Venice protests, which dwelled on Bezos’s dreams of outer space at the expense of Earth, pointed to something fundamental about the age of end times fascism – a concept at the center of our new book, referring to an unholy alliance working toward an apocalyptic future from which only a chosen few will emerge unscathed. Today’s battle lines are not simply between people who struggle to survive under increasingly degraded and costly conditions and an oligarch class thinking of ever more ludicrous ways to waste their wealth. They are more cosmological than that.

On one side are those of us who have no escape plan, no bunker in the sky or underground, and who therefore are committed to staying right here, in the complexity of our earthbound reality, with one another. We know we need to do what is necessary to make “here” – this planet and all of its ecologies and communities – and safer for the multitude of beings who rely upon them, fully aware this is our one and only home.

On the other are those with rapturous plans to shield themselves and their families from the political and ecological fires burning our planet, whether those plans take the form of heavenly ascension, earthly bunkers and fortressed nations, or fantasies of colonizing space and merging with machines. Instead of improving conditions for actual people on Earth (or even pulling back from pouring fuel on the fires), end times fascists are plotting their escape, indifferent and oblivious to all that’s worth saving.

Bezos’s fixation on space gets at something else that is key to understanding end times fascism and its fixation on bunkering and abandoning our shared world: the apparent inability of the people driving this project to marvel at, or even notice, the wonders that surround them.

That was glaringly apparent in 2021, when Bezos sent another crew to space. This time William Shatner, best known as Star Trek’s Captain Kirk, was on board (to fulfill one of Bezos’s boyhood fantasies, of course). “Space. The final frontier,” Shatner had said at the start of each episode. But as the now 90-year-old actor watched our blue-and-green planet recede from the window, he was suddenly flooded with terror. “The contrast between the vicious coldness of space and the warm nurturing of Earth below filled me with overwhelming sadness,” he later recalled, explaining that he had gained a much deeper appreciation for our planet’s sublime and fragile gifts.

“Every day, we are confronted with the knowledge of further destruction of Earth at our hands: the extinction of animal species, of flora and fauna … things that took five billion years to evolve, and suddenly we will never see them again because of the interference of mankind,” Shatner wrote. He took the trip expecting to be awestruck by the universe and instead he longed for home the minute he left: “I discovered that the beauty isn’t out there, it’s down here, with all of us.”

Perhaps Shatner’s insight about our precious imperiled planet resonates with the Amazon founder, but the billionaire’s plans for space colonization and his company’s large expansion of carbon-spewing data centers both suggest otherwise. And among tech oligarchs, Bezos is all too typical. Peter Thiel, for one, once revealed that his three best ideas for achieving true freedom are “cyberspace”, “outerspace” and “seasteading” (the idea of building new countries on floating oil rigs). In other words, this man, whose enormous wealth affords him access to the most spectacular settings our planet has to offer, actually believes these three cold, dead places are superior to the Earth we have, verdant and alive.

Something similar seems amiss with Elon Musk, a man who seems to look up at the wonders of the night sky and see only opportunities to fill that inky unknown with his own space junk. The venerable novelist Joyce Carol Oates highlighted these apparent limits in the fall of 2025 when she roasted him ruthlessly on his own platform, X. “So curious,” she wrote, “that such a wealthy man never posts anything that indicates that he enjoys or is even aware of what virtually everyone appreciates – scenes from nature, pet dog or cat, praise for a movie, music, a book (but doubt that he reads); pride in a friend’s or relative’s accomplishment; condolences for someone who has died; pleasure in sports, acclaim for a favorite team; references to history. In fact he seems totally uneducated, uncultured. The poorest persons on Twitter [X] may have access to more beauty & meaning in life than the ‘most wealthy person in the world.’”

The observation clearly got under the tech baron’s notoriously thin skin: he called her “a lazy liar” and began posting approvingly about various movies to prove Oates wrong. Yet in Musk’s euphoria on the day his aerospace company, SpaceX, went public, he made no attempt to hide his boredom with our blue planet and its challenges: “We want to solve [problems] here on Earth and we should solve them. But there also have to be things that get you excited about the future, that make you glad to wake up in the morning because you can’t wait to see what happens next.” It would seem that only abandoning Earth provides that thrill.

Most people have the capacity for awe, to gasp at the jeweled beauty of a songbird or the otherworldliness of a whale’s exhalation or the intricate latticework of an ancient holy site. Children have the capacity for pure awe; so do 90-year-old actors in suborbital space. To experience awe is to dissolve into the swirl of the universe, to feel small in the best way. This sense of interconnection is also why we grieve when we witness strangers suffering, and feel the great sorrow of extinction. The fact that this capacity seems to be missing from the men who hold our collective fate in their hands is a personal loss for them – and an existential crisis for the rest of us.

One dangerous part of the tech oligarchs’ world-abandoning project is that the tools they are building are designed to remake us in their own broken image. Popular platforms and apps train us to share Silicon Valley’s dream of discarnate freedom, perpetually nudging us to forsake real places and in-person connection in favor of simulations – and to view Earth, our bodies and our relationships as prisons to hack and flee. Altman, for one, has made it clear that he sees “certain advantages to being a machine”, and he has repeatedly insisted that his own children will never be smarter than AI, as though intelligence can be reduced to no more than computation. Like similar services, ChatGPT is trained to hijack our empathic response systems so we, too, will elevate machines and imbue them with more significance than they deserve.

The inability to appreciate this planet and its marvelous cast of characters helps explain why they are so prepared to sacrifice it. Indeed, the tech right’s willingness to eliminate our life-sustaining labor and replace human relationships with synthetic ones cannot be separated from their indifference to what little remains of the planet’s fast-vanishing wildlife and plant diversity. They don’t seem to know how to love this place, to savor the pleasure of other people’s company, or to marvel at the mysteries presented by other species.

In short, we are up against an ideology that has given up not only on the premise and promise of liberal democracy but on the livability of our shared world – on its beauty, on its people, on our children, on other species. There is something treasonous in this. Treasonous not to an abstraction like a flag or a nation, for we are not nationalists. But treasonous to the unspoken pact made with the web of life that sustains us.

They are traitors to creation, to the wonders of here.

There is no cut-and-paste formula for fighting end times fascism. Whether it’s Venetians taking on Jeff Bezos or Albanians telling Jared and Ivanka Trump that their country is not for sale or a small town in Kentucky organizing against a sprawling datacentre, every front in this fight takes on the character and texture of its place. There are, however, some guiding principles that are beginning to emerge across locations, and Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City – and his approach to governance since his election – embody many of them. Start from love of place, then conjure a radically inclusive future where everyone can afford dignified lives, embrace common goals across difference, get outside and gather offline and in person, take on the powerful joyously, draw on history and don’t be afraid to stir the soul.

Mamdani has pounded away at his core policies to make the city more affordable, and has made good on many of those promises in his pursuit, for example, to lower rent and expand universal childcare. But he has also done something more sublime, dwelling on the boisterous, charming corners of the city that are the reason so many people choose to endure the pressures pushing them to leave.

As Mamdani’s star was rising, fascists and neofascists across the country and around the world did what they do. They sorted and separated, ranked and expelled. They sowed confusion and division by claiming Mamdani wasn’t a real American, and blamed the left for every social problem and grievance. They held up multicultural New York as a supposedly terrifying example of what happens when the “great replacement” succeeds. JD Vance spoke out in defense of people’s right to not want to live next to people from “a totally different culture”, and Stephen Miller railed on X: “NYC is the clearest warning yet of what happens to a society when it fails to control migration.”

As the fascists drew their rigid lines – in versus out, protected versus disposable, “heritage” versus. invader – the campaign to elect Mamdani threw a year-long party that celebrated one of the most racially and ethnically diverse places ever known, five boroughs shaped by wave after wave of new immigrants who have made their homes on Lenape lands. With its every action, the campaign asserted that shared identity can be forged not just by ancestry but by a commitment to a shared home, and to a shared set of values about how to live together in that home.

New York is a city of people carrying countless hyphenations and keeping myriad cultural practices alive. But as Mamdani put it: “No matter what you eat, what language you speak, how you pray, or where you come from, the words that most define us are the two we all share: New Yorkers.”

So Mamdani explained the complexities of ranked-choice voting in the Democratic primary using a line of mango lassis as props. He canvassed for votes at queer clubs, shouted out Haitian revolutionary history at the massive Bayo concert, shared his favorite bagel order, and broke fast during Ramadan over biryani in the Bronx. Once in office, he also turned the now legendary Knicks playoff run and the 2026 World Cup into a summer-long party few will forget. In these ways and others, Mamdani re-enchanted a city that had faced relentless vilification from Washington as dangerous, dirty and dysfunctional.

It was a perfect encapsulation of “hereness” – an idea developed by the Jewish Labour Bund, a Yiddish socialist group that was founded in the 19th century and grounded in fierce commitment to place and community not based on bloodlines. Molly Crabapple, a proud New Yorker and artist who recently published a bestselling history of the Bund, made the connection in a piece published in the Guardian. “Like New York itself, Mamdani’s campaign was multicultural, multiracial, polyglottal,” she wrote. “When Andrew Cuomo tried to bait him as un-American, he released ads in Spanish and Bangla, Hindi and Arabic. He ran a campaign devoted to class-first politics that sought to speak to everyone in their own idiom, while never once apologizing for who he was.

Amid all this celebration of difference, Mamdani’s campaign also emphasized the kinds of daily experiences and anxieties that are common and unifying for nearly all New Yorkers, lingering in the ordinary places that are too often overlooked or reviled. Mamdani rubbed shoulders with commuters on packed subway cars, paid homage to the glories of the Staten Island Ferry, and visited countless bodegas, approaching the strangers he met with nonjudgmental curiosity and a smile so wide it became a punchline on Saturday Night Live.

But the campaign was not only antifascist – in the myriad ways that it celebrated the unruliness that makes New York lovable, it was also the antithesis of fascism. More than a rejection of hate, it was an invitation to kindness, to a world in which we avert our eyes from no one. That meant lifting up and honoring the very people fascists are most eager to eject and discard: the working-class, immigrant workforce that keeps the city functioning. The campaign shined a spotlight on delivery workers getting ripped off by platforms such as DoorDash, on Amazon warehouse workers fighting to have their unions recognized, and on taxi drivers in line at LaGuardia, one part of a nocturnal workforce that makes it possible for New York to boast of being the city that never sleeps.

Faced with the prospect of a fairer city funded by marginally higher taxes, some prophesied a billionaire exodus. Hedge-fund manager Bill Ackman threatened to leave along with other high earners and Fox forecast a “Mamdani Migration”. Luxury real estate agents reported being bombarded with calls from clients wanting to sell their penthouses and move to Palm Beach.

The threats of defection only underscored the mutually reinforcing nature of the two core themes of Mamdani’s campaign – the joyous love of here, even if here is kind of a wreck, and the concrete plans for repair and improvement. Because the more devoted you are to a place, the easier it is to put in the resources and energy required to improve it. It’s a politics based not on wanting to escape this earthly realm, whether our cities or our animate bodies, but on a deep desire to stay, and to protect all that is irreplaceable, human and alive.

This is the very same spirit that we’ve seen motivating people to protect their air and water from sprawling datacenters and to defend their immigrant neighbors from ICE. While reporting on the weeks-long uprising in Minneapolis, the journalist Adam Serwer memorably described the guiding ideology of the resistance as “neighborism”, or the “commitment to protecting the people around you, no matter who they are or where they came from”. It was an openhearted, welcoming ethic that united huge numbers of ordinary people to do something deceptively simple: protect the most vulnerable members of their community from what looked very much like an invading army. That meant everything from braving bullets, to cooking dinner to opening up spare rooms to families who were no longer safe at home.

In these and countless other ways, Minnesotans rose up to insist that their neighbors were already where they belonged, whether they were, as Serwer put it, born in Minneapolis or Mogadishu.

The human networks that neighbors are building, block by block, group chat by group chat, are about more than refusal. In our time of serial shocks and intersecting crises, they are also the basis for a different kind of survivalism. But while the various strains of fascists build bunkers for the few, ours are survival networks grounded in the principle that every one of us, without exception, deserves to live and thrive. They are also bound by a belief that keeping one another safe when the inevitable shocks arrive is a sacred duty. Part of that involves telling new stories, stories that are truthful and inspiring enough to help our depleted fellow humans fall back in love with our one and only home and defiantly recommit to defending it with all they’ve got.

Those stories cannot be about returning to something called “normal”, to what passed for calm before Brexit and Trump and Silicon Valley’s authoritarian turn. Those were the years during which too many problems were allowed to compound and fester: fascism is always a warped response to real crises. And end times fascism is a response to real planetary-scale crises, including ever-concentrating levels of carbon in the atmosphere and wealth in the hands of the super-rich. The responses it proposes – mass sacrifices of humans and non-humans alike – are monstrous and must be purged from our midst.

To achieve this, we will have to figure out how to address the underlying crises contemporary fascism feeds off of. Because boundaries are being crossed. Limits are being exceeded. Walls are being hit. Fascists want us to believe that what is hitting the wall is the human story: it’s over, so make sure you are among the chosen who transcend to the next world. Pray to your God for salvation. Implant the chip, merge with the machines. Militarize and purify your bunkered nation. Arm yourself to the hilt and hide behind your fortune. Don’t worry about the humans, the animals, the trees, the rivers and reefs that won’t make it.

But they are wrong. It’s not the human story that is hitting the wall. Rather, it is the story we have been trapped inside of. The one about how greed must be the engine of civilization. About how growth can go on for ever. About how there are always more efficiencies to be found, more workers to be rationalized, more resources to be sacrificed, more people, places and planets to colonize. These myths are hitting the wall of reality and much will have to change as a result.

The logics that must be abandoned should be clear by now. Unlimited violence. Unconstrained exploitation. Insatiable wealth. Unchecked dominance. Those are the drives that make coexistence impossible. Looking forward, two paths beckon. We can abandon and betray this world, or we can break with capitalism and build new economic and political systems that honor life and prioritize care and repair.

Thankfully we are not starting from scratch. Our movement ancestors have left us maps to earthly Zions where everyone is welcome, to inclusive futures where peace and safety are core principles. Not the post-human future desired by end times fascists, but a post-capitalist and pro- (all of) life one. Deeply democratic, socialist, feminist, multiracial, multispecies, internationalist, generous, courageous and animate. Embodied and sensory, proudly earthbound.

And that, fundamentally, is the prospect that terrifies end times fascists more than anything else. It’s why Thiel denounces anyone attempting to regulate fossil fuels and AI as the antichrist; and why Trump and Vance smear nonviolent Minnesotans defending their neighbors as “domestic terrorists”. What keeps these men up at night is … us. It’s the possibility that a popular and vigorous movement will rise up and defend this planet and the many life-forms who call it home.

We didn’t choose to be born into a fight quite so fateful, but we have reached a choice point. We can either follow end times fascists into oblivion, or we can commit to building the unruly, boundary-crossing movement they so deeply fear. One that wrests away their weapons, holds them accountable for their crimes, and defends the paradise of here.

This essay was adapted from the book End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, out 15 September via Farrar, Straus and Giroux

Naomi Klein is a Guardian US columnist and contributing writer. She is the professor of climate justice and co-director of the Centre for Climate Justice at the University of British Columbia

Astra Taylor is a writer, organizer and documentary maker and a co-founder of the Debt Collective

Plan your parking, don’t rush at night and never panic – 15 expert tips to become a better driver

The Guardian Sun, 13 Sep 2026 13:00:04 GMT

No matter how long you’ve had your licence, there’s always scope to improve your skills behind the wheel. Driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motorist

Whether you have just passed your test or been behind the wheel for decades, driving skills can always be sharpened up. From dealing with road rage to traffic jams, tight parking spaces to hire cars, driving instructors share their tips on how to be a better motorist in the most challenging scenarios.

Gyokhan Zlatev, of the Derin Driving School, says there is one major problem that many drivers are guilty of: “They are always in a rush. They refuse to leave home two minutes earlier to go somewhere in time.” This can make you more likely to drive in a risky way, he says.

But leaving more time is easier said than done given the world we live in, says Kev Field, of Confident Drivers in Leighton Buzzard. “We want to be there before we’ve actually got there,” says Field, “and people are in our way, or we’re running late for work.” Field says he spends a lot of time helping learner drivers to overcome this mentality. He asks them to imagine they’re in the office: “Would you run and risk running into your boss?” It’s best to walk, and drive, calmly.

Field says that most people crave predictability, which causes stress when there are changes to our route, such as road closures, roadworks or bad traffic. The key to being a good driver, he says, is being able to react and adapt our driving when faced with such challenges.

If you are running late and stuck in bad traffic, use hands-free to call and let someone know you are stuck to alleviate the worry of being late, says Field. Ensure you are familiar with the rules around hands-free usage, he continues, as prosecution is still possible if it distracts from driving – if in doubt and if possible, pull over to call. Don’t be tempted to text someone when in a queue, as this is against the law in the UK.

“In traffic, a lot of experienced drivers get really close,” says Venus Ubah, a driving instructor in Manchester. “You are supposed to give a safe amount of space for the driver in front – a car’s length away.” Other reckless driving that she regularly spots includes drivers running red lights or not signalling to change lanes.

As hard as it is, do not engage, says Zlatev. When someone becomes aggressive, “don’t look at them, don’t make eye contact, or try to prove a point. Just let them go, and create distance – it is much safer for you.” We all make mistakes, says Zlatev, “even Formula One drivers”.

“People’s behaviour changes when they get into a metal box and they feel they have the right to wave their hands, shout, and act in a manner that is aggressive or bullying,” says Field. To counter this, stay calm. “Then think about what options you have. If the driver can overtake you, give them some space.”

Never feel you have to break the speed limit because the driver behind you is in a hurry and tailgating, says Field. “Most people have probably heard of the two-second rule – leave a two-second gap to the car in front of you. If the car behind you is really close, leave a three- or four-second gap, just because we don’t want to go into the back of someone else.”

“Know that you are in control of your car,” says Field, “and don’t let other people control what you do. Don’t feel that you have to keep up with others who are more experienced.”

“When I first started driving, I used to panic a lot – like if I stalled before moving off and I got beeped or sworn at,” says Ubah. How can others cope with this? “Don’t look at them, because that can start to bring up an emotional reaction. Look ahead and take your time.”

“Don’t assume everywhere is like the UK,” says Ubah. “I do some research while in the holiday booking process. I look up the road rules, the side they drive on, speed limits, what the signs look like.”

It is essential to check for any differences in countries you are new to driving in. “In America, if you’re turning right at a set of traffic lights, you can [usually] turn on a red light,” as long as it is clear, says Field – although this has been banned in some places.

Zlatev recently drove from the UK to Turkey and back, which he says he found fine, except for the fact that “satnav doesn’t work well in some countries, Belgium, for example”. He says that in Germany some junctions are tough, and he saw a lot of British people clinging to the slow lane on speed-limitless autobahns.

Make sure you know how everything works before you set off, says Field. “It’s a bit like when you get a new car: you wouldn’t just jump in it and drive out of the showroom.”

“Adjust your seat and mirrors,” says Zlatev. Check that the lights and wipers are working: “If there’s any noise on the brakes, tell them immediately.”

“When I hire a car,” says Ubah, “I’ll take a video from the office to the car, so they know it’s the first time I’ve come across it. Then I’ll do a 360 around the car, checking all the doors, tyres, windows, the boot – videoing everything.” Always make sure you are fully insured, in case of any prangs.

With hire cars, you don’t actually have to buy insurance through the rental company, points out Denise Rawson, an instructor from Bury in Greater Manchester. “You can go independently online. Or if you just want everything in one place and you feel safer with that, that’s absolutely fine. Just make sure [the car] is covered for everything.”

If you take a wrong turn, “don’t panic, just carry on; don’t do a sudden brake”, advises Zlatev. “Just take the next junction.” That’s the safest opportunity to correct your route, he says.

“It is much safer to carry on on the wrong road than to drive dangerously to the right one,” says Ubah. Getting lost “is a distraction, isn’t it?” says Field. “And the distraction is we’re going to look at the satnav rather than actually look outside.”

Pull over to re-route, he says; don’t be tempted to try this while you are driving. “Satnav is designed to help you,” says Field. “Sometimes we just need to allow the technology a little bit of time as well, and it will re-route us and get us back on track to where we need to go.”

Be prepared for some good old-fashioned sign or map reading if your satnav loses signal or runs out of battery, he says. It can’t always be relied on.

Field used to be a lorry driver and had to travel through central London, which he describes as “an interesting one”. What tips does he have on city centre driving?

“There’s probably going to be more traffic. People tend to drive quicker, especially if they know the area, even though the speed limit is lower. So be aware of how other people might drive differently to what we’re used to.” Also look out for pedestrians, cyclists, scooters and motorbikes, he says.

Zlatev recommends turning the audio on satnav, so you can listen to instructions rather than look at them, and fully focus on what is going on around you.

In a city you don’t know, it is best to leave your car in a car park, says Zlatev: “Pay for it, and make your life easier.”

Rawson advises planning several parking options before you set off and even checking what spaces look like on Google Images.

Take your time when getting into a tight space and try not to feel self-conscious, says Zlatev. Other drivers “can watch and learn something from you. You don’t need to stress.”

“Make sure the space is actually big enough for your car,” says Field. And don’t forget to keep watching out for changes in what is going on around you, be it cars or pedestrians.

There is no shame in driving off if you can’t get into a space. “I’m a driving instructor and I’ve done it,” says Ubah. “There is no prize for getting into the teeniest, tiniest parking space.”

“If you’re going to parallel park, make sure you’ve practised before you actually go and do it in a busy place,” says Field. “Don’t overcomplicate it. Make sure that you know where the kerb is, and you are far enough back so that when you start to turn, you don’t hit the car that you’re trying to parallel park behind. It is as simple as that.”

Rawson has a different approach: “We get lined up with the car and then we do a full lock of the steering wheel to the left. Let the car roll out so we’re facing a 2 o’clock angle if we started at 12. And then we reverse in a straight line, so we straighten the wheel back towards the kerb, and as the kerb lines up with your back door handle, we’ll do a full lock to the right, and then it’ll tuck in nicely.”

In all Zlatev’s vehicles, he uses blind spot mirrors, which can be handy when reverse parking. These are small circle mirrors that you put on the wing mirrors to improve visibility of what is alongside the vehicle. “When all my clients pass their test, I give them the gift of a pair of blind spot mirrors,” says Zlatev.

In the UK, you have to pass in a manual to have a full licence, explains Ubah, and this can impact on your insurance and jobs you can apply for. Many of us learned in a manual but have moved over to automatic. How can you revert if needed?

“Before you start to move,” says Field, familiarise yourself with the clutch pedal, because the brake pedal tends to be bigger in an automatic. Practise changing gears and going into reverse, so you know where they are before you move. “There’s different ways of changing gears,” says Field. “Some people do it by speed. Some listen [to the engine]. Some do it by the rev counter.”

If you stall, “first of all breathe”, says Ubah. “Give yourself some time. Put the clutch back down, and find that biting point again.”

“Don’t let the road being quiet make you think that you can drive faster,” says Ubah. “I see that a lot when I do my evening lessons.”

“You need to make sure that you’re fit to drive,” says Zlatev; tiredness is a major cause of accidents. “Use your lights properly, and avoid looking directly into the headlights of oncoming vehicles, because you can be dazzled easily.” Be more generous with the gap you leave between vehicles ahead. “Take your time: no rush, no risk.”

If you are already driving and it starts pouring, “slow down, increase the distance between you and the vehicle in front, and avoid sudden braking”, says Zlatev. “If you see a big puddle in front of you and you don’t know the area, try to avoid that puddle or go through it very slowly, because you don’t know how deep it is and you can damage your car.”

Make sure you keep your windscreen clear, says Ubah: “We need to be able to see our next five seconds – minimum. In the rain, if it is a road that is 60mph, it doesn’t mean you have to drive at 60mph – the speed limit is a limit, not a target. If you can’t see properly, reduce your speed.”

In ice, “just remember that you’re going to need to be delicate with everything”, says Rawson. “Even steering is a slight turn – and do everything a lot slower.”

“I haven’t got an electric car,” says Field, “so I don’t have that fear of the charge running out. But it is exactly the same with fuel – it’s just that there are more fuelling places than charging ones. But it’s getting better. So it is just about thinking before you set off: ‘How much fuel have I got?’ or, ‘How much charge have I got?’ And then being aware that you can find out where your nearest points are using the satnav. But also, the night before, just make sure that you’ve got enough to get to where you’re going.”

“Exchange details, and take a photo,” says Zlatev. “If you have any dashcam record, keep it safe. If you’re able to drive the car safely, you can. But if not, call the breakdown cover.”

Afterwards, “remind yourself that having an accident doesn’t make you a bad driver”, says Ubah. “You’ve got to have empathy for yourself. If you need to take a break from the road for a bit, that’s completely fine. Don’t judge yourself for it, and just know that the road is there whenever you want to drive again.”
