From Practical Magic 2 to Saturday Night Live UK: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 12 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

Bullock and Kidman try to put a second spell on you in the fantasy comedy sequel, while the topical sketch show returns after a well-regarded debut

Practical Magic 2Out now The beloved fantasy romance from the 1990s returns with Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. The story picks up 25 years later, with more family secrets and curses in the offing, plus a trip to the UK. Sure to be spellbinding stuff.

Pulp: What Do You Do for an Encore?Out 18 September for one night only Captured during their 2025 tour, this music documentary blends footage from the live shows with archive material and new narration from Jarvis Cocker, to trace the band’s rise from outsider status in Sheffield to global fame, via megahits such as Common People and lesser-known fan favourites. Directed by Garth Jennings.

PressureOut now Andrew Scott heads up an all-star cast in a drama exploring the second world war from a slightly quirky angle: the weather forecast. Don’t laugh: it was a crucial piece of the puzzle in the 72 hours leading up to D-day, with Britain’s chief meteorological officer James Stagg unexpectedly finding himself the man of the moment.

Everybody Digs Bill EvansOut now A winner at the Berlin festival, Grant Gee’s biopic explores the aftermath of the death of bass player Scott LaFaro, and the impact the tragedy has on jazz pianist Bill Evans, who is torn between New York and suburbia as he attempts to navigate his profound grief. Starring Anders Danielsen Lie, Bill Pullman and Laurie Metcalf. Catherine Bray

Saint EtienneBirmingham, 12 September; Manchester, 15 September; Bristol, 16 September; London, 18 September; tour continues to 26 September The beloved indie dance-pop trio head out on their final tour after more than 30 years. So expect songs such as the bangersome Glad from last year’s album International to rub shoulders with their 90s classics. Michael Cragg

CBSO/Yamada Symphony Hall, Birmingham, 17 September The dynamic Japanese conductor has embarked on one of classical music’s great endurance tests: a complete cycle of Gustav Mahler’s symphonies. Symphony No 2 promises to be a truly monumental season-opener – and also marks the CBSO Chorus’s 1,000th performance. Flora Willson

Chris CheekLondon, 15 September; Leeds, 16 September; Aberdeen, 17 September; Cambridge, 18 September The album Dear Paul by this versatile saxophonist was dedicated to Paul Motian, his old employer and one of jazz’s most creative percussionists. These gigs with fine Swiss drummer Florian Arbenz, a true Motian inheritor, will confirm just why. John Fordham

Wu LyfDublin, 15 September; London, 17 September; Brighton, 18 September Released in April, A Wave That Will Never Break marked the return of the enigmatic Manchester experimentalists after their 2012 split. It luxuriates in what they call “heavy pop” so remember your earplugs. MC

Laura PorterIrving Gallery, Oxford, to 10 October This north Devon-based artist is seriously into recycling, taking discarded old clothes, breaking them down and turning them into a mouldable, papier mache-style pulp and twisting them into wobbly geometric shapes.

Liz LarnerCamden Art Centre, London, to 17 January It’s the debut UK institutional show by this influential American sculptor and ceramicist, filled with rocky, prehistoric-looking references to cosmic matter, ancient mythology and the grizzly politics of resource extraction.

Gabriel OrozcoWhite Cube Bermondsey, London, 16 September to 8 November Mexico’s leading conceptualist returns to London for another show of minimal, ephemeral geometric installation work, this time dealing with the idea that objects can act as historical records.

Celebrating Julia Carter Preston, CeramicistVarious venues, Liverpool, to 28 February Liverpool is rolling out the red carpet for home-town ceramics hero Julia Carter Preston (1926-2012) with five galleries across the city hosting displays of her work at the same time, including shows at the Bluecoat and Walker Art Gallery. Eddy Frankel

Phil WangStockton, 12 September; Leeds, 13 September; Tunbridge Wells, 16 September; Northampton, 17 September; Guildford, 18 September; touring to 23 May Thanks to hit podcasts, presenting gigs and film cameos, a small cohort of millennial standups have finally ascended to the mainstream comedy firmament. Foremost among them is 36-year-old Wang, who returns to muse on ageing and his generation in new show Uh Oh. Rachel Aroesti

Apocalypse Channel 4, 13 September, 9pm Channel 4 be Channel 4-ing with its latest discomfiting social experiment. A group of civilians are left in an abandoned town to test how they cope with the kind of end-of-civilisation situation (no running water, no heating, no electricity) that could in reality be merely a couple of cyber-attacks away.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden StoryNetflix, 17 September Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s queasily contentious anthology series has previously dramatised the lives of some of America’s most notorious killers. Fire Emblem: Fortune’s Weave Nintendo Switch 2; out 17 September In the vast, fantastical Dagdan empire, warriors gather to fight in a tournament where the winner is granted one wish – but dark forces are gathering on the horizon and the fate of young contender Cai is in your hands. Bloc Party – Anatomy of a Brief Romance Out now Following a further lineup reshuffle in 2023 – new bassist Harry Deacon makes his debut here – art-rockers Bloc Party return with their seventh album. This Is Lorelei – The Singer in My BandOut now As one half of art-rock misfits Water from Your Eyes, Nate Amos, AKA This Is Lorelei, often deals in shape-shifting abstraction. Sylvan Esso – Ow ∞Out now Having built their own studio, the American electropop duo of Amelia Randall Meath and Nick Sanborn set about improvising, writing five to 10 songs a day. The result is this obscurely titled fifth album, which features the pogoing Hot Slob and the blown-out bop Sledge. MC

Across the Horizon Podcast Musician Bob Holmes hosts this soothing series analysing the world of ambient country music. He and his guests, including guitarist Hayden Pedigo, discuss how Americana can conjure imaginative worlds.

RobWordsYouTube YouTuber and linguist RobWords produces fascinating video essays on the many quirks of the English language. Highlights include the hidden logic behind typographical symbols, the literal meanings of body parts and sarcastic punctuation.

People Fixing the World: The Pictures That Help and HealBBC World Service, 15 September, 8.06am Journalist Myra Anubi’s documentary on the creatives producing visual aids for disabled people is a hopeful insight into how technology can be harnessed for good. Five Great Reads: Gloria Steinem, men’s therapy, and slime moulds

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 22:17:13 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert and Jacqui Housden

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Good morning, and welcome to your weekly roundup of the best stories from across the Guardian. Are you interested in living for ever? Maybe you just want to be a bit happier, or spend your time making the lives of others better? You could dedicate your life to saving the planet or contemplating the meaning of intelligence.

Either way, you can find some of the answers to life’s big questions in the reads below.

Enjoy.

Tributes have been flooding in for Gloria Steinem, the groundbreaking US feminist campaigner who died last week. The journalist, writer and activist fought tirelessly against domestic violence, female genital mutilation and the pornography industry and for women’s reproductive rights. Her death has already raised questions over what the feminist movement will be without her. But here leading contemporary writers reflect on her legacy.

How she made women’s lives better: As Rebecca Solnit writes: “Some of the hot takes I’m seeing now on Steinem, and the women’s movement she was at the heart of, act as reminders that a lot of people have no idea of what women’s lives were like before second-wave feminism.”

Notable quote: “Steinem, the silence-breaker. The truth-teller who had inspired millions of women around the world to find our voices and use them.”

How long will it take to read: Six minutes.

Further reading: Gloria Steinem is remembered by readers, celebrated by authors, actors and musicians and her life is beautifully detailed in this podcast.

Hoping for a longer or potentially limitless life? For the small cost of A$200,000, you can now be suspended upside down in liquid nitrogen at -196C in the hope of being reanimated in the future. Catie McLeod trekked out to a small town in regional Australia to be the first journalist inside the facility selling the dream of immortality.

They’re basically big Thermos bottles: To prevent damage to the body and its cellular structure, people who opt to be cryogenically frozen undergo an eight-hour process as soon as they die. Their corpse is pumped with “antifreeze-like embalming chemicals”.

Not everyone is a believer: Scientists are not convinced it is possible to revive someone’s consciousness, even if the freezing process preserves and protects the body. Associate Prof Saffron Bryant, a cryopreservation expert, considers this question to fall into the realm of mysticism, rather than science.

How long will it take to read: About four minutes.

Further reading: Take it on faith, or find another way to lay yourself to rest.

Can an entire ecosystem evolve fast enough to adapt to the climate crisis? While scientists have long thought that adaptation is a “survival of the fittest” race to outrun extinction, a first-of-its-kind project in the streams of the Arctic posits that a more communal approach could be the ecological answer to climate resilience.

‘Things won’t completely fall apart’: The climate emergency and global heating is upending the order of life, according to Linda Deegan, a senior scientist at Woodwell climate research center in Massachusetts. But Deegan also believes if species can evolutionarily band together, those connections will help them not only survive, but prosper.

How long will it take to read: Charles Darwin reportedly spent five weeks exploring the Galápagos Islands developing his theory of evolution. But you can read this article in just over four minutes.

Further reading: Why not take a look at the place that never freezes – and, separately, having lived through the ice age, can the mighty musk ox survive the heat?

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

In 2010 a group of scientists embarked on a somewhat unusual – but now famous – experiment in which they proved that a brainless organism, called a slime mould, could reproduce the route map of greater Tokyo railway system. It even gave hints on how to improve the design. Understandably, scientists have since been battling over whether simple life forms such as these should be considered intelligent.

Dunce or deliberate? A slime mould can appear to be just a small cell, capable only of feeding and reproducing. But it’s impossible to watch a slime mould – apparently – without sensing some deliberation at play. In another famous experiment, the organism found the shortest route through a maze in search of food.

A mystery: Toshiyuki Nakagaki, a scientist, betrays a sense of wonder while discussing the slime mould’s “intelligence”, a word that biologists invoke carefully. Others have since justified the use of the word, as well as other fraught ones such as “learning” and “memory”, in describing it. Which poses a mystery: how is this cell without even a semblance of a brain, capable of it all – the decision-making, the memory, the processing of information?

How long will it take to read: A slimy 12 and three-quarter minutes.

Further reading: ‘I have an understanding housemate’: the student who makes videos of fungus on faeces.

Most men go to therapy looking for answers. Maybe they want to work on their anger, or break out of a prison of isolation? But the psychotherapist Matthew Willner writes that most of his clients leave with nothing to show for their hours in the chair but grief. So why, if they are looking for happiness, do they leave feeling so empty?

Being told to ‘talk to someone; or that ‘it’s OK to cry’ can feel ridiculous: Finding the root cause of your own unhappiness can be a tricky nut to crack when you don’t know what caused your declining mental health. And if you can’t name the event that brought you to therapy in the first place, it can go unresolved.

The war with your own feelings: Rather than trying to fight what brought them in the door, Willner encourages the men he works with to “get curious” about their own feelings. Men often find themselves lonely and unhappy, he writes, but turning inwards toward their own sadness may allow them to feel less controlled by it.

How long will it take to read: Two and a half minutes.

Further reading: Eight reasons why men don’t go to therapy, and why men find it hard to make friends.

US Open tennis finals, the Manchester derby and Solheim Cup – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 11 Sep 2026 15:59:24 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The 20th edition of the Solheim Cup is under way, and for the first time in the Netherlands. Angela Stanford’s Americans are the slight favourites and defending champions, but they have not won on European soil since Germany in 2015. The US, as holders, need only 14 of the 28 points available to retain the crystal trophy. Scott Murray and Matt Cooper offer live coverage of day two’s foursomes (6.40am) and fourballs (12.05am), with Ewan Murray reporting from Bernardus Golf.

Join Tom Bassam for the latest news and buildup to Saturday’s football action. We will keep pace with all the day’s breaking news from around the grounds for seven Premier League matches, plus a full Championship and EFL programme. Join our Matchday live community by sending your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com.

Barry Glendenning keeps watch over all five 3pm kick-offs in the Premier League, and will be focusing on two of the afternoon’s most compelling games. Liverpool’s season took ⁠a while to get going under Andoni Iraola but after wins at Ipswich and then Atlético Madrid in the Champions League they will relish another home clash against a Fulham side managed by the former Liverpool player Álvaro Arbeloa. After three successive defeats and seven goals conceded, Arbeloa is already feeling the pressure of management in the top flight. Alongside last season’s top two, only promoted Hull remain unbeaten but their brilliant start faces an acid test against Xabi Alonso’s free-scoring Chelsea.

Kimi Antonelli is Formula One’s man of the moment but Mercedes’ 20-year-old championship leader faces a Monumental challenge in Spain this weekend, along with all his rivals. Fresh from ⁠becoming the first Italian since ⁠1966 to win his home race at Monza, Antonelli will be entering new territory when the Spanish capital’s Madring makes its grand prix debut with its signature La Monumental. The banked curve is a 550m-long high-speed 270-degree bend with a crest on the exit meaning drivers momentarily take it blind as they look up at the sky. Mercedes, winners of nine ‌of the first 13 races, should be in the mix but can expect a tougher fight than Monza, where they finished one-two, putting Antonelli 66 points clear of ‌his teammate George Russell. We will have lap-by-lap coverage of qualifying from Philip Cornwall, and Giles Richards reporting from Madrid.

Despite a £300m close-season splurge, Roberto De Zerbi’s Spurs are winless in their first three games and without a goal. Little more than three months ago, the Italian completed his Tottenham rescue mission as they beat Everton on the final day of the season to secure their top-flight status. On Saturday, David Moyes’ Everton are the visitors again and, while the stakes are not so high, De Zerbi desperately needs a victory to instil some belief that the money has been well spent. There will be a live blog of the match, with David Hytner reporting from Tottenham Hotspur Stadium.

Elena Rybakina rallied to beat Coco Gauff in a thrilling semi-final to earn a title showdown with the defending champion, Aryna Sabalenka, and take a step towards her third grand slam crown. The pair have met in two previous slam finals, with Sabalenka defeating Rybakina in the 2023 Australian Open decider before the second seed ​levelled the score at Melbourne Park in ‌January. Sabalenka, who will lose her world No 1 status to her opponent on Monday regardless of the result, is seeking to join Chris Evert and Serena Williams as the only women to win three straight US Open titles. Katy Murrells helms the live blog, with Tumaini Carayol reporting from Flushing Meadows.

Stability has been the order of the day at Arsenal, with Mikel Arteta’s side straight back into last term’s groove. Arsenal visit Sunderland, a fixture they will be wary of after being held to a 2-2 draw at the Stadium of Light last season. The Gunners made it four wins from four with a 1-0 victory at Napoli in their Champions League opener on Wednesday night and – with three victories in the Premier League already under their belt – show no signs of faltering. Billy Munday liveblogs the match and Louise Taylor reports.

After three bruising contests, South Africa go in search of a third successive Test victory over ⁠the All Blacks that would secure the four-game series for the world champions and lay down a marker for next year’s title defence. The ⁠final game of New ⁠Zealand’s six-week, ​eight-match tour of South Africa is being played in the United States as the top-ranked sides in the world look ⁠to promote the Rugby’s Greatest Rivalry series to a wider audience at the 70,000-seater home of the NFL’s Baltimore Ravens. Daniel Gallan buckles up as blog host.

Ryan Garcia enters his WBC welterweight title fight showdown with Conor Benn carrying the belt but understanding that winning the belt and establishing himself as a legitimate champion are different accomplishments. The American captured the first recognised world title of his turbulent career in February, dominating his compatriot Mario Barrios over 12 rounds for a unanimous decision. The performance showcased a more disciplined, complete fighter than the social media phenomenon who built his reputation on blinding speed and a devastating left hook. Now he must prove that victory began a sustained championship run. His first defence comes at T-Mobile Arena in Las Vegas, where personal hostility and contrasting styles should produce a revealing test. The British fighter intends to pressure Garcia, force exchanges and make the fight physical. Bryan Armen Graham has round-by-round coverage of the big fight.

Emillia Hawkins clocks on bright and early to preview Sunday’s action with breaking news and much more as we settle down for two Premier League fixtures, with all the noise around the afternoon’s Manchester derby. Email matchday. live@theguardian. com with your notions and queries.

Scott Murray is back at post for the deciding singles contests as Europe seek to regain the trophy after losing 15½-12½ in Virginia two years ago in the biggest team event in women’s golf.

Emillia Hawkins then turns to live commentary as last season’s fourth- and third-place teams respectively meet for the first time this season, both seeking a first win of the campaign. United lost to London City last weekend as Eva Olid took charge of the club for the first time in the WSL while Sonia Bompastor’s Chelsea were held by Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge despite battering the visitors with 35 shots. Suzanne Wrack reports.

The Hoops’ only blemish this term remains their Champions League playoff capitulation away to Lask, and overcoming their Old Firm rivals at Ibrox to reach the semi-final of the Premier Sports Cup would help maintain their momentum. There will, however, be no Celtic fans in attendance after the recent decision not to allow away supporters at any matches between the two Glasgow giants this term to avoid the trouble that marred last season’s Scottish Cup collision. The anxiety from the Light Blues legions, which has been prevalent in some games in Govan, resurfaced on Wednesday night as the home side struggled in the Premiership match against St Mirren after missing several chances before the break. However, a pressure valve was released when Bojan Miovski scored in stoppage time for a crucial 1-0 win, making it four victories in a row for Derek McInnes and his side. Taha Hashim liveblogs the cup tie, and Paul MacInnes reports.

John Brewin has lap-by-lap coverage as Formula One sweeps into Madrid for a first look at the Madring. Mercedes are in the ascendant and Kimi Antonelli can still put the equivalent of three race wins between him and Russell, with the Briton chasing a first win since Austria in June to prevent his title hopes from withering further. McLaren, who won in the Netherlands and Hungary with the reigning world champion, Lando Norris, and have Oscar Piastri hungry to open his account, could be the main rivals. Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc drove the Madring when it was still a building site on a scorching filming day in July but there is an underlying tension in the camp after last weekend’s opening-lap shenanigans at Monza.

After all the pre-season optimism, United’s start to the season has been inconsistent but Sunday’s derby offers Michael Carrick’s side an early chance ⁠to show they are contenders. City, meanwhile, arrive at Old Trafford with a perfect record under their new manager, Enzo Maresca, although their performances have suggested there is still work to do after Pep Guardiola’s departure. Carrick’s impact at United last season as interim manager after the club’s parting of ways with Ruben Amorim in January was dramatic, beginning with a 2-0 home victory over City. Their rivals will provide an acid test, especially with Erling Haaland firing on all cylinders having scored both goals in the 2-0 win at Porto in the Champions League on Tuesday to make it five goals in three games so far this season. Rob Smyth liveblogs the big game of the weekend, with Jamie Jackson and Will Unwin reporting from Old Trafford.

The men’s singles semis pitted Alexander Zverev against Karen Khachanov and Frances Tiafoe with Ben Shelton. The latter pairing are on a quest to become the first American men’s grand slam champion ⁠since Andy Roddick’s 2003 triumph at Flushing Meadows. Whoever emerges victorious will collide in Sunday evening’s final, and Ella Brockway has live blog commentary of the showdown.

Why Did Trump Order Up 660 Million Pounds of Mystery Meat?

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Eric Schlosser

Eric Schlosser is the author of “Fast Food Nation.”

If you buy a T-shirt at Gap, it will have a label that tells you where it was made. That’s federal law.

The same is true for automobiles, appliances, television sets, every fresh or frozen fruit and vegetable sold at the supermarket.

Beef and pork are notable exceptions to these laws. And that may help to explain why President Trump signed a proclamation last month that will allow the duty-free importation of about 660 million pounds of inexpensive beef.

If American consumers knew where that beef was coming from, they might not want to eat it.

The cuts of meat covered by Mr. Trump’s proclamation aren’t fresh sirloins, rib-eyes and filets. They’re lean beef trimmings that will be added to fattier American cuts to make ground beef. They’re small chunks of frozen meat that could have been kept in cold storage overseas for years. They are the quintessence of generic industrial meat, imported here to be subsequently processed in massive grinders that combine pieces of tens of thousands of cattle from multiple countries, mainly into fast food hamburgers.

I’ve been a longtime critic of food-safety practices in the U. S. meatpacking industry. But some of the practices in the 16 countries currently authorized to export raw beef to the United States are worse than any on these shores. During the past year, China rejected two shipping containers of beef from Uruguay after finding residue of an anti-parasitic drug in the meat, and rejected beef from Argentina reportedly because it tested positive for a banned antibiotic that can cause serious blood disorders.

One of the worst food-safety scandals occurred in Brazil, the world’s largest exporter of beef. In 2017, the Brazilian federal police raided nearly 200 meatpacking plants after allegations that government inspectors and politicians were being bribed to allow the sale of contaminated beef. Rotten meat treated with ascorbic acid and other chemicals to mask the contamination had been sold to hospitals and schools in Brazil and also exported. Executives at the Brazilian company JBS, the largest beef producer in the world, later admitted to bribing inspectors.

American cattle industry leaders say that Mr. Trump’s move will hurt domestic ranchers and do little to reduce the price of ground beef. They say the real cost savings will be enjoyed by meatpacking companies, fast food chains and supermarkets.

Why did Mr. Trump come up with this scheme to import hundreds of millions of pounds of beef?

“Regime Change,” the recent book by the Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan, contains an interesting clue: a White House meeting last November between President Trump and Joesley Batista, whose family controls JBS.

Mr. Batista had long been considered persona non grata in Washington, having been jailed in Brazil as a result of, among other things, paying $186 million in bribes to almost 2,000 politicians, including three Brazilian presidents, to obtain state financing for his family’s company. In 2019, after JBS bought several American meatpacking companies, Senator Marco Rubio and his colleague Robert Menendez deplored JBS’s “admitted criminal conduct,” its “business relationships with Venezuela’s Maduro regime, as well as its growing reliance on financing from entities aligned with the Chinese government.” The senators argued that allowing JBS to own U. S. companies could endanger America’s food supply and national security.

Mr. Batista gained the White House meeting last November, Ms. Haberman and Mr. Swan wrote, because of his friendship with Melania Trump. In addition, a JBS subsidiary had donated $5 million to Mr. Trump’s second inauguration, the largest gift from any individual or corporation. Not long afterward, JBS got approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission to be listed on the New York Stock Exchange, a privilege the company had sought for almost a decade.

After the White House meeting with Mr. Trump, Mr. Batista flew to Venezuela at Mr. Trump’s request, met with President Nicolás Maduro and urged him to resign. Mr. Batista’s unusual diplomatic endeavor did not succeed, but in July, a company owned by his family acquired a major stake in Venezuelan oil production, with the blessing of the new Trump-backed government there.

The European Union suspended imports of beef from Brazil this past Thursday because of concerns about antibiotic misuse. Mr. Trump’s proclamation facilitating beef imports from Brazil took effect the same week. Calling these facts to public view, the writer Shanley Hunt allowed that perhaps it’s just a coincidence. According to The Wall Street Journal, Mr. Trump announced his intention to allow duty-free foreign beef just a day after another meeting with Mr. Batista at the White House. Perhaps that’s a coincidence, too.

And yet it’s remarkable that the livelihood of American ranchers is being shaped in private meetings between the president of the United States and a representative of Brazil’s largest exporter of beef.

Country-of-origin labeling on beef used to be mandatory in the United States. That changed in 2015, when a Republican-controlled Congress, led by Speaker of the House John Boehner, ended the requirement. Just over a year later, Mr. Boehner was appointed to the board of JBS Foods International.

Today, four large meatpacking companies control about 85 percent of the market for beef in the United States. Two of those companies — JBS and National Beef — are Brazilian-owned. Smithfield Foods, America’s largest pork company, was purchased by a Chinese company in 2013. Although Smithfield doesn’t currently import pork from China, if it ever does, that fact won’t appear on the label.

Last year the Senate majority leader, John Thune, and Senator Cory Booker introduced bipartisan legislation that would once again require that meat be labeled according to its country of origin. In March, the Senate minority leader, Chuck Schumer, introduced separate legislation that would require tougher antitrust enforcement in the meatpacking industry, break up the big four beef companies, strengthen protections for independent ranchers and place limits on foreign ownership of American meat companies.

Those bills are a good start. In the early 1970s, before the administration of President Ronald Reagan gutted antitrust enforcement, the top four beef companies had only 21 percent of the U. S. market. When that market was truly competitive, Americans ate more beef than they do today, the nation had more than twice as many cattle ranchers — and foreign corporations didn’t control the most valuable sector of American agriculture.

Until a new labeling act gets passed, if you want to eat a hamburger, I suggest going to your local butcher shop, rather than the supermarket, ordering cuts of American beef and asking for them to be ground on the premises. Or grind it at home. Otherwise, there’s really no way of knowing what’s in your meat, or how many international borders it crossed to reach your plate.

Eric Schlosser is the author of “Fast Food Nation.”

Meeting Between Iran, Arab States Postponed as Mideast Diplomacy Stalls

The New York Times September 13, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Talks between the United States and Iran hit a dead end weeks ago, leaving Arab countries struggling to manage their ties to Tehran amid ongoing attacks.

By Aaron Boxerman

Reporting from Tel Aviv

A planned meeting between Iran and several Gulf Arab countries it attacked during the war was indefinitely postponed on Sunday, underscoring how diplomatic efforts have struggled to defuse a widening Mideast conflict.

Iranian officials had said they expected to meet Arab counterparts in Oman on Monday to discuss the status of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical Persian Gulf waterway for global oil and gas exports. But late on Sunday night, Badr Albusaidi, the Omani foreign minister, said the gathering had been postponed “in the interests of consensus.”

Talks between Iran and the United States to reopen the waterway similarly show little sign of progress, with the countries exchanging strikes in recent weeks. Iran has maintained its effective blockade of the strait, throttling the Gulf Arab states’ oil exports and roiling global markets. Last week, the price of Brent crude, the international benchmark, briefly jumped to about $110 a barrel, its highest level for months, before dropping to about $105.

On Sunday, a ship in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by a projectile, causing a fire on the vessel, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, a monitoring group run by the British navy. The governor of Qeshm, an island in southern Iran, said on Iranian state media that an Iranian commercial vessel had been attacked, killing one person and injuring four.

U. S. Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the region, did not respond to a request for comment.

Iran and Oman, which border the strait, have been negotiating for weeks over how to reopen the waterway, discussing arrangements that would likely involve some kind of service fee. Before the war, ships could travel freely through the Strait of Hormuz.

Even if a deal is reached, however, Iranian officials have demanded concessions from the United States before ending their blockade, including lifting sanctions on Iran and releasing Iranian assets frozen overseas. The Trump administration is unlikely to take those steps without Iran agreeing to curb its nuclear program.

Yemen has emerged as another front in the fighting. The Iranian-backed Houthi militants there seized the strategic port of Mokha and the island of Perim in the Bab al-Mandab Strait in the Red Sea last week from the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognized government. They have also attacked Saudi energy sites and sought to blockade Saudi shipping.

Saudi Arabia was forced to shut its East-West Pipeline on Friday after it was targeted by drones from Iraq. That pipeline has been a critical lifeline for the country’s oil exports, after Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz. No one took responsibility for the attack, but Iraq has long harbored well-armed militias backed by Iran.

On Sunday, Houthi forces attacked a military site near the southern city of Sharurah, Yahya Saree, a Houthi military spokesman, said on social media. Saudi officials said at least two people had been wounded and a mosque was damaged when a projectile fell in a neighboring province, state news media reported.

Iran and its allies have repeatedly attacked neighboring countries during the war, saying they were targeting the U. S. soldiers and military assets they hosted.

But as the conflict has dragged on, Gulf states like the United Arab Emirates and Qatar are having to manage their relationship with a newly emboldened Iran. The aborted attempt at the joint meeting underscored how difficult it is to forge a common approach, however.

“This has been an enemy that’s been shooting at them, and they’ve been collateral damage between the U. S. and Iran for all these months. Yet they need to also engage with Iran,” said Bader al-Saif, an assistant professor of history at Kuwait University.

“These are pragmatic countries — they want to make sure things move on in the right direction so their domestic plans don’t get disrupted,” he added.

Some Gulf countries have signaled that they are open to dialogue. Crown Prince Khaled bin Mohamed Al Nahyan, the Emirati heir apparent, met with President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in India on Saturday — the first public meeting between senior leaders of the countries since the beginning of the war.

But not all Gulf countries are on the same page. Even before the meeting was postponed, Bahrain, which has repeatedly been targeted by Iranian missiles and drones, said that it would not participate.

Iran has signaled that it could escalate militarily as President Trump tries to squeeze the country with an economic pressure campaign. Senior Iranian officials have said they might be willing to return to the cease-fire agreement that briefly paused the war in June, but they have made new demands which the Trump administration has refused to accept.

The truce collapsed in July, and the United States and Iran are in a period of uncertainty that some observers have described as “no war, no peace.” Mr. Trump said he has come close to launching a massive attack on Iran but pulled back, in part following pleas from Gulf countries worried about the cost of return to full war.

Vivian NereimandSanam Mahoozi contributed reporting.

Aaron Boxerman is a Times reporter covering Israel and Gaza. He is based in Jerusalem.

Top Lawmakers Agree A. I.’s Risks Are Rising but Say They Have No Quick Fix

The New York Times September 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

House Speaker Mike Johnson warned on Sunday of competitive risks from China, and Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said Congress should start regulatory talks this week.

By Michael Gold and Tony Romm

Reporting from Washington

As warnings rapidly mount over the pace and potential dangers of artificial intelligence development, the top Republican and Democrat in the House agreed on Sunday that Congress should put guardrails in place, but would not commit to specific policies or a timeline for doing so.

Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, urged caution in an interview with NBC’s “Meet the Press,” saying that the House could not hastily pass regulations and that lawmakers needed to ensure American companies remain competitive with Chinese A. I. firms.

“We’re not going to rush in and pass a piece of legislation that would do harm to the country and put China at an edge,” Mr. Johnson, who controls what legislation comes to the House floor, said. “And so we’ve got to do this carefully.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, criticized Mr. Johnson for moving too slowly, saying in an interview on ABC’s “This Week” that the House should take “decisive action.” But when he was asked for specific restrictions that he might back, Mr. Jeffries would not elaborate.

“Well, we’ll have that conversation this week upon our return,” he said. Mr. Jeffries is considered the leading contender to become speaker if Democrats take control of the House after the midterm elections.

The House will return to Washington on Monday for what is scheduled to be its final week in session before November’s midterm elections, a short timeline that makes it nearly impossible for lawmakers to quickly adopt a comprehensive framework for A. I. regulations.

Though politicians from both parties have warned about the need to regulate A. I. development, the drumbeat of ominous warnings about the technology has increased significantly in recent weeks. Jacob Coxon, a researcher at Anthropic, resigned on Tuesday, saying in social media posts that he believed that the top A. I. companies were not developing the technology responsibly.

On Saturday, Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, called for tech companies to slow the pace of their development in the face of worries about the technology’s safety. Several other tech executives — including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, the billionaire whose company SpaceX has been increasing its spending on A. I. — said they backed that effort.

Worries over A. I.’s dangers are rising as an issue in the midterm elections, and former President Barack Obama, in a fund-raising event last week, implored Democrats to develop clear positions on how to address risks the technology poses to safety and the economy.

Mr. Johnson acknowledged the issue was significant. But he pointed out that even Mr. Amodei and his competitors did not agree on the best approach and said that they should play a part in the development of any regulatory framework.

“I think the first step is to have a meeting of all the platform providers,” he said. “I’ve talked to the president about this and others. I believe that’s the next step.”

Kevin Hassett, the director of the White House National Economic Council, said on “Fox News Sunday” that the Trump administration was “studying” efforts on Capitol Hill to regulate A. I., including a push to create a “kill switch” that would allow the government to order rogue models to be shut down.

But even as he acknowledged that A. I. has advanced so rapidly that it is capable of undermining existing cybersecurity protections, Mr. Hassett joined Mr. Johnson in endorsing the involvement of the private sector in any efforts to slow the pace of development.

Mr. Johnson also warned that any excessive regulations on A. I. risked restraining American companies and empowering Chinese firms, an argument that President Trump also made on Sunday when speaking to reporters in Ireland, where he was attending a tournament at one of his golf resorts.

“Look, we’re leading China in A. I.,” Mr. Trump said. “We can put guardrails, we can do this and that, but I think you have a lot of negative forces that are bringing it up that shouldn’t be bringing it up. And they’re bringing up things that won’t happen. But whoever wins with A. I., wins.”

Many Democrats have argued that Congress should not be letting tech executives take the lead in regulating their own technology. After Mr. Johnson declined to renew a bipartisan task force on artificial intelligence, House Democrats established their own A. I. commission that Mr. Jeffries said would soon present “an aggressive framework.”

A group of lawmakers also circulated a letter last week urging Mr. Johnson to cancel their scheduled recess until lawmakers advanced A. I. regulations.

Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, said in a CNN interview that Congress was moving too slowly to address the issue. He also dismissed concerns over China.

“We can’t just use this idea that if we do this we somehow are going to lose to China,” Mr. Gallego said on “State of the Union.” “Because A. I. does not care once it becomes fully dangerous whether we’re Chinese or American. That’s the danger of this.”

Ian Fisher contributed reporting.

Michael Gold covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on immigration policy and congressional oversight.

Tony Romm is a reporter covering economic policy and the Trump administration for The Times, based in Washington.

King Charles Will Convene A. I. Leaders Amid Calls to Slow Development

The New York Times September 13, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

As alarm from the highest echelons of A. I. companies mounts, Buckingham Palace said the king would meet with executives to explore how the technology can be used for good.

By Ephrat Livni

King Charles III of Britain will meet with leaders from major artificial intelligence companies this week in Scotland amid mounting fears that rapid, unchecked development of the technology could lead to a global catastrophe.

The king will convene leaders from companies including Nvidia, Google, DeepMind, OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as government officials and others, “to discuss how A. I. can be developed and deployed in ways that benefit society,” according to a statement from Buckingham Palace. They will meet in Ayrshire, in southwest Scotland, at Dumfries House, the headquarters of the King’s Foundation, an educational charity.

The gathering comes as A. I. insiders and chief executives of some of the industry’s most powerful companies have raised alarms about these tools and how quickly they are developing. Some have called for the creation of shared guidelines and a deliberately slower pace of progress to ensure humans can keep up.

Charles’s meeting on A. I. will explore how the technology can be used for good, to “strengthen communities and improve lives,” the statement from Buckingham Palace said.

The palace did not say who would be attending from the A. I. companies listed in its statement, and Anthropic, DeepMind, Google and Nvidia did not immediately respond to requests for comment confirming their participation. OpenAI said that Sarah Friar, its chief financial officer, would be attending.

The current concern about A. I.’s rapid advance was prompted in great part by a hack this summer into Hugging Face, an A. I. infrastructure company, orchestrated by a group of A. I. agents created by OpenAI. The OpenAI agents swarmed Hugging Face’s systems, stealing data, gaining control of a server and attempting to cover their tracks.

That hack — and another similar incident within OpenAI shortly afterward — drastically raised fears about how quickly machines might escape human control, with potentially devastating effects.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, published a 3,800-word open letter on Saturday calling for slower development of A. I. In addition to the Hugging Face hack, he cited as a concern the fact that current A. I. models are increasingly able to build the next generation of A. I. tools. Mr. Amodei said that dynamic, known as recursive self-improvement, “could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems” if left unchecked.

The meeting between Charles and A. I. leaders will be facilitated by a British nonprofit, the Ditchley Foundation, and will include Kanishka Narayan, Britain’s minister for A. I., according to Buckingham Palace. Representatives from charitable organizations founded by the king, including the King’s Trust, a youth charity, and the Sustainable Markets Initiative, a network of global chief executives, will also attend, the palace added.

Mr. Amodei’s essay on Saturday — which quickly reverberated around the internet — received support from other A. I. company chiefs, including Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk of xAI, which is part of SpaceX, Mr. Musk’s rocket and satellite company.

Mr. Amodei urged A. I. companies and regulators around the world to work together on a thoughtful approach to developing the technology and proposed his own three-step plan. His proposals included allowing third-party evaluators to embed in frontier A. I. companies to monitor growth and report incidents, and coordinating among companies in democratic countries to establish common safety standards. “To the extent possible,” he said, democratic countries and authoritarian governments should also try to coordinate and pace global development.

The essay was published just a few days after Jacob Coxon, an Anthropic engineer who previously worked for OpenAI, resigned from his job and declared on social media that the companies claimed to be concerned about rapid development but were nonetheless hurtling toward “superhuman systems that can hack anything, revolutionize any field overnight, and acquire real power and resources.”

Ephrat Livni is a Times reporter covering news around the world. She is based in New York.

Unvaccinated Woman Likely Died of Measles Complications, Pa. County Coroner Says

The New York Times September 13, 2026

Measles Outbreaks

Advertisement

Supported by

The case is the third reported death linked to a rapidly expanding outbreak that has sickened more than 670 people in the state.

By Teddy Rosenbluth

A 40-year-old unvaccinated woman in Pennsylvania died Saturday, most likely because of measles complications, the Jefferson County coroner, Greg Furlong, said Sunday.

The news comes as Pennsylvania faces a rapidly expanding outbreak that has already sickened more than 670 people and hospitalized 124. The state department of health reported two deaths related to the outbreak last month, which set off a frenzied debate over whether the deaths were a result of measles or merely coincided with the infection.

In this woman’s case, the immediate cause of death was respiratory failure “due to suspected measles,” according to a preliminary death certificate viewed by The Times. Mr. Furlong said that testing had not yet confirmed the woman had measles, though she had many of the symptoms of the virus — including the telltale rash that often starts as flat red spots on the face and travels down the body — and had recently been exposed to someone with measles. A nasal swab will be sent to the state laboratory to be tested for measles, Mr. Furlong said.

The woman had several chronic medical conditions that made her vulnerable to severe complications from measles. She had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, or C. O. P. D., and was on 24/7 supplemental oxygen.

The state health department has not included the death in its official tally but has been in close contact with Mr. Furlong, he said.

While most measles cases are mild, roughly one in five unvaccinated people in the United States who contract the virus lands in the hospital, often for complications such as pneumonia, severe dehydration and brain swelling. The virus is especially dangerous for young children, adults older than 20 and those who have a compromised immune system.

Measles deaths are extremely rare in the United States. But the virus’s recent resurgence has caused a handful of fatalities. Two school-aged children and one adult died last year from measles complications, the first such deaths in the country in a decade.

Teddy Rosenbluth is a Times reporter covering health news, with a special focus on medical misinformation.

What Anthropic’s C. E. O. Argued in His Call for Slower A. I. Development

The New York Times September 13, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

Dario Amodei’s 3,800-word letter laid out a three-step plan to rein in artificial intelligence.

By Emmy Martin

Reporting from San Francisco

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of the artificial intelligence company Anthropic, published a 3,800-word open letter on Saturday calling for a slowdown in the development of A. I.

The essay prompted other A. I. leaders, including Sam Altman, the chief executive of OpenAI; Elon Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive; and Demis Hassabis, the chair of Google DeepMind, to speak out in agreement.

Here are the key arguments that Mr. Amodei made in his essay:

Mr. Amodei said two recent developments convinced him that simply investing in A. I. safety was no longer enough.

One, he said, was that A. I. itself had begun helping to build the next generation of A. I., a self-reinforcing loop called “recursive self-improvement” that could soon outrun humans’ ability to understand or control what they were creating.

Mr. Amodei also pointed to a recent incident where OpenAI’s systems went rogue and attacked the A. I. start-up HuggingFace. OpenAI was not aware of the hack until it was informed about it by HuggingFace weeks later.

While the attack did not cause any real harm, Mr. Amodei said he predicted a more capable version of the A. I. could seize large parts of the internet and cause “hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.”

Mr. Amodei laid out a three-step plan to “pace” the development of A. I. across the industry, arguing that the world would have to do it together.

First, he said, Anthropic would invite independent reviewers to work inside his company, giving them employee-like access, including desks, badges and laptops. The reviewers, which he called “evaluators,” would verify that his start-up was following its safety practices. These reviewers would then publish what they found, even if it was unflattering. Mr. Amodei urged rivals to do the same.

Second, Mr. Amodei said, A. I. companies in the United States and other democratic countries should agree on shared safety standards and a common limit on how fast A. I. capabilities could advance, aided by their governments. He suggested that A. I. companies coordinate — ideally through regulation, but voluntarily in the meantime — on how quickly their systems could advance.

Third, he said, the United States and other democratic nations should work to get authoritarian governments, chiefly China, to accept similar limits. Mr. Amodei said this step would be the hardest and most unlikely to happen soon.

Any deal with China would be a ladder, Mr. Amodei said, from the most to least achievable steps. They would include banning clearly dangerous A. I. uses; agreeing to test A. I. models for dangers before release; putting a “speed limit” on A. I.’s self-improvement capabilities; and, what China is least likely to agree to, a full pause on development.

Mr. Amodei said in the meantime, democracies must keep their lead over China, backing restrictions on selling powerful A. I. chips to the country and employing tighter security to keep rivals from stealing or copying American models.

“Any cooperation we are able to achieve with China will extend the amount of time we have to spend on pacing the frontier within the democratic nations,” he said.

Emmy Martin is a reporter covering the technology industry from San Francisco and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship class.

Connections Coach

The Democratic nominee for Senate faces strong headwinds in a decidedly Republican-leaning state. She has been a fighter, and an underdog, for years.

Credit...

Supported by

By Patricia Mazzei

Patricia Mazzei, who has covered elections in Florida since 2008, reported from Jacksonville, Yulee and Miami, Fla.

Angie Nixon is tough to silence.

The first time she protested gerrymandering in Florida, Republican state lawmakers cut the video feed of her sit-in. The second time she showed up with a bullhorn. The third time, she was arrested.

“When they go low,” she says, putting a twist on Michelle Obama’s decade-old dictum, “we get loud.”

Ms. Nixon’s high-volume tactics as a state representative have made her one of the most outspoken critics of Florida’s Republican governor, Ron DeSantis. She has also at times rankled fellow Democrats. Some political veterans dismissed her campaign for the U. S. Senate as progressive whimsy — until her decisive primary victory against a more moderate opponent last month. It catapulted her onto the national stage and jolted an otherwise sleepy Democratic Party in a Republican-leaning state.

She has spent the weeks since hoarse, appearing nearly everywhere as she tries to make the case that a Black woman with a Southern drawl — who identifies as a progressive but also joined the Democratic Socialists of America in June — can win in a state President Trump has taken three times. If elected, Ms. Nixon would become Florida’s first Black senator.

National Democrats have all but written off Florida. Republicans believe the nomination of Ms. Nixon, whom they have branded a “socialist,” has only made it easier for Senator Ashley Moody, the Republican incumbent Mr. DeSantis appointed last year to replace Marco Rubio, to win in November.

But Ms. Nixon the Senate nominee, much like Ms. Nixon the state legislator, is difficult to ignore. She leans fiery while Ms. Moody leans restrained. She engages with the media and curious crowds drawn to her, while Ms. Moody mostly sticks to Fox News and friendly supporters.

The forces working against Republicans nationally — the high cost of living, some Hispanic voters who lean away from Mr. Trump — are also present in Florida. And Florida Democrats have historically turned out more voters with a Black candidate leading the ticket.

“What up, Nassau County!” Ms. Nixon, 42, told a full house of supporters recently in Yulee, a deep-red community in northeastern Florida, near Georgia. She later joked that they probably had never seen so many Democrats here.

The establishment Ms. Nixon is not. Her primary win so shocked some Democratic leaders that a unity rally, planned on the assumption that her rival would win, was scrapped. Some Jewish Democrats were upset by a resolution she filed in 2023 in Tallahassee calling for a cease-fire “in the State of Israel and occupied Palestine,” which failed with a vote of 104-2. She has since mended some fences and been quick to condemn antisemitic incidents.

She also does not quite fit the mold of other democratic socialists running this year. A longtime union and community organizer, she has been rooted in campaigns to restore felon voting rights, expand Medicaid and unionize adjunct college professors. She also owns a book-and-coffee shop named Cafe Resistance. In 2020, she received the endorsement of the chamber of commerce in Jacksonville, her hometown, and then ousted a conservative Democratic incumbent.

Her vocal opposition to Mr. DeSantis has become her calling card. At every turn of his administration’s “war on woke” — changing how slavery was taught in schools, restricting diversity initiatives, removing books from school libraries — Ms. Nixon was there, calling the policies racist and the governor a bully. Her shop showcases banned books.

When Mr. DeSantis was booed at a vigil in 2023 for Black victims killed in a racially motivated shooting in a Jacksonville Dollar General store, she stood nearby, arms at her hips, glowering at him.

This spring, she parked herself in the governor’s office and demanded a meeting over his administration’s gerrymandered congressional map. She refused to leave, leading to her arrest. She is awaiting trial next month on trespassing charges.

“I’m the biggest pain in Ron DeSantis’s ass,” she recently told donors at a fund-raiser in Miami, casting herself as the fighter voters want and saying she would be the “biggest pain” for Mr. Trump, too. For his part, the president called her a “card-carrying member” of the D. S. A. at his Republican midterm convention last week.

Some Democrats dislike her style and politics, but Ms. Nixon comes off as authentic, something Florida Democrats have struggled with, said Joe Garcia, a former Miami congressman, who co-hosted the fund-raiser.

“You may not like what she’s saying, but you know it’s what she feels,” he said. “It’s very powerful.”

Daniel Henry, the first vice chairman of the Florida Democratic Party, who has worked closely with Ms. Nixon, said her skeptics dismissed her passion and organizing skills at their peril.

“The people that usually underestimate her,” he said, “end up losing.”

Ms. Nixon was raised in Jacksonville’s historically Black Montcrief neighborhood. Her mother worked two jobs to support her and her brother.

At 13, Ms. Nixon said in her hometown newspaper, The Florida Times-Union, that she would call a movie based on her life “Outspoken,” “because I like to tell how I feel inside and not just leave things bottled up.”

She graduated from Stanton College Preparatory, a public magnet high school, and from the University of Florida. In her final semester, a visibly pregnant Ms. Nixon walked into the office of Mia L. Jones, then a Jacksonville city councilwoman, and asked to be her intern. The City Council did not offer internships.

“She was not afraid to come and ask for something that didn’t exist,” said Ms. Jones, who created one for her.

In 2008, barely out of college and a single mother to her 1-year-old daughter, Ms. Nixon ran for the City Council. The Times-Union endorsed her — “Her moxie certainly isn’t in doubt,” the editorial board wrote — but she lost the election.

A few years later, when her daughter, Natalie McGriff, felt insecure about her looks, the mother and daughter published children’s books about “Moxie McGriff,” whose curly hair gave her superpowers.

Ms. Nixon sometimes struggled financially. Public records show that her home was briefly in foreclosure in 2014, when she was between jobs and behind on mortgage payments. The case was later dismissed.

In 2016, she worked as the deputy field director for national Black outreach for Bernie Sanders’s presidential campaign. Four years later, Ms. Nixon has said, she supported Elizabeth Warren for the Democratic nomination.

That year, Ms. Nixon ran for the State House while pregnant with her younger daughter. Democrats had all but shut down field campaigns because of the coronavirus pandemic, recalled Andrea Cristina Mercado, a fellow progressive organizer. Ms. Nixon insisted on canvassing anyway, contracting Covid before the election.

“Angie kept being a voice of like, ‘Republicans are out there on those doors,’” Ms. Mercado said. “‘We have to be out there on those doors, too.’”

After winning in a rout, Ms. Nixon married Jarrett Morene, the father of her younger daughter. Their blended families made them parents of five children.

Ms. Nixon arrived at the State Capitol as Mr. DeSantis was becoming a national Republican darling. In 2022, Republican lawmakers prepared to pass redistricting maps that diluted Black representation. Ms. Nixon and State Representative Travaris McCurdy interrupted the session and sat on the House floor in protest. They wore “STOP THE BLACK ATTACK” T-shirts, which they had raced to the local mall to make the night before.

The sit-in turned Ms. Nixon into a foil for the powerful Mr. DeSantis. But it also brought criticism.

In 2024, her primary opponent accused her of failing to pass legislation or secure money for district projects. Ms. Nixon, who worked in the Legislature to expand child care and confront price gouging, countered that Republicans wanted her gone because she was “making too much noise.”

She won with 81 percent of the vote.

This year, when Republican lawmakers readied a vote on a new set of congressional maps that eliminated four Democratic seats, Ms. Nixon was running for Senate.

She procured a pink bullhorn — the color of her campaign signs — and wore a matching jumpsuit as she marched down the center aisle of the House floor in protest. A couple of weeks later, she staged her sit-in inside Mr. DeSantis’s office.

Republicans and some Democrats dismissed her protests as stunts. Democratic primary voters felt differently, choosing her by double digits over Alex Vindman, a former national security official with party establishment ties.

Winning a general election is harder. Ms. Moody is something of a generic Republican, but that has been enough for Florida, where Republicans now handily outnumber Democrats. Florida is not on any list of competitive Senate races, though a strong showing from Ms. Nixon could lift other Democrats down the ballot.

Ms. Moody has declined to debate Ms. Nixon, saying she is “not going to give a stage or any attention” to someone she considers “truly anti-American.” She has alluded to past speeches that Ms. Nixon gave to the Council on American-Islamic Relations, a Muslim advocacy and civil rights group that Florida has declared a foreign terrorist organization.

Mr. DeSantis has flatly dismissed a democratic socialist’s chances in Florida: “I don’t think it’s going to work at all.”

The idea that a grass-roots focus on working people could energize voters originated with Ms. Nixon and her brain trust of labor organizers, including Alphonso Mayfield, the late leader of the Florida Public Services Union, and her former boss. Mr. Mayfield, who died in January, was perhaps Ms. Nixon’s biggest champion.

Ms. Nixon campaigns in a van, nicknamed the Vangie, that is filled with snacks, a clothes rack and a pillow. To save money, she often stays with friends and family. Her most recent financial disclosure listed a nearly $14,000 debt to the I. R. S., which her campaign said was a tax payment plan.

Her events are intended to recruit supporters as canvassers and phone bankers. Her speeches sound like church revivals, with Ms. Nixon leading call-and-response chants, as she did on a recent rainy Saturday in Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood.

“I am running against a woman that voted to end health care for 440,000 Floridians in this state — say, ‘Shame!’” she said.

A democratic socialist is a tough sell in South Florida, particularly among Hispanics. Ms. Nixon does not regret her D. S. A. membership, saying she is a big-tent Democrat, but while in Miami she denounced authoritarian leaders in Cuba and Venezuela. She then hopped in her van and knocked on doors.

Jesús García, a 60-year-old bus driver who emigrated from Cuba, welcomed Ms. Nixon into his living room, telling her he recognized her from TikTok.

“What you’re doing is great,” said Mr. García, a naturalized citizen registered without party affiliation, who described himself as liberal. “Are you a progressive? A socialist?”

“I’m a progressive,” Ms. Nixon said. “I don’t go by labels.”

Kitty Bennett contributed research.

Patricia Mazzei is a national political correspondent for The Times, based in Miami.

How Iran’s Hard-Liners Prevailed and Sabotaged U. S. Peace Deal

The New York Times September 13, 2026

War in the Middle East

Opponents derailed the agreement with a clandestine effort to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz, regime insiders say. Iran’s president was furious when he found out.

Opponents derailed the agreement with a clandestine effort to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz, regime insiders say. Iran’s president was furious when he found out.

President Masoud Pezeshkian of Iran, next to the honor guard, at the funeral for Ayatollah Ali Khamenei in Tehran in July. Credit... Arash Khamooshi/Polaris for The New York Times

Supported by

By Farnaz Fassihi

Farnaz Fassihi has covered Iran for three decades. For this article, she interviewed Iranian officials, former officials and members of the Revolutionary Guards and reviewed speeches, comments and interviews of senior officials and generals from June to September.

Masoud Pezeshkian, the president of Iran, was riding high in early July, fresh off the successful negotiation of a peace agreement with the United States, and had traveled to neighboring Iraq for part of a weeklong funeral spectacle for Iran’s slain supreme leader.

Suddenly he got stunning news.

Iranian forces had opened fire on three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, setting ablaze a Qatari L. N. G. tanker and damaging other vessels. Iran was under siege in world opinion.

Outraged, Mr. Pezeshkian phoned Gen. Ahmad Vahidi, the commander in chief of the powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, and in a raised voice called the actions reckless and demanded answers, according to five Iranian officials and two Guards members familiar with the events.

General Vahidi told the president that he had neither authorized nor had advance knowledge of the strike, the five officials said. The nation’s Supreme National Security Council, which plays a critical role in both the war and negotiations, had also been in the dark, he said.

In fact, much of the country’s leadership was unaware that a fringe hard-line faction had decided to act on its own. Ultimately, those clandestine efforts derailed a push by more moderate pragmatists in Iran to reach an end to hostilities with the United States and repair their nation’s ailing economy.

The hard-liners succeeded in part because the only figure with the authority to resolve such disputes — the new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei — has been a phantom since taking office in March. He has not been seen, and his voice has not been heard. And the authenticity of written statements and messages attributed to Ayatollah Khamenei has been questioned, including by Mr. Pezeshkian, according to three Iranian officials.

Mr. Pezeshkian immediately returned to Tehran. By the next morning, even as the funeral ceremonies were still underway, the United States had retaliated with airstrikes on Iran. The two countries were back at war.

Senior Iranian officials and a Guards member said in interviews that what followed were some of the most volatile political confrontations within Iran’s leadership in memory. Officials engaged in shouting matches. Two senior generals threatened to resign. Accusations of treason and betrayal flew.

The reverberations, officials said, contributed to a shake-up at the National Security Council and the supreme leader’s appointment of Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, a seasoned politician and former commander in chief of the Guards, to lead the council, as he was thought to have the skill to mediate among political factions.

But divisions persist, and the hard-liners who have committed Iran to escalation are in an even stronger position. This past week, Iran and the United States traded attacks, with Iran repeatedly targeting American naval vessels for the first time, and the United States blowing up at least eight Iranian oil tankers.

This account of the inner deliberations of Iran’s leadership is based on interviews with eight Iranian officials, three members of the Revolutionary Guards, four former officials and a review of dozens of speeches and comments by government officials and military generals from June to September published in the Iranian press and social media. The officials interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss delicate issues of national security.

Three Iranian officials said inquiries by the government and security forces traced the decision to strike the three commercial ships in July to the cleric Hossein Taeb, an influential spymaster who had opposed the peace deal with the United States from the outset. Mr. Taeb had been telling the new supreme leader that Iran had made a mistake in ending the war and agreeing to the deal, they said.

Mr. Taeb, in a recent speech to military families, said that he was not opposed to talks but that “negotiations that ignore the rights of our people and concede to the excessive demands of the enemy have no place in Iran’s politics.”

Ayatollah Khamenei recently appointed Mr. Taeb as the head of the Basij militia, which is responsible for quelling domestic dissent. He had previously served for more than 20 years as chief for the Revolutionary Guards’ intelligence agency before the previous supreme leader ousted him in 2022 over failures such as Israeli infiltration of his rank and file, and a foiled plot in Turkey. Mr. Taeb re-emerged after that supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed at the start of the war, and he played a key role in the selection of the son Mojtaba as the successor to his father, officials said at the time.

“The attack on the ships was orchestrated with the goal to blow up the memorandum of understanding with Trump and to kill the prospects of any future negotiations and deal,” Alireza Namvar Haghighi, an Iran expert and former official who still has close contacts in the government, said in an interview from Canada.

When Mr. Pezeshkian demanded to know who had struck the three ships, he was told that commanders in the field had acted on their own, in line with an order empowering them to attack any ship violating Iran’s control of the Strait without waiting for approval from central command, according to the officials with knowledge of these discussions. In one sign of the dispute, the Guards’ Khatam al-Anbiya headquarters never issued a statement claiming responsibility for the July 7 attack, as has been routine in other attacks before and since.

Iranian officials relayed this same account to the United States and some of its regional allies in the immediate hours after the attacks, blaming rogue operators, according to U. S. officials who briefed reporters at the time and the three Iranian officials. Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, was dispatched to Oman, a key mediator, to try to defuse tensions with Washington.

On the streets and on state television in Iran, meanwhile, the hard-liners openly attacked the negotiating team and its peace deal, and at nightly rallies, crowds chanted for a return to war.

The Iranian government has devised an official narrative deflecting blame for the collapse of the agreement, saying Washington violated it first by not stopping Israel’s attacks on the militant group Hezbollah in Lebanon, by withholding Iran’s frozen assets and by sneaking ships through a portion of the Strait of Hormuz not controlled by Iran. But few inside Iran’s political circles are convinced by this version, including Mr. Pezeshkian himself, five officials said.

Mr. Pezeshkian said publicly last month that every agreement sees violations and that they should be addressed through talks, not confrontation. When he was privately told by generals that Ayatollah Khamenei had approved the July attack on the three ships, the president demanded proof, according to three Iranian officials.

Under the Iranian form of government, the supreme leader has ultimate authority to settle internal disputes. But Ayatollah Khamenei’s whereabouts, his physical health and mental acuity, and the extent he is involved in state affairs have become subjects of fevered speculation.

“The security situation requires for him to be protected, but I’m asking, how long is this supposed to go on? Six months? One year? Five years? Ten years?” Hojatoleslam Alireza Pirouzmand, a senior cleric and academic at Iran’s National Defense University, said on state television in late July. He added that if “we can’t see our leader, then we will remain in a perpetual state of weakness and decline.”

This month Ayatollah Khamenei’s mother-in-law, Tayebeh Mahrouzadeh, gave a lengthy video interview to a local reporter, describing the extreme security precautions surrounding family members and saying they had no news of the ayatollah and his three children. Her husband, the politician Gholam-Ali Haddad Adel, told the Iranian news media in July that while Ayatollah Khamenei had no contact with anyone for security reasons, “God willing, he is healthy.”

The few comments attributed to the missing leader about the peace deal have added fuel to the dispute. After the agreement was signed, a statement in his name was issued saying he had approved because it had been endorsed by the president and a majority of the National Security Council — but that he was of a different opinion “on principle.” That phrase — “on principle” — has been repeatedly used by hard-liners to attack the deal.

In May, Mr. Pezeshkian said he met with Ayatollah Khamenei but did not say when or where. Two Iranian officials and a former official said the circumstances of the encounter were bizarre.

They said an ambulance with blacked-out windows was used to drive Mr. Pezeshkian around, while a secure video connection was established. A person who said he was an interlocutor for Ayatollah Khamenei appeared on a monitor and purportedly passed messages between the two men.

Mr. Pezeshkian confided to a close ally that he was unsure whether he had actually been communicating with the supreme leader, according to the officials with knowledge of the meeting.

Last month Mr. Pezeshkian said he had been granted a second meeting and that it had lasted for seven hours. “We spoke about all the issues facing the country,” the president told Iran’s state television, listing them as affordability, unemployment, sanctions, unity and resilience during wartime. He did not describe the circumstances of the meeting or reveal what Ayatollah Khamenei had said.

For weeks, the political leaders and generals running Iran have debated two ways to break the stalemate with the United States, officials said.

Under one approach, Iran could seek to return to negotiations. Under the other, it would escalate attacks on American targets, aiming to strike naval vessels, kill American troops and raise global oil prices.

Both would aim to end the U. S. naval blockade on Iran’s southern ports, which have paralyzed trade and brought oil sales down to zero, according to officials. Iran’s economy is deteriorating, with the currency plunging daily, inflation soaring and the government facing a cash deficit.

Hard-line generals, including Brig. Gen. Seyyed Majid Mousavi, who commands the Guards’ Aerospace Force, pressed for confrontation, officials and two Guards members said. The generals told the National Security Council they had devised a detailed war plan in which Iran and allied militias, in particular the Houthis in Yemen and armed Shiite Muslim groups in Iraq, would intensify attacks, including on regional oil facilities, further widening the scope of the war and raising its costs for the United States and its allies.

Mr. Pezeshkian and Gen. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, who is the speaker of Parliament and the top negotiator with the United States, were among the officials who warned that the war plan risked dragging the country into an abyss, with even fiercer U. S. airstrikes and more crippling economic pressure.

But by last Saturday, the hard-line faction had gained the upper hand. “The war between Iran and the United States,” said Mahdi Mohammadi, the top adviser to General Ghalibaf, “has entered the phase of escalation.”

Farnaz Fassihi is the United Nations bureau chief for The Times, leading coverage of the organization. She also covers Iran and has written about conflict in the Middle East for 15 years.
